title: Attention Opportunity Cost and Ad Insertion in Synchronous Media: Evidence from Live Streaming
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Department of Supply Chain & Information Systems, Pennsylvania State University and

detail.title: Attention Opportunity Cost and Ad Insertion in Synchronous Media: Evidence from Live Streaming

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are no personal or financial interests to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Picture-in-picture (PiP) ads have emerged as a prominent format on live streaming platforms such as Twitch and YouTube Live, where they overlay advertisements on streaming content without interrupting the live broadcast. A central design question for the advertising intermediaries that deliver PiP ads is when during a stream to trigger an ad insertion. Prior work on engagement-triggered ad insertion, developed primarily in asynchronous video contexts such as YouTube and Netflix, prescribes targeting ads to moments of high viewer engagement on the reasoning that engaged viewers pay more attention to whatever appears on screen. We argue that this prescription does not transfer to synchronous live streaming. When a viewer attends to an ad during a live stream, the concurrent stream content, community reaction, and participation opportunities are forgone permanently rather than deferred. This generates an opportunity cost of ad attention that is endogenous to the viewer engagement state. Because higher engagement implies a higher cost of attending to an ad, the insertion prescription reverses in the synchronous context. We examine this framework using data from a third-party advertising intermediary that serves PiP ads on Twitch. An observational study of fixed-interval ad insertions provides early evidence, and a field experiment that varies the engagement state at which ads are triggered provides the primary test. Across both studies, ads delivered during low-engagement periods receive more clicks than ones during high-engagement periods. In the experiment, point estimates imply that a delivered ad receives roughly twice as many clicks under low-engagement insertion. Three moderation patterns, involving the opportunity cost premium in the stream content, weekday versus weekend streaming, and streamer age, align with the theoretical framework. Our work extends the economics of attention to the synchronous advertising context, identifies boundary conditions for the engagement-targeting prescription, and offers practical guidance for advertising intermediaries operating in live streaming ecosystems.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work: Automation, Labor Law, and the Redistribution of Economic Power

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Work: Automation, Labor Law, and the Redistribution of Economic Power

detail.abstract: Labor-law responses to artificial intelligence have converged on a single strategy: reclassifying platform and algorithmically managed workers as employees, or at least giving them access to employment-adjacent protections. The European Union's Platform Work Directive, Spain's Ley Rider, and the pending judgment of Brazil's Supremo Tribunal Federal on "algorithmic subordination" all pursue this classification strategy, now joined by the International Labour Organization's Convention No. 193, the first binding international instrument on platform work. This article argues that classification reform, however necessary, addresses only one half of the problem AI-driven automation poses for labor law. It corrects the question of who counts as a worker but leaves untouched the separate question of who controls the surplus that algorithmic management and automation generate. Because algorithmic systems continuously set prices, allocate tasks, and adjust compensation parameters unilaterally, correct employment classification does not, by itself, restore workers' bargaining power over the terms that most affect their income. Drawing on a doctrinal and comparative analysis of EU, United Kingdom, Spanish, United States, and Brazilian law, supplemented by empirical evidence on AI's uneven effects on wages and capital returns, this article identifies a "redistribution gap" in current reform and proposes a distinct regulatory category-the Algorithmic Surplus and Bargaining Parity Standard-designed to give workers enforceable, periodically audited rights over the compensation-determining parameters of algorithmic management, independent of and in addition to their employment status. AI Disclosure Statement: During the preparation of this manuscript, the author used AI-based language and research-assistance tools for drafting support, research organization, literature and source discovery, analytical structuring, and language refinement. The author critically reviewed, edited, verified, and assumed responsibility for all legal analysis, argumentation, sources, interpretations, data, and conclusions contained in the final manuscript.

title: A Cross-Engine Content Analysis of Brand Recommendation in AI Answer Engines: A Skincare Pilot with a Preregistered Confirmatory Design

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involved no human participants, patients, or personal data; it analyzed outputs generated by publicly available AI answer engines. An independent second coder assisted with reliability coding as a collaborator, not as a research subject.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding; it was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: AI answer engines increasingly stand between a consumer's question and the brands that would answer it, returning a short, ranked, confidently worded list that most users never scroll past. This study measures which skincare brands such engines recommend, how concentrated those recommendations are, how much the engines agree with one another, what sources they draw on, and whether a model with live retrieval recommends differently from the same class of model relying only on training memory. A stratified set of 25 natural-language skincare queries was submitted to four engines during an August 2026 collection window: Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT search, and a base GPT-4o model with tools disabled. A single coder applied a codebook fixed before analysis to 85 engine-query answers, recording every recommended brand and every cited source, yielding 115 distinct brands and 428 brand mentions. The results show a concentrated head (top three brands hold 26 percent of mentions, 95 percent CI 20 to 32; top ten hold 47 percent, 95 percent CI 40 to 57), low cross-engine agreement (mean pairwise Jaccard 0.22 to 0.35), sharply divergent sourcing profiles by engine, and a strong effect of query framing on whether any brand is named. Headline figures are bootstrapped for uncertainty; a test-retest on a query subset finds mean brand-set stability 0.77 and answer-type stability 100 percent; and an independent human second coder reproduces the coding on the checked subset (raw brand-set agreement 0.91, complete after reconciliation). These are pilot findings. A confirmatory study, preregistered before data collection, tests whether they replicate under a larger, volume-weighted query frame with multiple runs per query and full inter-coder reliability. The method, reliability checks, limitations, query frame, and analysis code are reported so the study can be reproduced.

title: When Success Splits: Emotional Variance Predicts Higher Ratings but Lower Popularity
affiliations: University of Toronto, Northeastern University (USA) and

detail.title: When Success Splits: Emotional Variance Predicts Higher Ratings but Lower Popularity
detail.abstract: Products people praise should be products people choose. Yet ratings and popularity can disagree. What predicts when they do? We propose that one answer lies in a cultural product's emotional variance-the degree to which distinct emotions (e.g., joy, fear, sadness) fluctuate over its duration. A multimethod investigation combines computational linguistics, machine learning, and experiments. We validate and apply a linguistic emotion classifier to more than 50,000 cultural products-over 3,000 movies, 12,000 TV episodes, and 36,000 songs. We find that products with greater emotional variance consistently receive higher ratings but are less popular, even after accounting for a broad set of alternative explanations. Two controlled experiments then manipulate emotional variance in written narratives. Before consumption, emotionally variable content seems more challenging to consume, discouraging consumption. During consumption, the same content is more engaging, leading to higher ratings. Together, the findings identify a predictable source of divergence between ratings and popularity and show how a single product feature can pull two common measures of success in opposite directions.

title: SEO & Ponto Futuro: Marketing Strategies for Higher Online Visibility in Non-Profit Journalism

detail.title: SEO & Ponto Futuro: Marketing Strategies for Higher Online Visibility in Non-Profit Journalism

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal affiliation with the founders or leadership of Ponto Futuro. The collaboration was undertaken solely based on the project's genuine interest in contributing to this research and advancing knowledge within the field.

detail.abstract: This applied article presents a study on the employment of structural Search Engine Optimization (SEO) strategies in Ponto Futuro, a non-profit journalistic-literary project dedicated to producing and sharing content about football. The project faced a fundamental dilemma: how to increase organic visibility in search engines without compromising editorial integrity and the authorial voice that distinguishes its production. To address this challenge, a marketing intervention was designed and implemented based on "non-content" SEO techniques, metadata optimization, taxonomic restructuring of the site, strategic definition of page indexing and de-indexing, continuous monitoring of technical health, and integration with social networks, all applied exclusively to the site's infrastructure and information architecture, without altering the editorial content. The results were evaluated using organic traffic and keyword data extracted from SEMrush for the period from August 2023 to September 2025. The findings indicate a consistent increase in organic traffic, with monthly visits rising from an average of 110 to 195, and a peak of 478 visits in September 2025-a growth of 73.2% compared to the pre-intervention peak. Although total keywords declined due to de-indexation (from 539 to approximately 200-300), the number of top 3 keywords remained stable (between 3 and 4), suggesting consolidation of the site's authority on relevant terms. The results are contextualized in light of Google algorithm updates during the same period. The study contributes to the marketing literature by offering empirical evidence that it is possible to reconcile algorithmic visibility and editorial integrity through structuring strategies that respect content as the untouchable asset of journalistic projects, particularly relevant for non-profit organizations with limited resources.

title: From Narrative Spectacle to Cold Identity: Cognitive Hegemony, Algorithmic Katechon, and the Disenchantment of L'Oréal Paris (1997-2026)
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: From Narrative Spectacle to Cold Identity: Cognitive Hegemony, Algorithmic Katechon, and the Disenchantment of L'Oréal Paris (1997-2026)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The L'Oréal Group has influenced this study : I worked for them between 1996 and 1998.
declarations.funderStatement: Author reports that this study has not been funded.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the structural and identity transformation of L'Oréal Paris within the French mass-retail market over three decades (1997-2026). Escaping conventional managerial narratives of seamless digital transition and adaptive organizational agility, we deploy a critical hermeneutic framework to critique the progressive cooling of brand identity-from the collapse of Debordian storytelling to the rise of automated Beauty Tech. Drawing on a multidisciplinary theoretical apparatus, we mobilize Weick's retrospective sensemaking, Schmittian political theology (Katechon), Ricoeurian identity philosophy (Mêmeté vs. Ipséité), and a critical re-reading of Resource Dependence Theory (RDT). We demonstrate that the mid-2010s eviction of key competitors (notably P&G's Pantene) through predatory product proliferation and combat isomorphism did not signal a return to consumer intimacy, but rather the brand's entry into an era of "cold identity." Facing market saturation and narrative exhaustion, the organization deployed AI diagnostics and Beauty Tech as an algorithmic Katechon-a technological shield designed to freeze market decline, delay margin erosion, and substitute scientific hyper-personalization for lost mythological resonance. This shift marks the absolute triumph of Sameness (Mêmeté) over Selfhood (Ipséité): the brand abandoned its narrative fidelity to become a automated mechanism for appearance optimization. First, this study challenges naive marketing models of consumer reenchantment and brand agility by revealing how global firms utilize technological interfaces to enforce cognitive hegemony rather than foster authentic engagement. Second, it extends critical RDT by demonstrating how symbolic resources (cultural diversity, green credentials) are forcibly internalized to asphyxiate external resistance. Third, it introduces a conceptual framework bridging Ricoeurian philosophy and digital branding, illustrating how the shift from emotional Customer Lock-on to existential Customer Lock-in relies on the systematic production of narcissistic anxiety. For marketing practitioners and strategists, this paper provides a sober diagnostic on the hidden costs of over-rationalization. It warns against the long-term erosion of brand equity caused by replacing brand ethos with technological prosthetics. Furthermore, it highlights the structural fragility of relying on price/mix inflation and shelf-smothering tactics in mature markets, demonstrating that the clinical management of narrative ruins ultimately exposes firms to deep consumer disillusionment when market conditions shift.

detail.abstract: Competency and skill-acquisition frameworks such as the Dreyfus five-stage model treat proficiency as a single scalar that a person accumulates and, absent practice, may lose. This treatment conflates two mechanistically distinct phenomena documented separately in the labor-economics and vocationaleducation literatures: skill decay, the erosion of a person's grip on a stable target through disuse, and skill obsolescence, the decline in a skill's value or applicability because the target itself has moved while the person's proficiency against it has not changed. A person can sit at the highest proficiency level on a decay-only model while being substantially misaligned with current practice, because decayonly instruments have no mechanism for detecting drift in the task definition. This paper proposes the Proficiency-Currency Matrix, a two-axis instrument that scores a competency independently on (1) a Dreyfus-style proficiency stage against a named task definition, and (2) a currency score reflecting how recently and how substantially that task definition itself has been revalidated against present practice. We define both axes operationally, derive four resulting quadrant states with distinct organizational implications, and work through an illustrative, sector-agnostic application. We close with limitations and directions for empirical validation.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: Open access funding provided by Széchenyi István University (SZE). This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: This article offers a comprehensive bibliometric analysis of research on physical work environments and maps its intellectual structure, thematic evolution, and collaborative dynamics over the past four decades from a business and management perspective. It reveals how previously fragmented streams of research on workplace design, employee well-being, and organizational performance are embedded in the broader management literature. The analysis provides insights into how the physical work environment has evolved from a peripheral topic to a topic of strategic concern in organizational research. Based on a dataset of 834 publications indexed in Scopus and Web of Science between 1978 and 2024, it captures the contributions of 1,906 authors publishing across 214 sources. Using advanced bibliometric techniques such as co-citation analysis, keyword co-occurrence, and strategic mapping, the study reveals a transition from early concerns with office layout and facility management to more recent emphases on employee well-being, workplace design, and the impacts of COVID-19. The thematic structure shows well-developed motor themes, such as office buildings and sustainability, alongside basic themes, such as workplace, productivity, and the physical work environment. Emerging topics include coworking spaces and workplace learning, while niche areas such as indoor air quality and workplace health highlight growing specialization. The results uncover the underlying knowledge structure of physical work environment research and highlight emerging research areas related to workplace transformation, hybrid work arrangements, and employee-centered workspace design. This study provides the conceptual foundation that enables researchers to better position future workplace research.

detail.abstract: This study examines how digital fan engagement strategies influence brand loyalty in emerging sports leagues in India, with fan engagement positioned as a mediating mechanism. The study operationalizes Digital Fan Engagement Strategies (DFES) as a second-order construct comprising Social Media Engagement, Personalized Content Engagement, Gamification and Interactive Rewards, and Live/Second-Screen Engagement. Primary survey data were collected from 523 eligible respondents aged 18-45 who followed an emerging Indian professional sports league and used at least one digital platform to engage with it. The data covered followers of the Indian Premier League, Indian Super League, Pro Kabaddi League and other emerging leagues. Measurement assessment indicated satisfactory internal consistency and convergent validity across all constructs, with Cronbach's alpha values ranging from 0.837 to 0.895 and composite reliability values ranging from 0.892 to 0.923. DFES had a significant positive association with fan engagement (β = 0.517, p < .001) and brand loyalty (β = 0.105, p = .012) after accounting for fan engagement. Fan engagement was strongly associated with brand loyalty (β = 0.523, p < .001). The indirect effect of DFES on brand loyalty through fan engagement was positive and significant (ab = 0.324, 95% bootstrap CI [0.254, 0.400]), indicating partial mediation. At the strategy-dimension level, all four digital strategies significantly predicted fan engagement, while Social Media Engagement and Gamification and Interactive Rewards were significant direct predictors of brand loyalty. The findings extend sport marketing research by showing that digital strategy is not merely a communication function; its value is realized through deeper fan engagement that subsequently strengthens loyalty in India's developing professional sports ecosystem.

title: Feedback Control-based Automation for Optimizing Economic Development: A New Political-Economic Algorithm as a Controller for the System of Division of Labor

detail.title: Feedback Control-based Automation for Optimizing Economic Development: A New Political-Economic Algorithm as a Controller for the System of Division of Labor

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that may have influenced or could be perceived to have influenced this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently without external funding or institutional affiliation.

detail.abstract: The degree of automation-which historically tends to rise and represents the replacement of economic labor with technical operations-is increasingly realized through software rather than hardware. This has a significant impact on the system of the division of labor, which, as part of the economic system, has a relevant function for economic development. This leads to the question of how a controlled or regulated automation of economic labor could be implemented to support the objective of a sustainable, socioeconomic development of a human or collective system. To address this, the concept of feedback control-based automation is introduced, and a politicaleconomic algorithm is proposed that-based on labor evaluation, economic sector ranking, technoeconomic automation effectiveness, and psychological principles-functions as a collective feedback control process, or more precisely, a controller. This controller determines in which sector, under which conditions, and in what sequence economic labor should be automated, whereby this has to be naturally in accordance with the relatively progressive human needs and states of consciousness. The proposed algorithm provides a new opportunity to reduce economic inefficiency and ineffectiveness while optimally harnessing the skills and potential for competence development of individuals, thereby contributing to systemic sustainability. With established theoretical foundations, the next step can be the real-world implementation of the political-economic algorithm to assess its objective utility on the economic system.

title: Navigating Arbitration in an Era of Expanding Sanctions: Legal Hurdles and Enforcement Risks
affiliations: Jindal Global Law School, O.P. Jindal Global University

detail.abstract: Growth in global economic activity has been accompanied by increasing geopolitical issues. In response, economic sanctions may be imposed against a State by one or more countries, thereby affecting cross-border transactions. This article examines the interplay between sanctions and arbitration through three dimensions: (i) their impact on arbitrability, (ii) contractual obligations and the arbitration process, and (iii) their impact on enforceability. It first analyzes arbitrability, considering the law of the seat, mandatory rules, the principle of separability, and emerging case law on UN, EU, and unilateral sanctions. Next, it examines contractual performance, including sanctions clauses, force majeure, illegality, frustration, and the procedural effects on arbitration. Finally, it explores enforceability, focusing on public policy objections, national practices, EU standards, and other practical challenges from licensing requirements. The article concludes that while disputes are not automatically rendered inarbitrable by sanctions, the increasing use of sanctions as jurisdictional and public policy tools places structural pressure on the transnational enforcement framework of the New York Convention. Despite uncertainty caused by sanctions, stakeholders, including parties, arbitrators, institutions, and courts, play crucial roles in safeguarding arbitration, which can continue to operate effectively with careful engagement.

declarations.ethicsApproval: The study involving human participants received an exemption determination from the University of Utah Institutional Review Board under protocol IRB_00140911, “Explaining the gender gap in self-promotion: labor market discrimination and social norms.” The exemption was granted on April 1, 2021, under Exemption Category 3. detail.abstract: Do employers account for the gender gap in self-promotion when making hiring decisions? We study this question using two pre-registered online experiments. Applicants complete a cognitive ability test, receive feedback on their test performance, and choose how much to self-promote in an applicant profile. Employers observe applicants' gender and self-promotion, but not their test performance, and make incentivized hiring decisions. We find that women self-promote less than equally performing men and, as a result, are less likely to be hired. This hiring gap is not driven by a gender-specific penalty for self-promotion; rather, employers do not sufficiently account for women's lower self-promotion when interpreting applicant profiles. In a second experiment, we show that employers substantially underestimate the gender gap in self-promotion. Providing employers with information about the actual gap updates their beliefs and increases the hiring and perceived performance of equally self-promoting female applicants. However, the information intervention only partially closes the overall hiring gap.

detail.abstract: In the wake of the pandemic, many financial firms rushed to change their business strategies, at times exposing deep structural weaknesses. This article examines an insurance company that attempted a change in business model and growth without the necessary governance and competence. The study details how supervisors shifted from passive monitoring to intrusive engagement, ultimately halting new business to force a rebuild of internal controls. This study bridges the gap between abstract theory of regulation and the applied day-today mechanics and challenges of supervising the implementation of regulation in practice to achieve the desired consumer protection and financial system integrity outcomes. It reaffirms that where critical situations arise a financial supervisor must quickly shift supervisory approach from a passive monitor to intrusive supervisory engagement.

detail.abstract: Bhupen Khakhar utilized visual art to express his life experiences and cultural observations, making significant contributions to Indian art by openly addressing themes of homosexuality. His work explored sexuality, vulnerability, and cultural identity, merging diverse influences to depict both ordinary and taboo aspects of life. Khakhar's courage in confronting these subjects has paved the way for newer generations to explore LGBTQ+ themes within Indian art, promoting inclusivity in contemporary society. His influence remains vital in the realm of modern art, particularly in narrating personal and taboo narratives.

detail.title: Exchange-rate Intervention and the Timing of Volatility: Evidence from Japan

detail.abstract: Foreign-exchange intervention is usually judged by the direction of the exchange-rate movement, yet an operation can move the yen without reducing the risk surrounding that path. This paper studies the timing of USD/JPY volatility around 69 Japanese intervention episodes between May 1991 and July 2024. Daily variance is measured against each episode's own 20-trading-day pre-event benchmark, and the intervention day is separated from the following 5-, 10-, and 20-day windows. Pooled daily variance is 4.2% higher on the intervention day, 19.0% lower over days 1-5, 11.8% lower over days 1-10, and 0.1% lower over days 1-20. No level estimate survives the frozen four-test Holm family, and the three post-event-minus-event-day transfer contrasts are all negative with adjusted pvalues of 1.000, so the data do not support the intuition that intervention buys calm and repays it later. The 20-day outcome is statistically equivalent to its pre-event benchmark inside a pre-specified ±0.20 log-variance region. The pooled path nevertheless conceals a historical contrast: the four 2022-2024 episodes show variance ratios 3.45 and 2.97 times those of the earlier episodes at 5 and 20 days, with exact permutation p-values of 0.033 and 0.006 after Holm adjustment. That contrast rests on four yen-purchase episodes, weakens under controls and leave-one-out checks, and is not reproduced by a locked 2026 holdout whose variance falls 16.7% and 47.4% below baseline at 10 and 20 days. Yield-curve alignment does not explain the volatility path, and intervention size predicts only the contemporaneous response before family adjustment. Because intervention dates are endogenous to market stress, every estimate is an event-time association rather than a causal effect. The evidence rejects a general delayed-risktransfer account and points instead to historically concentrated, nonpersistent volatility consequences.

detail.abstract: Tele-robotic surgery depends on communication infrastructure capable of maintaining predictable performance between geographically separated surgical locations. This observational network-engineering study evaluates production-network behavior during three real tele-robotic procedure windows. The central tele-robotic site used fiber access, while the three remote healthcare sites used microwave access over an IP/MPLS infrastructure. Operational dashboard evidence was examined for network delay, jitter, availability/reachability, bidirectional interface traffic, and packet loss when directly available. Across the three windows, typical monitored network delay was approximately 7-8 ms while visually observed input traffic reached approximately 29 Mbps and output traffic approximately 8-9 Mbps during higher-load periods. No sustained latency degradation was visible during the analyzed procedure windows, and availability/reachability remained at 100% in the monitoring views. For Remote Site B, the monitoring dashboard reported 0% packet loss during the observed period. Because the source evidence consisted primarily of operational dashboard screenshots rather than exported raw time-series data, numerical observations are reported conservatively as approximate values. The study separates production findings from network-readiness requirements supported by published telesurgery guidance and does not establish universal thresholds or evaluate clinical outcomes.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether information about issuer default risk shapes households' beliefs and choices among digital money issued by central banks, commercial banks, and non-bank private firms. We conduct a randomized survey experiment with 800 participants from France, Germany, and Italy. Participants report prior and posterior defaultrisk beliefs and complete nine stated payment choices in which issuer identity and interest compensation vary. Two treatments provide financial information about institutional differences in issuer risk, with one additionally presenting salient examples of financial distress. The treatments produce selective belief updating: they lower perceived centralbank default risk, leave commercial-bank beliefs largely unchanged, and raise perceived risk for non-bank private issuers. They also reduce selection of non-bank private digital money relative to both central-bank and commercial-bank alternatives. Under a structural random-utility model, participants require higher interest compensation to accept less-protected claims, revealing a differentiated hierarchy across issuer types: the required premium is higher for commercial-bank digital money than for a CBDC and substantially higher for non-bank private digital money. Assignment to either information treatment significantly increases the model-implied required annual interest-rate premium for commercial-bank digital money, with the increase approximately three times as large for non-bank private digital money.

detail.abstract: Most of cold weather's health burden is mild respiratory illness, managed at home and absent from administrative records. Using retail scanner data on over-the-counter cold remedies and a triple-difference design that nets out storm-driven shopping suppression, I find that a cold anomaly raises cold-remedy sales by 6.2% in the week it occurs. The response depends far more on when the anomaly arrives than on how deep it is: shoulder-season anomalies raise sales by 8.7% against 2.2% in midwinter, despite a smaller temperature drop. Adaptation to cold thus varies within the year, not only across climates, and shapes when the burden falls.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether household internet access affects maternal and reproductive healthcare consumption in India. Using the fourth and fifth rounds of the National Family Health Survey, we study the relationship between household connectivity and healthcare utilization during a period of rapid expansion in low-cost internet access. Results indicate that internet access is associated with higher rates of institutional delivery, skilled birth attendance, postnatal care, and modern contraceptive use. We also find changes in the composition of healthcare consumption: connected households are more likely to use private facilities for delivery and less likely to use public facilities. The results are consistent with internet access reducing information and search frictions, as connected households are more likely to obtain antenatal care from skilled providers, complete at least four antenatal visits, and initiate care earlier in pregnancy. Internet access is also associated with a shift away from spouse-only healthcare decision-making toward greater joint or female participation. The effects are heterogeneous across socioeconomic groups: the association with institutional delivery is stronger among poorer households, while substitution toward private care is more pronounced among wealthier, urban, and better-educated women. These findings suggest that digital connectivity affects both the level and composition of maternal healthcare consumption, with distributional consequences that differ across households.

detail.abstract:
Background:
Red blood cell transfusion decisions in critically ill patients remain largely protocol-driven, as conventional models fail to integrate volume resuscitation with oxygen delivery dynamics. We developed a novel circulatory model to assess erythrocyte value across hemodynamic states and evaluated its generalizability. From this model's methods, we derived two key indices: cyclic score (Plife) and relative lactate level (Rlac). Using retrospective data from a local hospital system, we examined their association with all‑cause mortality via Cox proportional hazards models, Kaplan–Meier analysis, and restricted cubic splines. Joint latent class trajectory modeling characterized longitudinal Plife and Rlac patterns. Machine learning identified key predictors, and an online dynamic risk calculator was developed. External validation used the MIMIC‑IV database. Rlac was associated with increased mortality risk (HR = 1.062, 95% CI: 1.035–1.090, p < 0.001), while higher Plife was protective (HR = 0.962, 95% CI: 0.942–0.982, p < 0.001). Using cutoffs of Rlac > 1 and Plife > 5, four risk groups were identified; the "low Plife & high Rlac " and "high Plife & high Rlac" phenotypes showed markedly elevated mortality. Three distinct joint trajectories were identified; transition to the "Persistent decompensation" phenotype marked poor prognosis. The parsimonious model (Rlac + Plife) demonstrated good discriminative ability in internal (AUC = 0.770) and external (AUC = 0.805–0.912) validation. 
Conclusion:
This circulatory framework links erythrocyte dynamics to mortality, with Plife and Rlac providing complementary long‑ and short‑term risk stratification to guide individualized transfusion decisions in critically ill patients.

detail.abstract: This study explores how changes in crude oil prices affect U.S. government borrowing costs through inflation and Federal Reserve policy. It focuses on the period from 200-2026 and uses WTI crude oil prices, CPI inflation, the federal funds rate, and the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield from government and FRED data. Regression analysis is used to study the relationships between these variables, along with a historical look at major events such as the 2008 financial crisis, the Covid-19 oil crash, the 2022 Russia-Ukraine energy shock, and the 2026 Iran conflict. Overall, the results show that oil prices can influence Treasury yields indirectly by raising inflation and increasing investor expectations of high interest rates. However, this relationship is not consistent in every period. Recessions, financial crises, and demand for safer investments can also strongly affect Treasury yields. One limitation of the study is that oil prices are only one of many factors that influence U.S. government borrowing costs.

detail.abstract:
Background: Lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) remain a major cause of mortality globally, disproportionately affecting children younger than 5 years. Despite substantial reductions in childhood LRTI mortality, progress across Africa has been uneven, and the extent to which individual countries are on track to meet the Global Action Plan for the Prevention and Control of Pneumonia and Diarrhoea (GAPPD) 2025 targets remains unclear. We assessed country-level progress towards the GAPPD mortality and incidence targets across all 54 African countries and projected trajectories to 2050 under continuation of historical trends. 

Methods: We conducted a secondary analysis of Global Burden of Disease 2023 (GBD 2023) data for 54 African countries, 1990–2023. Bayesian age-period-cohort models via Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation (BAPC-INLA) were fitted per country to project LRTI mortality and incidence rates to 2050. Countries were classified against the GAPPD 2025 mortality threshold (<60 deaths per 100,000 children under 5) and incidence target (≥75% reduction from 2010 baseline) as Achieved, Borderline, or Off-track. MIR were computed for 54 countries and seven regional groupings. Performance was assessed through holdout validation (training 1990–2018; holdout 2019–2023). 

Findings: In 2023, an estimated 741,759 LRTI deaths occurred across all ages in Africa, of which 327,033 (44·1%) were in children under 5 — comprising only 17% of Africa's total population. The under-5 LRTI mortality rate declined from 478·7 per 100,000 in 1990 to 158·0 per 100,000 in 2023 (−67·0%). Nine of 54 countries met the mortality threshold; 45 were Off-track; no country met the incidence target by 2025. Forty-two countries (78%) are not projected to achieve the mortality threshold by 2050. 

Interpretation: Most African countries are not projected to achieve the GAPPD 2025 targets under continuation of historical trends. Closing-the-gap timelines to 2050 provide an evidence base for post-2025 policy planning.

title: A Space–Time Theory of Recovery Location in Heterogeneous Mines
affiliations: Pontificia Universidad Catolica de Chile

detail.title: A Space–Time Theory of Recovery Location in Heterogeneous Mines
detail.abstract: Choosing where a mine should advance is an intertemporal allocation problem: mineral value is unevenly distributed in space, and high-value material may become accessible only after lower-value waste or development is removed. Resource economics explains separately the opportunity cost of depleting a finite stock, the proportion of a heterogeneous resource ultimately recovered, and the shadow value of scarce mine, plant, and market capacity. Mine-planning models represent geometry and precedence in detail, but generally do not yield a portable economic rule for allocating a shared bottleneck among competing extraction fronts. This paper develops a space–time theory of recovery location that integrates these dimensions. A finite-horizon continuous model derives a local condition in which each front’s current netback is adjusted by a signed location co-state and a common bottleneck rent. A separate stationary benchmark represents the orebody as independent extraction chains competing for one transferable bottleneck. Under its restrictive assumptions, the established discounted-allocation theorem implies an exact rule: advance the front with the largest maximum discounted prefix-average netback. The index values a feasible spatial package rather than the next parcel alone, distinguishes current quality from access continuation value, and yields capacity-conditioned inclusion and sequencing thresholds when negative-value access precedes hidden ore. A three-front illustration reproduces the Bellman solution, and 3,000 randomly generated small problems confirm implementation consistency. The contribution is a resource-economic account of how spatial access enters the user cost of extraction and the intensive recovery margin, with implications for endogenous recovery, capacity design, fiscal incidence, and destination allocation.

title: Who decarbonizes? Effects of uniform and differentiated carbon pricing on carbon inequality
affiliations: University of Oldenburg

detail.title: Who decarbonizes? Effects of uniform and differentiated carbon pricing on carbon inequality
detail.abstract: In many countries, consumption-based emissions are increasingly concentrated at the top of the distribution, and there are growing calls in public debate for climate policy to target emission-intensive luxury consumption more strongly. Yet while financial distributional effects of carbon pricing are well studied, its impact on the distribution of emissions across households remains less well understood. This paper first characterizes the demand-side conditions under which uniform carbon pricing increases or decreases consumption-based carbon inequality within countries in a simple partial-equilibrium setting with heterogeneous households. Applying the main result to Germany suggests that uniform carbon pricing would slightly reduce carbon inequality, while a stylized approximation of carbon pricing in Germany increases it. The paper then compares differentiated carbon pricing, where luxury goods are priced at a higher rate than necessities, with the standard benchmark of uniform carbon pricing. While the latter is attractive in terms of efficiency, it does not necessarily outperform differentiated pricing, both regarding financial and emissions-based distributional effects.

detail.abstract:
Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) tools analysing tumour morphology from routine pathology images are a new method for risk stratification of breast cancer to guide decisions on adjuvant chemotherapy. Combined use of AI followed by a gene expression assay (GEA) is a novel implementation approach. This study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of an AI-based risk tool followed by a GEA in post-menopausal patients with estrogen receptor-positive (ER+), human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-negative (HER2−), node-negative (N0) breast cancer in Sweden.

Methods: Lifetime costs and health outcomes were simulated using a semi-Markov model from a healthcare perspective. The decision to use adjuvant chemotherapy was based on the AI tool followed by a reflex GEA or on GEA alone. Transition probabilities were estimated with parametric survival models based on Swedish quality register data. Outcomes were measured in life years (LYs) and quality-adjusted life years (QALYs). Cost-effectiveness was assessed using the incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (ICER). Uncertainty was explored through scenario analyses, a probabilistic sensitivity analysis, and value of information analyses.

Findings: In the base-case analysis, the AI+GEA strategy resulted in cost savings of €756 per patient and an incremental gain of 0.0154 LYs and 0.0061 QALYs, compared with GEA alone. At a cost-effectiveness threshold of €43,736 (500,000 SEK), the probability of the AI+GEA strategy being cost-effective was 87%, and the prognostic performance of the two tests accounted for 70% of the expected value of the perfect information.InterpretationThe addition of an AI-based risk stratification tool to GEA appears to be cost-effective for guiding adjuvant chemotherapy decisions for patients with ER+, HER2-, N0 breast cancer in Sweden. Limited data on the joint test characteristics require further research.

detail.abstract: This article examines whether contemporary large language models (LLMs) are capable of assisting with parliamentary committee scrutiny of legislation. Parliamentary scrutiny is a structured process requiring the identification and evaluation of issues by reference to established scrutiny principles and committee practice. Recent advances in artificial intelligence have prompted interest in whether such technologies might support aspects of this work. This article considers whether LLMs are capable of producing legal and technical analysis of an acceptable standard in the context of parliamentary scrutiny, and what limitations and risks arise from their use in this setting. To explore these questions, this study tested several leading LLMs against real scrutiny tasks drawn from the work of two Senate committees: the Scrutiny of Bills Committee and the Scrutiny of Delegated Legislation Committee. The outputs generated by the models were then assessed against a structured rubric designed to reflect committee practice. The findings suggest that, while current models are capable of producing outputs that resemble committee analysis in some contexts, significant limitations remain, particularly in relation to threshold judgment, consistency and alignment with institutional practice.

detail.abstract:
Background: Maternal mortality rose sharply in Brazil during the COVID-19 pandemic, but whether the decline after 2021 represented recovery or mainly the disappearance of the COVID-19 component remains unclear. We assessed national maternal mortality from 2015 to 2024, estimating excess deaths, COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 contributions, residual excess by cause and timing, and regional trajectories.

Methods: We conducted a nationwide ecological time-series study using mortality records and live-birth denominators. Maternal deaths among women aged 10–49 years occurring during pregnancy, childbirth, abortion, or within 42 days postpartum were included. Quasi-Poisson models fitted to the 2015–2019 baseline, with log live births as an offset, estimated counterfactual mortality for 2020–2024.

Findings: We identified 16,882 maternal deaths. Mortality exceeded counterfactual estimates throughout 2020–2024, peaking in 2021 with 2,983 observed versus 1,347·0 expected deaths, 1,636·0 excess deaths, and 121·4% relative excess. COVID-19-related deaths accounted for 51·8% of maternal mortality in 2021 but declined sharply thereafter. Positive non-COVID-19 deviations in 2022–2024 persisted in the puerperium and selected underlying-cause groups.

Interpretation: Brazil’s decline in maternal mortality after 2021 did not represent complete recovery. Although the COVID-19 shock subsided, selected components remained above expected trajectories, consistent with persistent vulnerabilities in maternal care and regional inequalities.

detail.abstract: The improvement of urban living quality is not driven by a single factor, but rather is a comprehensive project involving the energy structure, industrial ecology, and public service provision. Under the symbiotic logic of 'planetary health–human health,' energy use constitutes the metabolic foundation of the Earth's ecological cycle, and its structural transformation—through improving soil quality, reducing pollution, and optimizing the overall ecosystem—generates positive spillovers to residents' health and well-being. This article focuses from a theoretical perspective on the systematic impact of energy transition on the livability of cities, constructing a "institutional support - ecological competitiveness - incentive compatibility" triple framework to clarify the relationship between innovation and the utilization of renewable energy, and identify the specific paths through which energy transition can enhance the quality of population development. Methodologically, using China's Innovative City Pilot Policy (ICPP) as a quasi-natural experiment, we employ difference-in-differences (DID) to examine the effects of renewable energy consumption on population development and its transmission channels. Findings reveal that the environmental dividends of renewable energy significantly enhance resident employment, income, and education, with innovation amplifying this effect; the ICPP, as an exogenous institutional arrangement, helps compensate for market-driven innovation deficiencies. Heterogeneity shows that policy effects on healthcare are more pronounced in northwestern and smaller-population cities. Our results suggest that whether energy transition translates into quality improvement depends on establishing a synergistic mechanism of "market innovation, policy support, and context-specific resource allocation," providing critical evidence for coordinated green development and new urbanization.

title: Prevalence of visual impairments in children with cerebral palsy in South-East Asia: A systematic review and meta-analysis

detail.abstract:
Aim: To estimate the prevalence of oculomotor dysfunction, binocular vision anomalies, and refractive errors among children with cerebral palsy (CP) in South-East Asia (SEA).

Methods: This systematic review followed the JBI methodology and included studies (2010–2025) of children (2–17 years) with CP in the SEA reporting visual impairment prevalence. Research was conducted in MEDLINE, Scopus, Cochrane Central, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and reference lists. Study selection (Covidence), data extraction (piloted Excel form), and ROB assessment (Newcastle–Ottawa Scale) were performed independently. Statistical analyses were performed using Stata 18.5. Prevalence estimates were stabilized using the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation and pooled using a random-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood estimation.

Results: Of the 166 unique records, 37 studies were included. The pooled prevalence of myopia was 13%, hyperopia 28%, astigmatism 38%, strabismus 36%, nystagmus 11%, optic atrophy 9%, ptosis 2%, Cortical Visual Impairment 21%, congenital cataract 2%, disc pallor 6%, and reduced VA 25.0%. Sensitivity analyses confirmed robust findings. Hospital-based studies generally reported higher, but non-significant, prevalence than school-based studies.

Interpretation: Visual impairment is highly prevalent among children with CP in SEA, highlighting the need for routine vision screening and early intervention, particularly in special schools.

detail.abstract:
As AI systems come to write, store, retrieve, summarize, and interpret institutional records, nearly every integrity check available — hashes, logs, timestamps, signed manifests — is itself a digital artifact verified by software of the same class as the thing being checked. 
The verification chain no longer terminates outside the system it examines. 

This paper argues that records whose authenticity rests on institutional assertion alone are becoming "fiat records," and that the primary risk is not forgery but drift: the gradual divergence of the working record from what was recorded, with no external reference against which the divergence could be observed. Evidence of present-tense contamination is reviewed, including model collapse (Shumailov et al. 2024), measured growth of synthetic text in newly published web content, and documented error propagation in AI-drafted clinical records.

The paper proposes a "Cold Standard": a fixed, sealed corpus of record digests held beyond the executable reach of any connected system, opened only through governed human action, whose sole function is to answer whether what an institution holds today matches what was sealed then — an instrument for use while systems work, not a backup for after they fail. 

Two historical precedents (metrological reference artifacts; monetary convertibility) supply the design logic; an isolation ladder ordered by adversary cost, from logical isolation to extraterritorial and off-world custody, situates existing infrastructure. 
The paper distinguishes the instrument from fixity checking and preservation copies, states its own weakest point — verification's last mile — and proposes an OAIS profile as a standards path. 

It is the companion to "Decision Custody", which established the obligation this paper's instrument serves.

detail.abstract: AI enabled crime is transforming identity theft from a largely manual or semi-automated activity into a scalable, persuasive and increasingly autonomous threat. Recent developments in generative and agentic AI allow attackers to produce multilingual phishing messages, synthetic voice and video impersonations, adaptive malware and data poisoning attacks that can compromise individuals, organizations and public trust. AI-powered phishing, deepfake scams, AI-driven malware, model manipulation and criminal LLMs are expanding the enterprise attack surface and eroding digital trust. A human-rights-centered privacy framework is needed to protect identity, dignity, autonomy, due process and informational self-determination in the age of AI-powered identity theft. The chapter proposes a multilayer defense model combining privacy-enhancing technologies, AI bills of materials, deepfake detection, multi-channel verification, zero-trust identity governance, employee awareness and rights-based policy controls. It concludes with a practical governance framework for organizations seeking to defend against synthetic identity crimes while preserving civil liberties and human rights.

detail.abstract: AI agents are a class of autonomous systems capable of goal-directed planning, tool use, and multi-step action. They are presently being deployed at a scale and speed that render manual compliance assessment practically impossible, which creates a structural paradox: The only credible path to assessment automation relies on large language models (LLMs) of the same class as the agents under review. This paper examines whether LLM-based assessment is technically sound, consistent with regulatory objectives, and legally tenable. We survey the principal assessment approaches and situate them within a systematic framework of four LLM roles: trajectory critic, multiagent cross-examiner, adversarial simulator, and semantic data synthesiser. We further identify a regulatory transparency deficit and the digital sovereignty risks created by concentrated assessment capacity and analyse liability implications. We conclude with a proposal of three governance principles: independence at model, context and commercial level; repeatability and reproducibility; and risk-proportionality as minimum conditions for trustworthy AI-based assessment.

detail.abstract: Cloud transformation has evolved from a predominantly technical infrastructure initiative into a strategic organizational capability that influences how enterprises design, coordinate, and execute business operations. Unlike basic cloud adoption, which may involve migrating selected applications or infrastructure to cloud environments, cloud transformation encompasses the redesign of information technology capabilities, organizational processes, data architectures, governance mechanisms, and business models around cloud-enabled operating principles. This paper examines the relationship between cloud transformation and enterprise operational efficiency and develops a conceptual framework for understanding how cloud-enabled capabilities translate into improvements in organizational performance. Drawing on the Resource-Based View (RBV), Dynamic Capabilities Theory, and the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, the study conceptualizes cloud transformation as a multidimensional capability consisting of cloud infrastructure modernization, data and application integration, automation, scalability, cloud governance, security, and organizational readiness. Operational efficiency is examined through dimensions including process efficiency, cost efficiency, decision-making speed, service quality, resource utilization, organizational agility, and innovation capability. The paper argues that cloud transformation does not automatically generate efficiency gains. Instead, its value depends on the organization's ability to integrate cloud technologies with business processes, workforce capabilities, governance structures, and strategic objectives. The framework proposes that cloud-enabled automation, integration, scalability, and data accessibility directly and indirectly improve operational efficiency, while organizational readiness and effective governance moderate these relationships. The study contributes a theoretically grounded framework that can guide future empirical research and provide managers with a structured approach to evaluating the operational consequences of cloud transformation. It concludes that enterprises should treat cloud transformation as an enterprise-wide operating-model transformation rather than simply an information technology migration project.

detail.abstract: Lawyers play a crucial role in representing litigants in court and providing legal counsel on their rights, obligations, and the procedural steps involved in complex pre-trial and trial proceedings. However, the excessive costs of legal services and the absence of (sufficient) legal aid mechanisms can exclude certain citizens from seeking a dispute settlement before courts. Chatbots based on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become popular due to their user-friendly way of communicating information on substantive and procedural law and on court proceedings. Nevertheless, LLM-based chatbots can mislead users by providing inaccurate information, ultimately affecting the progress of their case before courts. The present paper asks to what extent Large Language Models-based chatbots are designed in a human centric way to support self-represented litigants in accessing legal information. To address this question, the paper explores the concept of 'human centricity' under the EU's framework for trust worthy Artificial Intelligence, in order to develop a set of functional requirements against which the performance of LLM-based chatbots is assessed in the context of landlord-tenant disputes.

title:
The Experience Paradox
Task Automation, Hiring Automation, and the Market That Stopped Evaluating
affiliations: and Chiang Mai University

detail.title:
The Experience Paradox
Task Automation, Hiring Automation, and the Market That Stopped Evaluating

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No
declarations.ethicsApproval: NA
declarations.funderStatement: Self

detail.abstract: Three prominent 2026 studies of artificial intelligence and employment appear contradictory: (1) occupation-level employment declines among young workers in AI-exposed occupations, (2) firm level hiring increases among heavy AI adopters, and the (3) attribution of rising graduate unemployment to remote work. They also share a limitation, for each measure only the extensive margin of employment. None asks whether the work that survives still builds, or still rewards, accumulated judgment. This paper develops a two-axis framework distinguishing execution (codified task performance, subject to physical or algorithmic ceilings) from judgment (consequence-bearing discretion, which compounds with experience), and separates two conditions that current data cannot tell apart: (1) the destruction of experience's value and (2) the failure of the market that prices it. Evidence that generative AI transmits the practices of experienced workers to novices implies that the transmissible component of experience is depreciating; the consequence-bearing component is not, and its complement is expanding. Drawing on the litigation record of Mobley v. Workday, which makes the algorithmic screening layer observable at unprecedented scale although no finding on the merits has been made, we identify a paradox: task automation is raising the relative value of consequence-bearing judgment at precisely the moment hiring automation is reducing the probability that judgment is ever evaluated. The two failures compound across generations: with the formation of judgment disrupted among the young and its evaluation gated for the experienced, the judgment supply chain is severed at both ends, and an economy can run short of experience while excluding the people who have it. Rational adaptations to this collision, signal degradation and reversion to patronage channels, carry costs of their own. We close with five testable propositions and a measurement agenda for the experience margin.

title: The Industrialization of Intelligence: How Scalable Artificial Intelligence is Transforming Modern Defense Organizations
affiliations: , Lusófona University, Lusófona University and Lusófona University

detail.title: The Industrialization of Intelligence: How Scalable Artificial Intelligence is Transforming Modern Defense Organizations

detail.abstract: For most of human history, intelligence has been an inherently biological capability. Human cognition has always been constrained by the number of trained individuals available, their expertise, physical presence, cognitive limitations, and the time required to acquire and apply knowledge. Consequently, defense organizations have traditionally treated intelligence as a scarce resource that could only be expanded through recruitment, education, and organizational growth. Artificial Intelligence fundamentally changes this paradigm. AI is enabling the industrialization of intelligence itself. It transforms cognitive capabilities into scalable, reproducible and continuously available assets. Identical to how the Industrial Revolution multiplied human physical labor through machines, AI is multiplying cognitive capacity by allowing organizations to generate, replicate, and deploy intelligence at unprecedented speed and scale. This paper introduces the concept of the "Industrialization of Intelligence" as a new framework for understanding the digital transformation of defense organizations. It argues that AI is viewed as the emergence of a new production factor that is improving the decisionmaking processes. Building upon a systematic literature review the paper examines how scalable AI changes the economics of cognition and enables defense organizations to move from human-limited decision support to continuously operating cognitive ecosystems. The discussion also explores the implications for command and control and human-AI collaboration. The paper concludes that future military advantage will increasingly depend on possessing advanced AI technologies, but also on the organizational capability to industrialize intelligence across all defense functions. Organizations capable of integrating scalable cognitive systems into their processes will gain significant advantages in speed, adaptability, and decision superiority within increasingly complex security/defense environments.

title: The Timing Problem: Conditions for a Response to an Adaptive Rogue AI

detail.title: The Timing Problem: Conditions for a Response to an Adaptive Rogue AI

detail.abstract: This paper asks under what conditions a defending AI could constrain an attacking one, and, separately, whether a government could act on those conditions before an adaptive adversary moves past them. The objection that "we could just use a good AI to stop the bad AI" only becomes operationally relevant once society has already handed AI systems enough responsibility that losing control of one would materially matter. Even then, the objection assumes away a timing problem that this paper treats as the harder question. The framework is developed in two parts. First, it identifies six conditions under which a defending AI could plausibly constrain an attacking one: relative defensive capability, the durability of a capability lead, the ordering of defensive and offensive capability arrival, independent oversight, deployment speed, and meaningful human override. Second, it models a government response lifecycle alongside a mirrored, adaptive rogue-AI response lifecycle, treating each government intervention as an observation that can change the adversary's subsequent behaviour. The framework is deliberately speculative and is not presented as an empirical model of future AI behaviour; its purpose is to identify the assumptions, timing relationships, and observable signals that would need to be tested if such a scenario became operationally relevant. The paper therefore treats the lifecycle as a planning hypothesis rather than a forecast.

detail.abstract: We ask whether e-commerce and transport infrastructure substitute for one another, and which modes matter for online retail. Using bilateral online transactions across 279 Chinese prefectures matched to the road, freight-rail, and high-speed-rail (HSR) networks, we document a causal asymmetry: HSR raises online sales while conventional freight lowers them. A calibrated heterogeneous-firm spatial model with online-offline channel choice shows that e-commerce and infrastructure are substitutes, since the online channel is worth more where connectivity is worse, and yields a 2.1% welfare gain from e-commerce. HSR complements the online channel; freight crowds it out.

title: When AI Speaks for the Crowd: A Field Experiment on the Design of AI-generated Summaries
affiliations: China Europe International Business School (CEIBS), Tianjin University, China Europe International Business School (CEIBS) and China Europe International Business School (CEIBS)

detail.title: When AI Speaks for the Crowd: A Field Experiment on the Design of AI-generated Summaries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No funding

detail.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly use generative AI to convert large volumes of dispersed reviews, comments, and opinions into decision support for consumers. This deployment creates an operations-design problem: how should a platform configure AI-generated summaries (AIGS) to reduce customers' information-processing burden while improving downstream conversion? We argue that AIGS affect these operational outcomes through designed social influence. By replacing directly observable peer signals with an algorithmically authored account of "what the crowd thinks," AIGS allow platforms to configure two design choices: whether the summary renders underlying opinions as consensus or divergence-a normative cue-and whether the AI remains descriptive or expresses an evaluative stance-an informational cue. We test these choices in a 2×2 randomized field experiment with 35,625 users on a major consumption platform. Emphasizing consensus reduces viewing time by 10% and increases product clicks by 24%, indicating that the same design choice can improve information-processing efficiency and conversion. AI stance reshapes this operational tradeoff: it attenuates the consensus-induced reduction in viewing time but further amplifies product clicks. We attribute this pattern to a normative interpretation mechanism-AI evaluation helps users translate the prevailing social view into implications for their own decisions. The findings position AIGS configuration as a scalable operational lever for managing the customer decision process and platform performance, while highlighting governance risks when platforms algorithmically construct perceived consensus.

detail.abstract: Traditional Model Risk Management (MRM) practices are insufficient on their own for governing generative and agentic AI systems, which are stochastic, opaque, and often built on third-party-hosted foundation models. The April 2026 U.S. interagency supervisory guidance, SR 26-2, refreshed MRM principles but placed generative and agentic AI outside its scope, leaving institutions to determine appropriate governance and controls. This paper addresses that gap by providing a practical playbook for governing these systems. The playbook outlines four properties of a governed AI system: correctness, consistency, robustness, and predictability. It then sets out a governance lifecycle, from system design through monitoring and revalidation, for achieving and sustaining those properties. The lifecycle incorporates nine key concepts that address governance challenges arising from the distinctive characteristics of generative and agentic AI systems. The playbook is designed for two audiences: executive risk leaders who need the overarching framework and frontline risk managers who need detailed implementation guidance.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Social, Behavioral, and Health Sciences 2026, Volume 20, Pages 1–17 https://doi.org/10.5590/JSBHS.2026.20.1828 [undefined]

detail.abstract: Public online communication has increasingly included violence-related content that is meme-based, ironic, visually stylized, multimodal, and only partially ideological. This comprehensive literature review synthesized research on online extremism, extremist memes, toxic multimodal content, dehumanizing digital communication, nihilistic violent extremism, warning behaviors, platform affordances, and youth-facing online environments. The purpose was to clarify what the literature had established; identify where the scholarship remained fragmented; and map research domains relevant to social, behavioral, public safety, and human services scholarship. The review used a structured, comprehensive literature review strategy supported by integrative synthesis procedures. The final corpus contained 34 scholarly sources, including 32 topical sources, one ethics-oriented source, and one methodological source. The synthesis identified six recurring themes: (a) hybridized online violent communication; (b) memes, aesthetics, and multimodal violent meaning; (c) irony, humor, and ambiguity; (d) dehumanization and anti-human framing; (e) platform affordances and youth-facing digital environments; and (f) warning-behavior-adjacent signaling. The review found that existing research explained important parts of the problem but remained fragmented across studies on terrorism, criminology, communication, public health, digital platforms, and threat assessment. Five research domains were recommended for future empirical study: (a) meaning collapse, (b) anti-human or dehumanizing orientation, (c) aestheticized violent communication, (d) irony and ambiguity, and (e) warning-behavior-adjacent signaling. These domains were presented as research concepts rather than diagnostic, predictive, or surveillance tools. The review concluded with implications for researchers, practitioners, policy and platform audiences, and future empirical work.

title: Trustworthy Enough for What? Governing AI as an Operational Claim in Critical Infrastructure: A Practice-Focused Operational Synthesis for AI-Dependent Essential Services

detail.abstract: "Trustworthy AI" is useful as an aspiration, but in critical infrastructure a model-level label can outlive the evidence that justified a particular use. Data, retrieval, tools, permissions, staffing, connectivity, and common providers can change what an AI-enabled system can cause even when the base model does not. This Perspective argues that trustworthiness should be governed as a bounded, evidence-backed, revisable, and revocable operational claim about a system-in-context. It organizes the argument around five principles: govern consequence pathways and effective authority; bound claims to a validated operating envelope and explicit invalidation triggers; design degraded modes and require evidence before authority returns; preserve reconstructable evidence across decisions and artifacts; and treat resilience as an ecosystem property that includes common-mode dependencies and resource contention. A compact Claim Card and failure-first stress test translate these principles into practice. The proposal is not a new certification regime or an empirically validated framework. It is a synthesis that connects established risk, assurance, human-factors, continuity, incident-response, and resilience practices to AI dependent essential services.

detail.abstract: Japanese foreign-exchange intervention is often evaluated by the exchange-rate movement on the intervention day. This paper argues that the relevant policy outcome is the persistence of the intended-direction response after the initial operation. Using the official intervention chronology, daily USD/JPY observations, Japanese and U.S. short-rate measures, and strictly lagged market controls, the analysis constructs 69 pre-2026 intervention episodes and separates first-day response, continuation, decay, and reversal. Episodes preceded by an aligned short-end yield-curve state show mean intended-direction responses of 0.78 percentage points on the intervention day and 2.06 percentage points at the 20-day horizon, compared with 0.26 and -0.05 percentage points for misaligned episodes. Conditional regressions associate a one-standard-deviation increase in alignment with responses of 0.41, 0.60, and 0.83 percentage points at 5, 10, and 20 days. Raw wild-bootstrap p-values are near conventional thresholds, but Holm adjustment across the frozen horizon family yields 0.109. Alignment is also associated with a 25.2% larger first-day operation and lower continuation odds, although the two-outcome family does not reject. The estimates therefore support a positive state-dependent persistence gradient, not a confirmed causal effect of intervention. The findings show why an immediate currency movement should not be treated as evidence of durable policy effectiveness.
