detail.abstract:
Emerging market central banks frequently maintain aggressive policy rate differentials to attract foreign portfolio investment ("hot money" carry trade) as a primary stabilization lever to anchor the domestic currency and accumulate foreign exchange reserves. However, this currency defense strategy generates an understudied macro-fiscal friction: an endogenous fiscal-financial feedback loop linking speculative carry trade inflows, domestic debt repricing, and sudden-stop vulnerability. Positioning our analysis within the "Original Sin Redux" framework [10, 22], we utilize a monthly dataset of Egypt's sovereign debt operations, central bank balance sheets, maturity-decomposed foreign Treasury bill holdings, and sovereign credit default swaps (CDS) from 2010 to 2026 (T = 200) to develop a causal identification and macroprudential policy framework. We establish five core findings. First, foreign investors enjoyed an annualized carry trade excess return
peaking at +22.4%, expanding foreign T-bill holdings to a historical peak of $33.6 billion
in September 2021, with over 72% concentrated in ultra-short 91/182-day tenors. Second,
utilizing Neyman-orthogonal Instrumental Variable Double Machine Learning (IV-DML)
with 5-fold temporal blocked cross-fitting and a 3-month purging window (F = 30.05,
Partial R2 = 0.142), we isolate the causal fiscal gradient: every $1 billion USD in foreign
T-bill holdings increases the annual state budget interest expenditure bill by EGP 22.40
billion per year (p = 0.0012), derived from a 12-month distributed lag cumulative response. Mediation analysis reveals that 78.4% of this fiscal penalty is mediated through the
uniform debt auction repricing channel. Third, using Hansen’s (2000) sample-splitting
threshold regression with slope switching, we identify a structural concentration tipping
point at θ∗ = 22.5% (95% bootstrap CI: [20.8%, 24.2%]), which tightens to θ∗
stress = 18.2%
during high global volatility regimes (VIX > 25). We formalize this non-linearity in
Proposition 1, proving that the sovereign debt-CDS feedback dynamic transitions from
stable (ρ(A) = 0.78 < 1, 95% CI: [0.643, 0.895]) to explosive (ρ(A) = 1.58 > 1, 95% CI:
[1.335, 1.810]) when foreign concentration exceeds θ∗. State-dependent local projections
(ST-LP) confirm that a +100 bps policy rate shock induces a +EGP 55.4 Bn interest
explosion and +195 bps CDS spike under high concentration (θ > θ∗) compared to
a stabilizing trajectory under low concentration (θ ≤ θ∗). Recursive pseudo-real-time
out-of-sample holdout forecasting validates this mechanism across the 2018 (-$10B), 2020
(-$18B), and 2022 (-$22B) flight episodes (ROC-AUC = 0.942, PR-AUC = 0.891, Brier =
0.068), with TreeExplainer SHAP interactions confirming that VIX shocks act as violent
hazard catalysts exclusively above θ∗. Fourth, we formulate the Hot Money Laffer Curve
and analytically derive the optimal foreign portfolio buffer F ∗ ≈ $14.20 Billion USD
([$12.5B, $15.5B]), establishing that maintaining a $25 billion buffer pushes the economy
into the destructive downward-sloping region where marginal fiscal costs dominate reserve
benefits. Fifth, we design a state-contingent Maturity-Tiered Dynamic Unremunerated
Reserve Requirement (Dynamic URR) with a 60-day grandfathering transition path to pre-
vent front-running fire sales, combined with sovereign Quanto-indexed T-bills with capped
spread protection and debt reprofiling. Counterfactual simulations demonstrate that
this macroprudential framework delivers EGP 579.8 billion (95% Monte Carlo CI: [EGP
535.0 Bn, EGP 625.2 Bn]) in cumulative budget savings over 2016–2026 and compresses
12-month Fiscal Debt-at-Risk (F -DaR0.95,12) by EGP 522.3 billion.

title: Optimal sequential EAF-BESS investment for China's steel decarbonization based on a compound real options framework
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Optimal sequential EAF-BESS investment for China's steel decarbonization based on a compound real options framework
detail.abstract: The iron and steel industry contributes over 7% of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas emissions, and the transition from conventional blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace (BF-BOF) to electric arc furnace (EAF) coupled with battery energy storage systems (BESS) is a feasible low-carbon transition pathway. Existing studies mostly assessed single technologies in isolation, failed to resolve high-dimensional uncertainty analytically, and lacked quantitative evidence on China’s provincial heterogeneity in paired EAF-BESS investment. This study developed a two-stage compound real options framework with relative-price dimensionality reduction, deriving closed-form optimal investment thresholds and timing rules, and conducted case and scenario analyses in China. Results showed standalone EAF lacked cost competitiveness under China’s current scrap, iron ore and carbon price regime. Co-located BESS proves economically viable only when valley-period green electricity discounts were sufficiently steep. Reduction of price volatility, especially for electricity, can drive larger threshold decreases than long-term drift rates. Carbon price drift showed an inverted U-shaped relationship with EAF thresholds, where moderate rises lower barriers while excessive escalation induces deferral. Analysis across 30 provinces confirms marked provincial heterogeneity. Stringent carbon constraints could significantly cut the national average waiting period for EAF and boost BESS deployment in western renewable-rich regions. Feedstock shocks accelerated EAF uptake with insignificant effect on BESS thresholds. Power market reforms elongated EAF waiting periods in high-tariff, high-volatility regions, while triggering a binary distribution of BESS investment timelines.

title: From Nudges to Nudge+: Exploring Personal Norms in Residential Energy Behaviour
affiliations: University College London, University College London, affiliation not provided to SSRN and University College London

detail.title: From Nudges to Nudge+: Exploring Personal Norms in Residential Energy Behaviour
detail.abstract: Behavioural interventions promise low-cost ways to reduce residential energy use—but how well do they work outside controlled settings? This study offers one of the first real-world comparisons of standard nudges and Nudge+ reflective prompts, using smart-meter data from ten UK student accommodation buildings. Over six weeks, we implemented personal-norm interventions and evaluated their effects through a difference-in-differences design with climatic and structural controls. Neither treatment produced statistically significant reductions in electricity use. Short exposure, purposive building allocation, limited clusters, missing engagement data, and the absence of financial incentives likely constrained responsiveness. The findings highlight the practical limits of norm-based interventions in low-incentive residential environments and clarify when behavioural tools require stronger reinforcement or complementary policy measures.

title: Occupational Green Potential: A Continuous Task-Based Measure of Green Work
affiliations: Clemson University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Virginia Tech - College of Engineering

detail.title: Occupational Green Potential: A Continuous Task-Based Measure of Green Work
detail.abstract: The green transition is changing what workers do by creating new occupations and adding green tasks to existing jobs. Yet there is no agreed-upon way to measure how green a job is. We close that gap by developing a task-based measure of occupational greenness that uses the textual content of job tasks. Using natural language processing, we represent each O*NET task description as a vector, cluster similar tasks across the economy, and assign each cluster a greenness score from O*NET's green-task labels. Aggregating these task-level scores to the occupation level yields the Occupational Green Potential index, a continuous measure for all 923 U.S. occupations that reflects how closely an occupation's tasks and underlying skills resemble green work. Comparisons with four existing measures yield consistently high correlations, indicating that the index captures the same underlying variation in occupational greenness. Our approach also detects green potential in occupations not typically classified as green, whose tasks involve environmental controls and land remediation. Because it requires only task descriptions, the index can be re-estimated for other countries and updated as the content of work evolves.

title: Attention Traps

detail.title: Attention Traps

detail.abstract: Standard models of misspecified learning take the agent's information structure as given. This paper allows that information structure to be endogenous. Rationally inattentive agents choose which statistics to process using the maintained model itself, so a misspecified model can direct attention away from evidence that would challenge it. In a dynamic asset market with capacity-constrained traders, the pseudo-true model is the spectral projection of the truth onto the affordable class where a persistent but transitory "hype" factor is capitalized at the permanent-growth multiple. The misspecification is not revealed within that class, which is just identified by the moments traders already track; it surfaces only in an over-identifying restriction whose evaluation costs capacity. The resulting threshold rises with the market's coordination motive, with the mass of traders in the low-monitoring state and, perhaps less intuitively, with fundamental uncertainty. Mispricing need not vanish as capacity grows, as additional capacity can reduce inattention without resolving misspecification. We apply the framework to the artificial-intelligence valuation debate.

title: Spatial Spillovers in Power Outage Duration: Weather Exposure and Transmission-Network Effects in Swedish Municipalities
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Spatial Spillovers in Power Outage Duration: Weather Exposure and Transmission-Network Effects in Swedish Municipalities
detail.abstract: Electricity reliability is a spatially interdependent good: the transmission network that carries power between regions also carries disturbances. We estimate the determinants of annual power outage duration, measured by the System Average Interruption Duration Index (SAIDI), for all 290 Swedish municipalities over 2018–2023, a balanced panel of 1,740 observations, using Spatial Durbin Models with municipality and year fixed effects under a spatial weights matrix built from the physical topology of the 220/400 kV transmission backbone and, for comparison, geographic contiguity. Outage duration exhibits robust positive spatial dependence: [[EQUATION]] ([[EQUATION]]), lying between 0.305 and 0.430 across both weights matrices, both fixed-effects structures and the main robustness checks; the choice of weights matrix affects which coefficients are separately identified more than the magnitude of [[EQUATION]]. The total impact of annual mean snow depth on [[EQUATION]](SAIDI) is 1.59 ([[EQUATION]]), of which 44 per cent operates through spatial spillovers, implying an equilibrium amplification of 78 per cent over the direct local effect; a one-standard-deviation increase in snow depth (0.17 m) corresponds to roughly 31 per cent longer annual outage duration. No robust within-municipality income gradient is detectable, although a marginally significant income effect emerges for unplanned outages. Municipal grid-hardening therefore generates positive externalities on grid-connected neighbours that decentralised investment decisions will not internalise.

title: Strategic Redeployment as a Dynamic Capability: A Multi-Level, Mechanism-Based Theoretical Framework

detail.title: Strategic Redeployment as a Dynamic Capability: A Multi-Level, Mechanism-Based Theoretical Framework

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NIL
declarations.funderStatement: NIL

detail.abstract: Internal talent mobility, the deliberate, strategically governed movement of employees across roles, functions, and business units is a pervasive organizational practice whose theoretical foundations remain underdeveloped. Existing scholarship treats mobility as either an efficiency mechanism within internal labour markets or a career-development tool within strategic human resource management systems. Neither framing explains how, why, and under what conditions redeployment generates sustained organizational adaptability and competitive advantage. This paper addresses that gap by developing an explicit, mechanism-based theory of strategic redeployment as a dynamic capability. Integrating insights from strategic HRM, internal labour market theory, the resource-based view, and the dynamic capabilities perspective, the study proposes that redeployment creates organizational value through three sequentially ordered mechanisms  skill reallocation, knowledge recombination, and capability reconfiguration, and that these mechanisms are jointly moderated by organizational justice, skill transferability, and managerial incentive alignment. The research further theorizes the dark-side boundary conditions under which redeployment destroys rather than creates value, generating propositions about knowledge drain in sending units, identity disruption costs, and the inverted-U relationship between mobility frequency and adaptive capacity. The paper advances a multi-level, process-based understanding of how organizations reconfigure human capital across institutional, organizational, capability, and individual levels, and offers a falsifiable set of ten theoretical propositions to guide future empirical inquiry.

detail.abstract: Public infrastructure prototypes often receive grants, institutional attention, or pitch-stage recognition, yet fail to move into everyday public-service operations. This paper examines that gap through a qualitative, practice-informed case study of a municipal streetlight monitoring prototype developed in relation to the Greater Chennai Corporation, Chennai, Tamil Nadu, under the Naam Mudhalvan Niral Thiruvizha student innovation programme. The prototype secured seed grant support and pitch-stage recognition but was not deployed in a live municipal system. Rather than treating non-deployment as simple failure, the paper uses the case to examine how recognised public infrastructure prototypes become, or fail to become, adoption-ready. Drawing on prototype records, development reflections, demonstration experience, practitioner inputs, and literature on public service operations, socio-technical systems, absorptive capacity, institutional risk, and innovation translation, the study develops an Innovation Translation and Adoption-Readiness Framework. The findings show that technical functionality is only the first layer of adoptionreadiness. For public adoption to become realistic, prototype outputs must be translated into field usability, operational workflow, managerial interpretation, institutional ownership, policy enablement, and public value. The case suggests that translation may fail through misaligned stakeholder success logics, boundary-spanning gaps, institutional risk logic, and limited absorptive capacity. For Atmanirbhar Bharat-oriented innovation policy, the study argues that self-reliance requires more than domestic prototype creation; it requires institutional pathways through which locally developed technologies can be tested, adapted, maintained, governed, and absorbed into public-service systems.

detail.abstract: Scholarly optimism over the global proliferation of Rights of Nature legislation systematically overlooks how legal grammar functionally grants or withholds these rights. This paper introduces "grammatical trusteeship", a structural semiotic condition where human agents serve as indispensable grammatical mediators of non-human personhood, reinstating anthropocentric ontology syntactically even when legislative intent nominally dismantles it in policy. Grounded in Jane Bennett's Vibrant Matter, this study applies a corpus-driven Systemic Functional Linguistic (SFL) transitivity analysis to 147 clauses from the Te Awa Tupua (Whanganui River Claims Settlement) Act 2017, cataloguing Material, Mental, Relational, and Verbal processes alongside the river's participant roles. Findings reveal Te Awa Tupua is positioned as Goal, Phenomenon, or Carrier in 76.2% of clauses, but as Actor or Senser in only 8.8%. This asymmetry constitutes a textual regime conditioning the river's legal personhood upon continuous human activation, narration, and representation. Exposing the disjuncture between the Act's decolonial ontological ambitions and colonial grammatical architecture, this paper argues that post-anthropocentric law requires a grammatical reorientation in encoding ecological agency, not merely new legislative intent. The study contributes a replicable analytical methodology to Environmental Humanities and intervenes in debates on the performative efficacy of Rights of Nature frameworks.

detail.abstract: While scholarship on South Asian climate fiction has begun to engage questions of voice and representation, it has done so in scattered and largely unsystematic ways, without developing a sustained analytical framework for identifying how the speech of climate-displaced communities is encoded, mediated, or silenced in the formal strategies of the text. This essay addresses that gap through the concept of ecosubalternity, a structural position produced at the intersection of ecological dispossession and representational mediation. Extending Spivak's subaltern theory into the context of climate displacement, the essay operationalizes eco-subalternity as an analytical method with identification criteria and formal features. Through close readings of three Amitav Ghosh novels, The Hungry Tide (2005), Gun Island (2019), and The Living Mountain (2022), the essay argues that Ghosh's fiction does not merely represent eco-subaltern silencing but enacts it through focalization, narrative mediation, and genre. Drawing on postcolonial ecocriticism, environmental justice, and subaltern theory, the essay traces how the formal strategies of these novels produce the eco-subaltern condition, with particular attention to the geopolitics of climate displacement in Bangladesh.

detail.abstract: The economic consequences of party membership may reach people outside members’ house holds. Using the China Education Panel Survey, I exploit quasi-random assignment of stu dents to classrooms and find that exposure to CPC-parent peer share leads to increases in academic performance and cognitive ability. The results remain sound after adjusting for peer ability, friendship networks, and parental socioeconomic advantage. No significant spillover arise from exposure to peers whose parents belong to China’s democratic par ties. The accompanying changes in homework effort, cooperative behavior, and parental engagement suggest several channels, while non-cognitive outcomes show no detectable de terioration.

title: Liquidity without Liquidation: Tax-efficient Withdrawals from Tax-aware Strategies
affiliations: AQR Capital Management, LLC, AQR Capital Management, LLC, AQR Capital Management, LLC and AQR Capital Management, LLC

declarations.declarationOfInterest: All authors are employees of AQR Capital Management.

detail.abstract: We examine whether tax-aware equity strategies can provide meaningful liquidity without full liquidation or material impairment of their investment objectives. We find that substantial capital can be withdrawn while preserving tracking error, leverage, and pre-tax information ratios. Tax-efficient withdrawal capacity is generally greater for long-short strategies than for direct indexing and increases with the strategy’s tracking error and leverage. An optimized withdrawal process can adapt withdrawal amounts to the strategy’s capacity to offset withdrawal-related realized gains with realized losses, given the strategy’s age and the prevailing market environment. Partial withdrawals can provide substantial tax-efficient liquidity while preserving the economic characteristics of the remaining portfolio and, in some scenarios, its ability to continue realizing net capital losses. Liquidity without liquidation is therefore an important dimension of the flexibility of tax-aware long-short investing.

detail.abstract: We document strong co-movement in firm-level idiosyncratic skewness. We show that the common component in idiosyncratic skewness (CIS) is a powerful non-linear predictor of market returns, in and out of sample; it is not subsumed by existing predictors, and adds economic value for mean-variance investors after transactions costs. Results are robust across observation frequencies and evaluation periods. Within a standard valuation framework, CIS forecasts through the discount rate channel. Using a simple stochastic discount factor formulation, we infer that the predictability evidence is consistent with a state-dependent SDF. Further analysis suggests that the state-dependence may originate from investor recency bias induced by fading memory, offering a new channel to illustrate the impact of experience-based learning on asset prices.

detail.title: Disentangling Tax Avoidance and Effective Tax Planning: Implications for Firm Risk

detail.abstract: Theory predicts that tax aggressiveness raises firm risk because aggressive tax choices generate cash savings today at the cost of a contingent future tax liability. The empirical evidence, however, is either null or contradictory. A central challenge is that the cash effective tax rate conflates productive tax planning with tax aggressiveness. To isolate tax aggressiveness, we decompose the cash effective tax rate against the effective tax planning measure of Schwab, Stomberg, and Williams (2022). Consistent with theory, we find robust evidence that tax aggressiveness increases firm risk. Moreover, the effect appears in the systematic as well as the idiosyncratic component of return volatility, so the risk tax aggressiveness creates is not confined to firm-specific noise. Corroborating evidence shows that our measure also predicts higher future unrecognized tax benefit balances, tax settlements, and financial distress. The decomposition resolves the empirical puzzle in favor of theory.

detail.abstract: Inequality of opportunity (IOp) measures the extent to which income inequality is driven by circumstances-factors beyond an individual's control-rather than effort. Drawing the boundary between circumstances and effort requires a normative criterion; in practice, most empirical studies determine it by data availability or researcher judgment. I use the age of majority-which in the US context I take to be 18-as the circumstance cutoff: all measurable pre-18 attributes of an individual's life constitute circumstances beyond her control. I further structure circumstance sets around developmental milestones motivated by the technology of skill formation, which predicts that early skill gaps persist and compound across childhood stages. Using PSID data on cohorts born 1978-1983, I estimate IOp in adult labor income using OLS and four machine learning methods. MLD estimates indicate that approximately 29-30 percent of total income inequality is attributable to observed pre-18 circumstances; the share attributable to circumstances measured through age five is disproportionately large, accounting for over four-fifths of the full pre-18 estimate. The evidence points to the developmental structure of the circumstance sets as consequential for IOp measurement.

detail.abstract: Workforce aging generally decreases labor mobility and bargaining strength even when older workers remain valuable hires, because they search less and are harder to poach. For example, U.S. industry-level evidence shows that aging reduces employer-to-employer (EE) flows, job creation, labor share, and firm's vacancy creation, while individual-level evidence shows that wage gains from EE flows decline with age. In a general-equilibrium life-cycle search model with on-the-job search and endogenous bargaining, aging explains half the 1995-2015 decline in labor share. The shift in workforce composition toward older workers accounts for 40% of this decline, while the balance reflects the resulting decline in vacancy creation responses by firms. Vacancy subsidies and moderate unemployment-benefit cuts substantially restore the labor share.

detail.abstract: We estimate a two-state Gaussian-mixture hidden Markov model for daily Brent crude, gold, silver, and natural gas futures in which transition probabilities depend on lagged geopolitical risk (GPR). Using the threat and act components of the daily GPR index, we find that realised geopolitical acts are associated with greater stress-regime persistence: a one-standard-deviation increase in act elevation is associated with roughly 45 to 51 percent higher odds of remaining stressed. Threat effects are concentrated on entry from calm but are weaker and not robust to the full control set. Nested likelihoodratio tests reject dropping the geopolitical block from the transition kernel. The results indicate that the geopolitical association is strongest through regime duration rather than through a simple level effect on volatility.

detail.abstract:
Goal setting is a widely used practice for performance improvement; however, recent studies and numerous corporate scandals have highlighted the dark side of goal setting, whereby goals can induce unethical behavior. Although previous studies have shown that participation in goal setting may encourage ethical behavior, they have not explored the simultaneous effects of participation in goal setting on both performance and reporting behavior. This study examines the simultaneous impact of participation in goal setting on both performance and unethical behavior, particularly focusing on the unintended consequences of participation in goal setting and the role of employees’ goal-related sense of responsibility as a psychological mechanism.
An economic experiment (N = 378) was conducted to examine these simultaneous effects. We compared participants’ performance and reporting behavior between conditions with and without participation in goal setting. Our experimental results show that participation in goal setting does not have a direct effect on task performance but indirectly improves task performance through a sense of responsibility. With respect to reporting behavior, we focus on participants who fail to meet their goals. Among these participants, unethical reporting behavior is more prevalent with participation in goal setting than without it; however, a stronger sense of responsibility mitigates this tendency, reducing the prevalence of such behavior. This study makes academic and practical contributions by highlighting the simultaneous impact of participation in goal setting on performance and misreporting and by identifying sense of responsibility as a key psychological mechanism when goals are not achieved.

title: Do Central Bank Statements Forecast Policy? A Calibration-Centred Framework with Evidence from the Bank of Korea

detail.abstract: We ask whether central-bank policy statements predict future committee rate decisions beyond macroeconomic fundamentals. We develop a framework for evaluating and repairing text-augmented probability forecasts: a joint multi-horizon rationality test with simulation-based finite-sample properties, a decomposition-guided recalibration procedure, and a directional-and-sectional text measure certified against a real-time look-ahead audit. Using the Bank of Korea Monetary Policy Board, we report two findings. First, undirected language-change measures add no predictive value alone, but once separated by direction (hawkish-dovish tone) and section (the paragraph on global conditions), a text signal survives at every horizon. Second, forecast difficulty is non-monotone in horizon, and skill concentrates in crisis episodes. Negative skill in raw machine-learning forecasts reflects miscalibration, not absent signal: the decomposition predicts which forecasts recalibration will repair. For committee communication, the binding question is calibration, not discrimination, and the framework transfers to any committee-type decision with dated communication and a decision record.

title: The Synthetic Economy: Can Small Language Models Generate Research-grade Economic Microdata?

detail.title: The Synthetic Economy: Can Small Language Models Generate Research-grade Economic Microdata?

detail.abstract: Synthetic microdata are increasingly proposed as a privacy-preserving substitute for confidential survey data, yet most generative approaches require substantial compute and access to real training records. We investigate whether small, low-cost language models—Ling 3.0 Flash, DeepSeek V4 Flash, Solar Pro 4, and Qwen 3.7 Flash, priced at under $0.03 each—can generate research-grade synthetic economic microdata from a text prompt alone, with no fine-tuning and no access to real records. Using public aggregated statistics from the U.S. Current Population Survey as ground truth, we generate 800 synthetic household records per model per condition (2,400 per model) across three prompt conditions (minimal, structural, priors) and evaluate them along four dimensions: statistical fidelity, downstream econometric utility, internal consistency, and diversity. We find that the models reproduce conditional economic structure remarkably well—education–income gradients within 5.1–11.6% mean absolute relative error, Mincer wage regressions with R² = 0.87–0.90, and high internal consistency between employment, hours, and income for most models—but systematically distort unconditional marginals, mis-calibrating the employment rate (61.6–82.6% vs. 63% reference, overstated for three of four models) and overstating the share of advanced degrees. A three-condition prompt ablation isolates the contribution of the models' latent economic knowledge from explicit priors supplied in the prompt, revealing that explicit priors substantially improve income fidelity (MARE reduction of 36–77%) while having limited effect on econometric utility (R² changes < 0.04). Compared with two non-LLM baselines (uniform and marginal sampling), the LLMs' unique value lies in their joint structure (R² ≥ 0.86), not their marginals—a marginal sampler achieves MARE of 4.0% but R² of only 0.23. We then demonstrate that the paper's recommended remedy works: a single poststratification step that reweights records to match the public education distribution drives the education-distribution total variation distance to zero while leaving the Mincer R² essentially unchanged (within ±0.03), confirming that the LLMs' joint structure survives marginal calibration. Cross-seed analysis demonstrates high reproducibility (coefficient of variation < 3.4% for R²), and Wasserstein-distance analysis reveals that the synthetic income distributions are within 15–21% of the reference in normalized earth-mover distance. Our results establish that small language models can serve as cheap, zero-shot generators of structurally coherent economic microdata, and that a lightweight, fully public calibration step renders them fit for research use—at a total cost of under $0.10.

title: The Cost of Fairness in Electricity Markets
affiliations: University of Mannheim

detail.title: The Cost of Fairness in Electricity Markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: ZEW – Centre for European Economic Research Discussion Paper No. 26-040

detail.abstract: European policymakers argue that bidding zones with uniform prices ensure fairness in electricity markets. Since the outcome of such a fair spot market is often infeasible due to network constraints, a second stage is needed: the redispatch. I establish a mechanism design result showing that even a minimal fairness restriction on the first stage strictly increases procurement costs for asymmetric dispatches. In detail, I analyze a market-based redispatch mechanism where inc-dec gaming creates arbitrage profits for those producers that benefit the network the least. These results identify a general cost of fairness in sequential markets and question uniform bidding zones in electricity markets.

title: The New Keynesian Term Structure of Interest Rates
affiliations: Universität Hamburg, Department of Economics

detail.title: The New Keynesian Term Structure of Interest Rates

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of the nominal term structure of interest rates in the New Keynesian model with Calvo pricing and recursive preferences. The central mechanism is endogenous inflation: unlike models with exogenous inflation, where inflation is separated from real allocations, sticky prices make inflation jointly determined with real allocations, monetary policy, and the stochastic discount factor. We classify structural shocks as "good" or "bad" according to their contributions to nominal bond risk and show that sticky prices can alter or even reverse bond exposures relative to the flexible-price benchmark. Real and nominal long-run risks each lower the nominal term premium in isolation, whereas negative dependence between them can overturn these effects and generate a positive premium. Preference shocks instead generate sizeable positive term premia, while convexity effects can imply negative expectations-based measures despite positive yield-based term premia. We solve the equilibrium globally and use nonlinear Feynman-Kac equations to price bonds and trace bond risk premia to structural shocks.

detail.abstract: A recent NBER working paper (Domínguez-Iino, Elliott and Hsiao, "Critical Minerals, Geopolitics, and the Green Transition", NBER WP 35654, August 2026) provides the first structural quantification of how the geographic concentration of lithium, nickel and cobalt supply shapes prices, policy spillovers and green technology adoption worldwide. This policy note summarises the paper's main findings and reads them against the European regulatory response, the Critical Raw Materials Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1252) and its Italian implementation (Decree-Law 84/2024, converted into Law 115/2024). Three implications follow for EU industrial policy: diversification priorities should be set on the joint mineral structure of battery chemistries rather than mineral by mineral; the 2030 CRMA benchmarks address the right margins but their bite depends on the strategic-projects pipeline; and firm-level exposure to critical mineral risk should be treated as an investment variable, with long-term contracts, supplier diversification and end-of-life recovery as the operational levers.

title: Dynamic Merger Control after Draghi: A Critical Appreciation of the Oxera Study on the Dynamic Effects of Mergers

detail.abstract: The European Commission's two-volume Economic Study on the Dynamic Effects of Mergers, prepared by Oxera with Professors Otto Toivanen, Yassine Lefouili and Leonardo Madio, is an ambitious and valuable contribution to the modernisation of EU merger control. It synthesises an unusually wide literature and gives dynamic harms and benefits a common language based on expected consumer welfare. I am particularly grateful for its careful and generous engagement with my recent work on merger efficiencies. My central criticism, however, is that the Study is more successful as a map of mechanisms than as a decision rule. Its operative framework excludes the ex ante effects of merger policy; applies merger specificity through a potentially inconsistent counterfactual; states evidentiary symmetry more clearly than it implements it; and treats balancing and remedies too lightly for the weight they must bear. It is also dynamic mainly on the expansion margin. Zombies, flailing divisions, declining industries, structural excess capacity, orderly restructuring and resilience remain peripheral. In light of the Draghi Report, this matters: Europe's productivity challenge concerns diffusion, scaling and resource reallocation as well as invention. The revised Merger Guidelines should use a single, probability-weighted counterfactual for harms and benefits, integrate efficiencies into the competitive assessment, recognise contraction and reallocation mergers, treat uncertainty symmetrically, and provide a disciplined framework for investment remedies. That would not make merger control permissive. It would make it neutral, economically complete and more faithful to the SIEC test.

title: Public Credit and the Financial Cycle
affiliations: Princeton University

detail.title: Public Credit and the Financial Cycle

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Bank of France and Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations

detail.abstract: This paper studies lending by state-led institutions (i.e., public credit). Using a comprehensive database covering thirteen countries since 1950, we document that public credit shifts from strongly procyclical relative to private credit to increasingly countercyclical as countries liberalize their financial systems. After liberalization, public credit compensates on average 10% of private credit contractions and moderates the output cost of private credit cycles. We show that, before liberalization, credit controls jointly drove public and private credit cycles. Liberalization removes these controls while making private credit cycles more damaging, prompting the state to turn public credit into a macroprudential tool.

title: Money, Lobbying, and Political Power

detail.title: Money, Lobbying, and Political Power

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any individual or organization that influenced this study. This is independent, self-directed research conducted without external sponsorship.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author without financial support from any institution, organization, or grant.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a framework for evaluating how economic resources convert into political power in the United States, distinguishing legitimate political participation from unequal influence and corruption using a stage model — money converts into capacity, visibility, access, attention, and influence before it can plausibly constitute corruption. Drawing on Federal Election Commission data, randomized and quasi-experimental studies, and current litigation including the June 2026 National Republican Senatorial Committee v. FEC decision, the paper finds that campaign spending predicts electoral success without reliably causing it, while donor status causally affects access to congressional offices and political relationships carry measurable market value independent of any legislative vote. Post-2010 natural experiments exploiting Citizens United's invalidation of state corporate-spending bans produce mixed evidence: some studies find meaningful state-house electoral effects and movement toward corporate-preferred policy, while others find no significant effect on state tax or environmental policy. That evidence undermines the categorical claim that independent corporate election spending is constitutionally immune from regulation, without supporting the opposite claim that such spending routinely purchases elections or legislation. The paper further documents that the Federal Election Commission has lacked the quorum necessary for consequential enforcement since May 2025, showing that formal campaign-finance rules can persist even as enforcement capacity is impaired. The paper's central argument is that campaign-finance reform should be evaluated by the same evidentiary and symmetry standards applied throughout the analysis: any proposed restriction or restored regulatory authority must be tested against how it would function if administered by the political faction the reader trusts least.

title: The Long Term Effects of School Prayer
affiliations: University of Cambridge,  and University of Cambridge

detail.title: The Long Term Effects of School Prayer

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: This paper studies whether school prayer and Bible reading affect adult beliefs and behavior. We exploit the U.S. Supreme Court’s early-1960s school-prayer decisions, which removed these practices only from states where they were still legal. Linking this state-by-cohort variation to adult outcomes in the General Social Survey, we estimate the long-run effects of removing school prayer on religiosity, family formation, labor-market outcomes, gender attitudes, and social views. The abolition of school prayer lowers adult religiosity; reduces marriage and fertility; increases employment; and shifts gender and selected social attitudes in a less traditional direction. The employment effect is driven by women, and may operate partly through decreased full-time homemaking and less traditional gender roles. A decomposition indicates that school prayer bans explain more than half the decline in American religious attendance, and roughly one quarter of the decline in fertility and rise in female labor force participation. The findings show that even brief daily devotional practices in childhood can shape adult beliefs, family life, and economic behavior.

title: Naive Diversification and the Opportunity Set: Long-Only Equity Factor Indices

detail.title: Naive Diversification and the Opportunity Set: Long-Only Equity Factor Indices

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that could have influenced this study. detail.abstract:
For twenty years the argument over whether portfolio optimization beats equal weighting has gone unresolved. We show that both sides are right on their own data. What divides them is the menu of assets on offer.


On the menu a real equity investor can reach, twenty-eight long-only regional factor indices, no optimization rule beats equal weighting by a margin this much data can settle. We race seventeen rules over 210 months out of sample, testing every comparison for significance. The optimizers are not at fault: these indices are close to being the same bet. Long-only factor tilts within a region move almost in lockstep, so the whole menu carries barely more independent risk than one index, and no weighting scheme can manufacture diversification the menu does not contain. Three asset classes, Treasuries, gold and cash, add more of it than all twenty-eight equity indices combined.


For a retail investor, widening the menu is the only move with measurable evidence.

title: Exchange Controls and The Segmentation of International Currency Markets
affiliations: Princeton University

detail.title: Exchange Controls and The Segmentation of International Currency Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: Thanks are also due to the Bank of France, the Louis Bachelier Institute, and Natixis for their generous financial support.

detail.abstract: This article relies on a new hand-collected dataset of end-of-month exchange rates quoted in 17 national financial centers (i.e., countries) over the 1900-1999 period. By measuring deviations from the Law of One Price in international currency markets, this article puts forward two contributions. First, I provide a new long-run measure of financial integration. I reveal that currency markets were well integrated except during the Bretton Woods period when foreign exchange controls were widespread. I find that controls were also used, to a much moderate extent, during the interwar. My second contribution is to measure currency market integration at the currency level. I show that, during the Bretton Woods period, virtually all countries in my sample maintained controls against the US and Canadian Dollars. These controls split the world into two independent currency zones: a Dollar zone (including the US and Canada) and a non-Dollar zone (including Western Europe, Japan and Australia). Within each zone, the market for non-Dollar zone currencies was integrated. The two zones progressively merged starting in the early 1960s as exchange controls were abandoned.

title: Selection Before Effect: Yield-Curve Alignment and Japanese Foreign-Exchange Intervention

detail.title: Selection Before Effect: Yield-Curve Alignment and Japanese Foreign-Exchange Intervention

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available financial and policy data and involves no human participants, animals, personal data, or interventions. Ethics approval and informed consent were therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Japanese foreign-exchange intervention is selected in response to market stress, clustered across days, and conducted under monetary regimes that differ sharply in their policy signals. These features make average effectiveness difficult to identify and leave open a narrower question: does the market state that precedes intervention condition the persistence of the intended exchange-rate movement? Using the Ministry of Finance daily intervention record from 1991 through 2024, daily USD/JPY, Japanese and U.S. two-year yields, and strictly lagged controls, this paper constructs 69 intervention episodes and a direction-signed measure of pre-intervention yield-curve alignment. The empirical design separates policy selection, first-day intensity and continuation, and post-intervention persistence. A conditional-logit reaction function across 61 direction-matched stress risk sets finds no association between alignment and intervention entry (bootstrap p = 0.577). Conditional on intervention, a one-standard-deviation increase in alignment is associated with a 25.2% larger first-day amount and lower odds of continuation, although the two-test Holm family does not reject. Intended-direction responses rise with alignment by 0.41, 0.60, and 0.83 percentage points at 5, 10, and 20 days. Raw wild-bootstrap p-values are near conventional thresholds, but the frozen three-horizon family does not reject (Holm p = 0.109). The 2026 holdout is pre-misaligned and displays substantial decay. The evidence supports a state-dependent persistence association, not causal effectiveness: selection precedes effect, and common support determines what can be claimed.

title:
Ontological Shift of Money

From Metal to Virtual and the Collapse of the Being-Nonbeing Concept

detail.title:
Ontological Shift of Money

From Metal to Virtual and the Collapse of the Being-Nonbeing Concept

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: This research examines the transformation of currency from physical commodity toward virtual representation and its implications for the three classical pillars of trade: transfer of rights (*right*), payment (*payment*), and delivery of goods (*delivery*). Using a historical- critical and juridical-sociological approach, this paper finds that the abstraction of money has severed the direct connection between intrinsic value and nominal value. This transformation brings remarkable economic efficiency, yet simultaneously creates new vulnerabilities: legal uncertainty of ownership, concentration of power in ledger managers, and social alienation. The era of fiat and virtual money marks a phase where the concepts of being and nonbeing are no longer relevant, because ownership is no longer determined by physical possession, but rather by records in centralized databases.

title: Beyond Related Rights for Deepfakes: Strict Retention of Control, With Fair Remuneration for Limited Exploitation Desire? Empirical Insights from Dutch Music Creators

detail.title: Beyond Related Rights for Deepfakes: Strict Retention of Control, With Fair Remuneration for Limited Exploitation Desire? Empirical Insights from Dutch Music Creators

declarations.funderStatement: Parts of this research build on the project "Fair Remuneration in Times of Generative AI" which the University of Amsterdam funded as part of its Responsible Digital Transformations community.

detail.abstract: The growing opportunities and risks associated with deepfake technology have led to legislative proposals following a copyright and related rights approach in countries including the Netherlands and Denmark. First, this article compares the (private member's) bills from both countries. The Dutch approach, which involves a related 'deepfake right' for everyone, is particularly inappropriate, not least given the risks of such a proprietary regime and the adequate existing legal framework for non-artists. Second, based on the results of a recent survey among music creators in the Dutch music sector, the analysis in this article demonstrates that the related rights approach is equally unsuitable for performing artists specifically. Third, alternative solutions are set out to address the legal challenges facing the creative sector with regard to consent and fair remuneration for the use of deepfakes, such as the risk of signing away rights. In particular, residual remuneration rights and unfair contract terms regulation are conceptualised for this context.

title: Strategic Interaction by Boundedly Rational Players: Structure, Selection, and Computation of Exponential Satisficing Equilibria
affiliations: Tilburg University and Nanjing University

detail.title: Strategic Interaction by Boundedly Rational Players: Structure, Selection, and Computation of Exponential Satisficing Equilibria

declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable.

detail.abstract: We study strategic interaction by boundedly rational players and introduce an algorithm to compute exponential satisficing equilibria that is effective for an open set of normal-form games of full Lebesgue measure. To do so, we analyze the structure of the cognitive tracing procedure, which is used to select an exponential satisficing equilibrium for each value of the preference resolution parameter. As a by-product, we find that there is generically an odd number of such equilibria. To develop a differentiable homotopy algorithm, we design new tools of variable transformations to deal with the non-differentiabilities inherent in the rank-dependency of exponential satisficing. We apply the algorithm to a model of heterogeneous Bertrand competition as well as to a connections model of network formation.

title: The Limits of Delta Hedging: Transaction-Cost Thresholds and Basis Risk in Futures-Hedged Autocallable Notes

detail.title: The Limits of Delta Hedging: Transaction-Cost Thresholds and Basis Risk in Futures-Hedged Autocallable Notes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study uses publicly available financial market data and involves no human participants, patient data, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Dealers of spot-linked autocallable notes (“snowballs”) hedge principally with stock-index futures whose basis is stochastic. This paper quantifies when increasing the delta-rebalancing frequency stops being economically optimal, and how the futures basis moves that threshold. We embed a mean-reverting annualized basis state in the futures price, prove that the single-futures delta hedge inherits a risk floor that faster rebalancing cannot remove, and decompose that floor into three channels: discrete barrier monitoring, the level of the basis (a path-dependent carry whose dispersion is frequency-insensitive and—we show—invariant to the hedge’s futures-maturity mix), and basis volatility, which a calendar-spread hedge can span in the model only by multiplying gross turnover. With a single proportional cost rate c, the risk–cost objective is affine in c, so the optimal interval is a lower envelope of lines and switches at break-even thresholds c ∗ that we estimate by simulation calibrated to CSI 500 index and IC futures data from April 2015 to August 2026, including the January–February 2024 knock-in episode (term-structure basis state reaching −16% annualized; single-contract prints below −40%). At the calibrated normal regime, refining from daily into the sub-hour range is cheap risk reduction (break-even one-way costs of 0.9–2.7 bp, above CFFEX’s ∼0.23 bp open/close fee), the 30-to-15-minute step breaks even at the fee itself (0.23 bp, CI [0.07, 0.39]), and no refinement below 15 minutes pays at any positive cost rate; once same-day closes attract the ∼2.3 bp intraday-close fee, the optimal interval retreats to about two hours. Raising basis volatility from its median to its 90th percentile compresses the sub-hourly thresholds by a quarter, and at extreme-but-observed volatility even the daily-to-two-hour step barely pays; yet persistence matters as much as amplitude—the violent but fast-reverting January 2024 episode itself left thresholds slightly wider than normal. On realized paths, replaying 24 year-long episodes through 2023–2025 at minute frequency, episode-level dispersion is flat across intervals while turnover rises ninefold—the frequency-insensitive floor in the data itself. A ten-million path–day panel regression shows basis instability is disproportionately costly near the knock-in barrier. The framework turns a structural model into an operating rule for hedging desks and clarifies how exchange fee policy implicitly caps economic hedging frequency. Keywords: aut

title: Ownership or Licence? Reassessing The Doctrine of Copyright Exhaustion for Digital Works Under Indian Copyright Law

detail.title: Ownership or Licence? Reassessing The Doctrine of Copyright Exhaustion for Digital Works Under Indian Copyright Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no personal or financial relationships with any individuals or organizations that could have influenced, or could be perceived to have influenced, the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The doctrine of exhaustion, also known as the first sale doctrine, states that when a lawful copy of a copyrighted item is sold, the copyright holder no longer has control over how that particular copy is distributed. Historically conceived for tangible property, the doctrine presupposes the existence of a single, identifiable material object-a "copy" in the physical sense-whose boundaries define the scope of what has been sold. This paper argues that this presupposition continues to hold for physical copies of video games, where a disc or cartridge functions as such a discrete object capable of outright sale and transfer, but breaks down for video games purchased through digital storefronts such as Steam or Epic Games. Drawing on the ontological distinction between a physical copy as a "token," capable of only one instantiation, and a digital copy as a "type," capable of indefinite instantiation whose scope is defined not by physical boundaries but by the terms of the license under which it is released, this paper contends that digital game transactions structurally resist the very premise on which exhaustion operates: there is no fixed material object corresponding to the physical copy whose transfer traditionally gives rise to exhaustion, and the consumer's rights are instead often structured through a licence whose scope the rights holder defines. Drawing further on the doctrinal position under the Indian Copyright Act, 1957, the paper examines the resulting divergence in how Indian copyright law treats functionally identical consumer transactions-the purchase of a video game-based solely on the mode of delivery. It concludes by evaluating whether India's copyright framework should reassess the exhaustion doctrine to address this physical-digital divide, or whether the license-based model for digital works is doctrinally justified.

title: How Climate-induced Resource Competition could Trigger Localized Conflict that Reverses Decades of Peacebuilding in Fragile States

detail.title: How Climate-induced Resource Competition could Trigger Localized Conflict that Reverses Decades of Peacebuilding in Fragile States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no personal or financial relationships that could have influenced the research. All analysis was conducted independently using publicly available datasets (ACLED, Pacific Institute, ND‑GAIN, WRI, UNEP).
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study synthesizes secondary data from peer‑reviewed sources and multilateral datasets; no human participants were involved, so formal ethics approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was self‑funded through institutional support from H Heuristics and independent consulting income. No external grants or sponsorships were received.

detail.abstract:
Climate change is already functioning as a measurable threat multiplier in fragile states, intensifying pastoral–agricultural clashes, sharpening transboundary water disputes, and accelerating institutional breakdown in regions where peacebuilding gains were hard‑won and structurally fragile. As the report states, “climate change is not a distant threat… it is an active, measurable multiplier of the pressures that already push pastoralists against farmers, downstream states against upstream dam‑builders” .

Across Nigeria’s Middle Belt, shifting rainfall, desertification, and conflict‑driven displacement have compressed grazing and planting seasons, producing nearly 5,500 deaths across 2,200 incidents since 2023 . In Kenya’s Rift Valley, drought‑driven livestock collapse has pushed pastoralists toward cattle‑rustling and armed violence. These dynamics illustrate a core mechanism: climate variability disrupts the seasonal logic of transhumance, overwhelming customary institutions that historically mediated land‑use friction.

Transboundary water stress shows a parallel pattern. Water‑related conflict events rose from 21 in 2010 to 420 in 2024—a twenty‑fold increase . Modeling published in Nature Communications projects that 35–41% of the world’s transboundary basins could face scarcity‑driven conflict risk by 2041–2050 absent new cooperation mechanisms. Yet cooperative water‑sharing arrangements can cut that risk to under 10%, a three‑quarters reduction .

The Lake Chad Basin demonstrates how these pressures converge: a 95% collapse in lake surface area since the 1960s has intensified competition among fishing, farming, and herding communities, while extremist groups exploit livelihood collapse for recruitment. As the report notes, “each element of the loop reinforces the next: environmental collapse reduces livelihood options… creating an opening that armed groups exploit” .

The report’s most consequential finding is that adaptation investment is conflict prevention. Analysis of 320 adaptation projects shows returns exceeding 10:1, with early‑warning systems and water infrastructure generating even higher dividends . Basin‑level cooperation delivers the strongest conflict‑risk reduction identified in the literature. Yet adaptation finance remains profoundly insufficient: $26 billion in annual flows against a $310–365 billion need, a twelve‑to‑fourteen‑fold shortfall .

The report concludes that climate‑resource shocks are degrading the very institutions peacebuilding programs rely on—customary land councils, grazing agreements, basin commissions—and that closing the adaptation finance gap in fragile states is not adjacent to peacebuilding; it is peacebuilding.

affiliations: Graduate School of Economics, Sophia University

detail.title: Global Safety Valves: Diaspora Networks and the Allocation of Crisis Migration

detail.abstract: Macro-financial crises increase pressure to leave, but they do not determine which destinations are accessible. This paper studies how predetermined diaspora networks allocate crisis migration, combining annual bilateral flows for 231 countries and territories over 1990-2023 with crisis onsets from the Global Macro Database. PPML models with dyad, origin-year, and destination-year fixed effects compare destinations within the same origin-year while absorbing destination-year conditions. During crisis windows, flows shift toward destinations holding larger shares of the origin's 1990 diaspora; the baseline interaction is 0.477 (standard error 0.081). A P90 positive-network corridor receives 3.40 percent more crisis-window flow than a zero-share corridor. The result is stable across crisis types, timing windows, network definitions, inference choices, and measurement audits, and it is replicated using Eurostat administrative inflows. Formal interactions are larger without colonial or linguistic ties and are not materially changed by EU free movement. Under the maintained conditional parallel-routing assumption, historical diaspora corridors operate as mobility infrastructure during macro-financial distress.

title:
Whose Water Body is this?
Decentralization, Administrative Distance, and Institutional Trust in the Governance of Non-River Water Bodies in Telangana, India

detail.title:
Whose Water Body is this?
Decentralization, Administrative Distance, and Institutional Trust in the Governance of Non-River Water Bodies in Telangana, India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There are none whatsover.
declarations.funderStatement: I have funded it myself, moreover it is secondary research and not primary research.

detail.abstract: Decentralization is widely assumed to bring governance closer to citizens, yet a growing body of scholarship shows this assumption does not always hold: reallocating authority across levels of government can just as easily widen the psychological and administrative distance between the state and the people it governs (Murali, 2026). This paper examines that dynamic through the case of non-river water bodies (locally called "cheruvu" or "kunta") in Sangareddy district, Telangana, India, where ownership is assigned by a simple rule: water bodies with a command area of 100 acres or less belong to the local Gram Panchayat, while larger ones fall under state authority. Drawing on the author's earlier archival and documentary research into this governance structure, the paper reinterprets the findings through the lens of institutional trust, the tradition of scholarship popularized by Fukuyama (1995), and recently revisited through performance-based (Murtin et al., 2026) and measurement-focused (Estadieu et al., 2025) frameworks. It argues that Telangana's acreage-based ownership rule, combined with the informal but powerful hierarchy running from state irrigation authorities down to Gram Panchayats, and further complicated by caste and gender dynamics within village-level decision-making, produces a distinct and under-studied mechanism of trust erosion, one rooted in a bright-line legal rule rather than, as in Murali's Tamil Nadu case, scheme implementation failure. The paper closes by proposing this comparison as the basis for a mixed-methods doctoral research agenda that would test these mechanisms empirically across multiple districts.

detail.abstract: We propose GeoSkew, a new measure of global geopolitical risk asymmetry constructed from the cross-sectional skewness of global geopolitical risk across 44 countries and regions. GeoSkew predicts commodity futures returns both in-and out-of-sample, and its predictive power remains robust after controlling for business-cycle, macroeconomic, and uncertainty indicators, as well as competing measures of geopolitical risk. Portfolio analysis shows that GeoSkew generates economically significant gains for mean-variance investors. We further show that elevated GeoSkew predicts lower GDPat-Risk quantiles and higher future global supply chain pressures. Taken together, our findings highlight the importance of crosscountry asymmetry in geopolitical risk for commodity pricing.

title: Future Mobility: Electric, Autonomous, Connected, Shared -How Investors Can Take Part in the Remaking of Transport

detail.title: Future Mobility: Electric, Autonomous, Connected, Shared -How Investors Can Take Part in the Remaking of Transport

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal or financial relationship influnced this study
declarations.funderStatement: No funder

detail.abstract: Transport is undergoing its greatest transformation since the horse carriage gave way to the motor car: in 2025 one in four new cars sold worldwide was electric, driverless taxis complete roughly half a million paid rides a week in American metropolitan areas, and software is turning the vehicle from a product of mechanical craftsmanship into a computer on wheels. This paper — the first of five devoted to the great megatrends — orders the field of future mobility along its five arenas: decarbonisation and alternative drive systems, autonomous driving, connectivity, shared mobility, and the urban transformation including micromobility. The paper examines market positions and timetables: battery prices have fallen by more than 90 per cent since 2010 (2025: USD 108 per kilowatt-hour), five-minute charging is series production reality in China, driverless lorries have been running in Texas since 2025, and the robotaxi market could grow to more than USD 400 billion by 2035 — while the privately owned Level 4 car is, by broad agreement, unlikely before the 2030s and will dominate the vehicle fleet only decades later. For investors, the paper names listed companies along the entire value chain — large and mid caps exclusively — with their business ideas and trading venues, and identifies two ETFs that pass the selection checklist developed in the text. The investment conclusion cuts both ways: the megatrend is real, but its returns are unevenly distributed and have historically flowed to the suppliers of scarce key technology rather than to the car brands. Thematic ETFs launched near peak sentiment have lost roughly 30 per cent in risk-adjusted terms over their first five years. Whoever wants to take part therefore diversifies across the value chain, weights platform and technology leaders above hopeful newcomers, avoids naming small specialists, and measures success in decades, not quarters.

title: Associate Commissioners
affiliations: Wayne State University Law School and

detail.title: Associate Commissioners

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Some interviewees were personally known to authors; nothing else to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Multimember regulatory commissions—including the Federal Trade Commission, Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Consumer Product Safety Commission, and Federal Reserve Board of Governors—have long been mainstays of federal administration. Yet both before and after Trump v. Slaughter (2026), in which the Supreme Court overturned Humphrey's Executor (1935), research has focused on these bodies as institutions or on their chairs, largely neglecting the associate commissioners who make up most of their membership.

We present semi-structured interviews with twenty-four current and former officials across fifteen federal multimember agencies who served between the 1990s and 2025. We confirm that most commissions have strong chairs, whose control over agency agendas and career staff frequently gives them decisive influence over regulatory outcomes. Genuinely equal-commissioner arrangements are rare. But associate commissioners, even in chair-dominated commissions and even from the minority party, are often far from passive. They wield influence through negotiations, delegations, separate statements, and pre-commitment instruments, such as strategic plans and budget proposals. Although their effectiveness depends on access to timely information and the chair’s management style, associate commissioners play a real role in governance. Moreover, notwithstanding deep skepticism in prior scholarship and in Slaughter, most interviewees from both parties perceived their commissions as genuinely independent. The vast majority of interviewees believed that overturning Humphrey’s Executor would rupture commission governance and impair agency performance.

Our findings are particularly significant after Slaughter. They provide an account of independent commission governance from what may be the last generation to engage in it. They undercut claims that such agencies were never truly independent; that bipartisan commissions are inherently dysfunctional; and that associate commissioners play little meaningful role. And they suggest paths for Congress and agencies to preserve some benefits of the commission form, despite Slaughter's devastating blow to agency independence. To make remaining structural features, such as partisan-balance and quorum requirements, effective, we recommend policy reforms to empower associate commissioners. These include reducing information asymmetries between chairs and their colleagues, reforming the Sunshine Act, and developing onboarding programs tailored to the distinctive demands of the associate-commissioner role. Such steps might avert Justice Sotomayor's fear that commissions will fall under "absolute partisan control."

title: Preparation and Characterization of Rice Husk-derived Activated Carbon for Vanadium Redox Flow Battery Applications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work
declarations.funderStatement: Funded by HEC Pakistan, NRPU Project no. 16709.

detail.abstract:
In this study, activated carbon was prepared from rice husk using acidolysis, carbonization and chemical activation. The prepared activated carbon was characterized using BET, Raman, SEM, TEM and XRD analysis. The BET results showed a high surface area of approximately 747 m²/g. Raman analysis confirmed the presence of both graphitic and disordered carbon structures. SEM and TEM images showed a rough, porous and interconnected structure, while XRD confirmed the mainly amorphous nature of the activated carbon. 
The electrochemical performance of activated carbon-modified carbon felt (AC-CF) was compared with pristine carbon felt (PCF) in a VRFB. Both electrodes showed high current efficiencies of approximately 95-98%. Although PCF showed a slightly higher discharge capacity, AC-CF showed improved energy and voltage efficiencies. The energy efficiency of AC-CF was 85-87%, compared with 82-84% for PCF. Similarly, AC-CF showed higher voltage efficiency of approximately 86-88%. It can be seen that the high surface area and porous structure of rice husk-derived activated carbon provided additional active sites and improved the electrochemical performance. Overall, rice husk-derived activated carbon can be considered a promising, low-cost and sustainable material for VRFB electrode applications.

detail.abstract: This paper examines a critical vulnerability in the methodology of sub-sovereign ESG (Environmental, Social, and Governance) ratings, utilizing Chiba Prefecture, Japan, as a primary case study. While global ESG frameworks increasingly evaluate local government bonds, rating agencies predominantly rely on macro-level socioeconomic indicators and overarching policy frameworks, creating a significant "measurement gap." We demonstrate how this macro-dependence obscures micro-level governance failures-specifically, the indefinite suspension of complaint processing and the systemic non-creation of official records within police administration. By applying an axiomatic approach grounded in administrative law and corporate governance principles, this study empirically proves the existence of a structural "Accountability Gap" at the operational entry point. The findings highlight the critical need for institutional investors and ESG rating agencies to discount the reliability of sub-sovereign sustainability representations when auditable management evidence is structurally absent.

title: Identity Without Identifiers: Node Lineage and Longitudinal Measurement in Nodal Electricity Markets

detail.title: Identity Without Identifiers: Node Lineage and Longitudinal Measurement in Nodal Electricity Markets

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors

detail.abstract: Electricity system operators publish locational prices against identifiers that can change when the network model is revised. Across six United States nodal markets we examine, most price records carry no market-wide persistent identity key, despite an industry data standard that already specifies persistent object identifiers. Using eighteen years of PJM model-update records covering 1,354 documented renames, we measure how much of the correspondence the published cues determine. The most informative cue, the equipment unit number, sharply reduces ambiguity yet is frequently inconsistent with documented continuity, an information–validity tradeoff that survives conservative parsing; the typical model update resolves none of its contested renames from published cues alone. A rule frozen on MISO transfers blind to PJM documentary labels at 93.5% precision over 34.7% of events, falling to 85.2% outside the single dominant update. MISO remapping workbooks retrieved only after that rule was frozen corroborate 47 of the 48 links underlying the economic analysis, while showing that operational remapping cannot itself be read as persistent identity. The economic consequence is concentrated rather than average. Successor-only identifiers omit a median 66.4% of the congestion record and raise the sampling variance of the historical mean by a median factor of 2.53, while short-window estimates that do not cross the boundary are unaffected. Because truncated histories produce extreme ratios, a screening rule selects them: all twelve corrected nodes in the naive top hundred by mean-to-volatility leave it once lineage is restored. Persistent identity and event-typed transition metadata belong with market objects at source.

title: A Theory of Bullying Under-reporting
affiliations: Universidad Loyola Andalucia

detail.title: A Theory of Bullying Under-reporting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a theoretical paper and does not involve human participants, personal data, or experimental procedures requiring ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by the Spanish Ministry of Science, Innovation and Universities through projects PDC2025-165775-I00 and PID2024-156629NB-I00

detail.abstract: Bullying is difficult to detect because victimization is not directly observed as a single objective state. This paper develops a simple theory of bullying under-reporting. Motivated by four descriptive regularities from Spanish classroom data, the model explains why peer-reported victimization can exceed self-reported victimization while most students nominate no victim and most peer-identified victims receive only one or two nominations. We start from a latent victimization state and model how it becomes, or fails to become, a report. Victims observe their own suffering but may not self-report because disclosure carries identity and psychological costs. Peers observe noisy social signals and report only if they classify the situation as bullying and are willing to bear the cost of speaking. The model also explains why self-and peer-reports often disagree and why silence by victims or bystanders should not be interpreted as absence of harm. A public-good extension shows that more potential observers need not eliminate under-reporting, because individual pivotality falls when bystanders can freeride on others' reports. A simple static extension connects these reporting decisions to the aggressor's incentives: when harm is unlikely to generate an effective institutional response, aggression carries a lower expected institutional cost. The theory yields practical implications for measurement, reporting systems, institutional response, and early detection.

title:
The Unequal Genome:

A Sociological Approach to Genetic Engineering and the Ethics of Health Equity
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title:
The Unequal Genome:

A Sociological Approach to Genetic Engineering and the Ethics of Health Equity

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable.
declarations.funderStatement: Not applicable.

detail.abstract:
Emerging technologies involved in genomic medicine have the potential to revolutionize prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of diseases. There are, however, key ethical considerations that are illuminated by the field of sociology. These issues include concerns about who is allowed to participate in genomic research and technology development, who has power over these technologies, and who will have access to the benefits of these technologies. This paper begins by highlighting opportunities and potential ethical considerations with genomic medicine, genetic engineering, and human-directed modification of biological inheritance. It then summarizes concerns regarding representation and bias within genomic datasets as well as how a lack of representation may worsen health inequities when translating genomic innovations into the clinic. 

This paper continues by discussing sociological considerations related to structural racism and historical medical misconduct, medical mistrust, privacy and informed consent, and other structural issues impacting underserved communities. This paper’s recommendations highlight several key themes: effective communication, transparency, and partnership-building; safety and technological regulation; responsibility in scientific application; standardized and equitable reference datasets; access to appropriate follow-up resources and care; as well as community governance. Finally, this paper suggests working towards creating systems that are accessible, equitable, and trusted to fairly disseminate the benefits of genomic medicine.
