detail.abstract: This study aims to evaluate the quality of PT Telkom Akses Kendari services in the implementation of the Fiber to the Home (FTTH) network development project using the five-dimensional SERVQUAL approach. The results of the study show that the company's service quality is in the good category with a total observation score of 66. The main findings indicate that the Reliability aspect is the most dominant dimension, reflected in the company's ability to complete projects on time, maintain consistency in installation quality, and comply with strict technical standards. In addition, the Tangibles dimension is realized through the provision of modern infrastructure and equipment, while Responsiveness is shown by the speed of handling field disturbances. The Assurance and Empathy dimensions have also been implemented effectively through the competence of professional workers and efforts to distribute services to various residential areas in Kendari City. The company has successfully implemented Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) and maintains good work safety. However, an in-depth evaluation revealed that there are gaps in the standardization of project documentation and uniformity of competencies among technical team members. Improvements in these areas are crucial to drive the transition of service quality from good to excellent. This conclusion confirms that although the overall performance is satisfactory, administrative optimization and human resource development are still needed to increase customer satisfaction and trust in a sustainable manner in the midst of dynamic competition in the telecommunications industry.

title: Mobilising Household Savings for Long Shot Innovation: Financial Product Design and Governance for European Research Funding
affiliations: and University of Antwerp

detail.title: Mobilising Household Savings for Long Shot Innovation: Financial Product Design and Governance for European Research Funding

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The current study results from a collaboration that is exclusively academic.
declarations.funderStatement: unfunded research

detail.abstract: Long shot innovation projects, including fundamental research, are persistently underfunded because they combine long investment horizons with low probabilities of success and highly skewed, often binary, payoff distributions. Financial engineering theory suggests that pooling such projects and allocating cash flows across tranches that differ in seniority can transform these uncertain outcomes into more conventional risk-return profiles. While the existing literature has focused almost exclusively on the potential of such structures for institutional investors, this article examines their eligibility for European retail investors operating under the current investor protection regime. We show that retail eligibility depends on a non-linear interaction between regulatory risk classifications, the allocation of success across tranches, and the degree of diversification within the underlying research portfolio. Carefully designed portfolio and tranche structures can satisfy retail eligibility requirements while preserving exposure to innovation related upside potential, also when including mandatory liquidity reserves and representative fees. Building on these findings, we outline a governance framework for a dedicated funding vehicle capable of managing the resulting asset and liability structure. Mobilising household savings to finance research and innovation complements existing public funding instruments and contributes to the objectives of the European Savings and Investments Union.

title: Techno-Economic and Environmental Assessment of Solar Photovoltaic System for Energy Autonomy at Chittagong University of Engineering & Technology, Bangladesh

detail.title: Techno-Economic and Environmental Assessment of Solar Photovoltaic System for Energy Autonomy at Chittagong University of Engineering & Technology, Bangladesh

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: The research was self-funded by the researcher

detail.abstract: This study evaluates the technical, economic, and environmental feasibility of a grid-connected solar photovoltaic (PV) system at the Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET), Bangladesh. The proposed system utilizes available rooftop areas and campus water bodies to reduce dependence on conventional grid electricity and support national renewable energy goals. Historical electricity consumption data from 2013–2025 were analyzed to forecast energy demand up to 2050 using a linear regression model. The solar PV system was designed and simulated using PVsyst, while RETScreen Expert was employed to assess environmental benefits. Financial performance was evaluated through Net Present Value (NPV), Internal Rate of Return (IRR), Return on Investment (ROI), Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE), and Payback Period analyses. The proposed installation consists of a 10.296 MWp solar PV system with a total AC capacity of 9.075 MW, combining rooftop and floating PV technologies. Simulation results indicate that the system can meet a significant portion of CUET’s electricity demand while exporting surplus energy to the national grid. Economic analysis yielded a positive NPV of USD 2.92 million, an IRR of 17.33%, an ROI of 192.03%, and an LCOE of USD 0.0681/kWh, with simple and discounted payback periods of 5.0 and 6.18 years, respectively. Environmental assessment revealed substantial greenhouse gas emission reductions through the displacement of fossil-fuel-based electricity generation. The findings confirm that large-scale solar PV deployment at CUET campuses is technically feasible, economically viable, and environmentally sustainable, offering a practical pathway toward energy security and sustainable development in Bangladesh.

detail.abstract: Why do studies of transportation infrastructure often reach conflicting conclusions? We investigate this question using China's high-speed rail expansion as an empirical setting and systematically implement leading empirical strategies from the literature. We find that empirical implementation can generate substantial disagreement even within a common economic setting: conventional historical-route and inconsequential-place IVs produce sharply divergent estimates, whereas long-difference (LD) specifications with appropriate controls yield stable results. A quantitative spatial equilibrium model provides independent support for the LD estimates and implies meaningful national welfare gains. More broadly, our results demonstrate the value of systematically comparing empirical designs when evaluating major policies.

title: Does Artificial Intelligence Reduce Investor Disagreement? Evidence from Human-AI Interactions Data
affiliations: The University of Hong Kong - Faculty of Business and Economics, , , Tsinghua University, School of Economics and Management and Tsinghua University - Tsinghua University School of Economics and Management

detail.title: Does Artificial Intelligence Reduce Investor Disagreement? Evidence from Human-AI Interactions Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: We acknowledge research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China.

detail.abstract: We use proprietary microdata on human user-generative AI (GAI) interactions to study how AI-assisted information processing affects investor disagreement. Disagreement rises over the course of a conversation, driven by increasing dispersion across topics despite declining dispersion within topics. This disagreement is economically meaningful: dispersion in beliefs formed after GAI interaction predicts higher subsequent abnormal trading volume, whereas initial-round dispersion does not. GAI responses also contain value-relevant information. The tone of GAI answers shapes users' subsequent expressed beliefs and predicts future stock returns, while the tone of user prompts does not; within-topic response noise declines as conversations progress. Yet users persistently pursue previously activated topics, and later-round GAI responses are not systematically more informative about future returns. These findings suggest that GAI improves the information content of investor beliefs without generating convergence: heterogeneous and persistent information search creates disagreement across topics. Consistent with this mechanism, broader U.S. evidence around ChatGPT's deployment shows greater disagreement following earnings announcements even as information asymmetry declines.

title: AI Volatility Forecasts Under Stress: Performance, Tail Risk, and Ranking Reversals

detail.title: AI Volatility Forecasts Under Stress: Performance, Tail Risk, and Ranking Reversals

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Machine-learning volatility forecasts are usually judged by average out-of-sample accuracy, but their practical value depends on whether relative performance survives stress. This paper studies state-dependent forecast ranking rather than unconditional loss alone. Using the full 2,615-observation archived S&P 500 realized-volatility file preserved from the Oxford-Man Realized Library, I compare EWMA, HAR-RV, and XGBoost in a walk-forward design whose state thresholds use only information available through t-1. XGBoost outperforms HAR-RV in normal observations, but the ranking reverses under high volatility. The paired XGBoost-minus-HAR QLIKE differential is-0.0097 in normal states, +0.679 in Stress90, and +1.167 in Stress95; the Stress90-minus-Normal deterioration is +0.689. The pairwise reversal survives log-MSE and log-MAE, Holm adjustment, chronological subsamples, and a pre-specified top-5% one-day realizedvolatility-ratio state with 148 events. Moving-block bootstrap and leave-one-event-out diagnostics indicate that the jump-state result is not driven by any single observation, although the five largest events account for about 42% of the cumulative differential. By contrast, the primary Q50-to-Q90 transition definition identifies only eight events and remains descriptive under the pre-specified power gate. The evidence reveals a forecasting-risk paradox: a model can look competitive under unconditional average-error criteria while becoming materially worse when volatility is high or rising abruptly. The results motivate evaluating AI volatility forecasts by state-conditional ranking stability, not average accuracy alone.

title: Exploring Migration Governance Gaps: The Case of Ugandan Labor Migration to the UAE

detail.title: Exploring Migration Governance Gaps: The Case of Ugandan Labor Migration to the UAE

detail.abstract: Drawing from extensive interviews with migrants and policy document analyses, we argue that Ugandan government’s incoherent policies on migration have increased the vulnerability of the migrants in host countries and limited the capacity to optimize migration as a national development strategy. This paper is divided into six sections. The first section explains the Sub-Saharan African migration to the GCC from the era of slave trade up to current labor migration. The second section contextualizes the patterns of Ugandan migration to the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The third section analyses the Ugandan migration policy framework and institutions while the fourth section examines the Ugandan government’s role in implementing migration policies with a focus on labor protection in the UAE. The fifth section explores migration as a co-responsibility of both Uganda and the GCC countries in addressing labor issues. The final section broadly offers some policy recommendations to increase protection measures for Ugandan and other Sub-Saharan African migrants in the host country.

title: Jameel–Ternyik Model of Historical Applications
affiliations: University of the Punjab and Techno-Logos) Educatis. CH.) Sharing Knowledge among Professionals

detail.title: Jameel–Ternyik Model of Historical Applications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest. This research was conducted independently with no financial or personal relationships influencing the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study involves no human subjects, patient data, or empirical experiments. It is a philosophical and conceptual analysis based entirely on publicly available information.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was self-funded by the author as an independent scholarly contribution.

detail.abstract:
Initiated by international scholar Dr. Stephen I. Ternyik, who encouraged Arif Jameel to synthesize classical political economy with his foundational civilizational framework, this joint paper develops the Jameel–Ternyik Model of Historical Applications. The model bridges macroeconomic long waves, biological generational change, ethical development, and institutional governance.

At its centre is a sociological paradox: although an older scholar may construct a long-range theoretical map of historical cycles, the legitimacy and renewal of a 50–60-year civilizational wave depend on the cognitive and ethical participation of the 15–25 age cohort, termed the Architect Generation.

By integrating Schumpeter’s theory of creative destruction, Kondratieff’s long-wave analysis, Ternyik’s Spiral Wave Theory, and Jameel’s theory of biological generational shifts, the paper argues that economic collapse is rarely a purely mechanical failure. It more often reflects a divergence between structural forces—money, technology, energy, and settlement patterns—and ethical forces, including moral legitimacy, social responsibility, and generational renewal.

Through historical applications ranging from the Late Roman Empire to the post-2000 digital economy, the model examines how these structural and ethical engines interact. It proposes that long-wave transitions should be analysed not only through technological and financial variables but also through generational psychology, institutional legitimacy, and ethical governance. The paper further argues that the 2000–2060 period represents a major historical transition shaped by digitalization, algorithmic markets, demographic change, declining institutional trust, and the emergence of new ethical demands.

The framework does not claim that youth should govern without institutional safeguards. Rather, it proposes that the Architect Generation should participate meaningfully in institutional redesign through an Ethical Passport framework that links leadership, technological power, and civilizational responsibility. The paper concludes that sustainable civilizational development requires the alignment of structural innovation with ethical legitimacy, enabling societies to move from coercive, high-entropy statecraft toward more accountable, low-entropy forms of leadership.

title: The EU Needs Semiconductor Supply Security to Achieve Digital Sovereignty
affiliations: Bruegel and Natixis Research

detail.title: The EU Needs Semiconductor Supply Security to Achieve Digital Sovereignty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: With the growing geopolitical tensions, the European Union (EU) will not be able to achieve its goal of maintaining security and digital sovereignty without a stronger focus on semiconductors. The EU is heavily reliant on imports, with 92% of global manufacturing capacity located in Asia, and the US leading high-level chip design. Such dependence can be a more important issue than ever, as advanced semiconductors are almost a prerequisite for Artificial Intelligence (AI) development, leading to problems for competitiveness and supply chain resilience. The heavy concentration of manufacturing capacity in Taiwan may also face disruption from natural disasters and geopolitical risks from China. We argue that the EU should consider producing some chips domestically as a safety net and climb the supply chain participation ladder by R&D, especially in design, meaning industrial policy is necessary. In this regard, China’s policies to reduce its external dependence on semiconductors were introduced before the US, and therefore, more lessons can be drawn about their effectiveness. The comparison with the world will help in analysing the current EU measures, namely the Chips Act. We conclude that a clearer distribution of responsibilities at the EU and the national level is needed to avoid excessive competition among member states through subsidies. A good model could be the Airbus project applied to the semiconductor supply chain, not only because it is pan-European but also open to the rest of the world. Finally, partnerships with existing high-end chip producers from like-minded governments and guaranteeing access to abundant critical raw materials are equally important.

publicationDetails.detailsText: “Shifting Boundaries in Georgia—Cultural Factors of Abkhaz Disintegration,” in Boundaries Revisited: Conceptual Turn in European Border Practices, Thematicon, Vol. 25, pp. 177–188.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines the Georgian–Abkhaz conflict through a constructivist and cultural perspective, shifting attention from conventional geopolitical and historical explanations to the changing identities, perceptions, and cultural relationships that made territorial separation possible. It develops a conceptual framework distinguishing frontiers, boundaries, and borders and uses the idea of a “separatist cycle” to trace Abkhazia’s movement from emerging grievances and self-determination to frontierization, de facto boundarization, and the pursuit of international recognition. The chapter argues that Abkhazia’s historical integration within Georgia rested substantially on cultural ties, particularly among political and intellectual elites. Sovietization weakened these ties by shifting the principal cultural centre from Tbilisi to Moscow, institutionalizing ethnic difference, and encouraging competing national narratives. These transformations intensified mistrust and contributed to the political disintegration that culminated in war and the consolidation of Abkhazia’s de facto statehood. The chapter also examines the Gali district as a distinctive cultural and political frontier, where ethnic Georgian residents remain caught between Georgian citizenship and Abkhaz institutions. It concludes that shifting territorial boundaries are not merely products of military conflict or external intervention but also the culmination of long-term changes in cultural identification, political trust, and perceptions of belonging.

title: Pensions from Capital: How Pension Funds in the United States, Japan and Europe Invest -and What Private Investors Can Learn from Them

detail.title: Pensions from Capital: How Pension Funds in the United States, Japan and Europe Invest -and What Private Investors Can Learn from Them

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal and no financial relationship to anyone
declarations.funderStatement: No Funder

detail.abstract: This paper examines the pension funds of the large industrial countries — with more than USD 68 trillion between them, the heaviest group of investors in the world. It compares how funded retirement provision is organised in the United States, in Japan and in Europe: how state, occupational and private provision differ, who grants which tax advantages to whom and at what level, and why equity quotas diverge so widely across regions — from 25 per cent in Japan and 27 to 29 per cent in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and Switzerland to 50 per cent in the United States and 52 per cent in Australia. A chapter of its own is devoted to Switzerland: there, companies invest their employees' pension capital themselves through their own provident institutions, the employer bears at least half of the contributions, and pension assets of more than CHF 1,220 billion reach 152 per cent of economic output — the highest figure in the world. The paper also describes the awarding practice: many funds tender their asset management externally, controlling firms rank the mandates every six or twelve months, and whoever comes last usually loses the mandate — a greyhound race that palpably raises investment discipline along the agreed strategy. The paper further shows that states and central banks, too, appear as securities investors — from Japan's pension reserve fund through the Swiss National Bank, which holds a quarter of its currency reserves in equities, to the Bank of Japan, which will unwind its equity fund holdings only over generations — while states continually replace their maturing bonds with new ones. For private investors, concrete conclusions are derived: employer contributions are the safest return there is and should be exhausted before any other investment; tax-favoured vehicles pay off in almost every situation; the equity share belongs tied to the investment horizon — high in youth, declining by plan towards retirement; and the most important institutional virtue, the regular verifiable review of one's own investments against a written strategy, costs nothing.

title: Strategic Voting When Winning is <u>Not</u> All

detail.title: Strategic Voting When Winning is <u>Not</u> All

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A

detail.abstract: Elections do not just pick a winner; they produce a full ranking. Standard strategic-voting models assume nonetheless that voters care only about who ranks first. We show that this restriction matters. Even a slight concern for who ranks second, third, and so on changes strategic incentives: generically, voters support their preferred candidate in the pair whose score tie is most likely. In three-candidate elections, this implies that two-candidate equilibria can exist only when the race is sufficiently competitive; arbitrarily small stakes in lower ranks eliminate lopsided Duvergerian equilibria. With four or more candidates, this necessary competitiveness condition tightens to exact balance. That is, with preferences over rankings (i) Duvergerian outcomes are more sensitive to perceived closeness, and (ii) strategic coordination does not disappear, but the strategically relevant margin can shift down the electoral ladder.

detail.abstract: Public authorities increasingly delegate eligibility determinations, fraud adjudication, and benefit-revocation decisions to statistical systems whose outputs are treated as administrative acts. This article argues that the central legal problem is not opacity or bias, the two failure modes that dominate existing scholarship, but attribution: the doctrinal apparatus of the rule of law-legality, motivation, contestability, and proportionality-presupposes that a sovereign act can be reconstructed to an identifiable decisional moment and an accountable decision-maker. Continuously retrained, vendor-controlled, statistically averaged systems dissolve that presupposition along three axes simultaneously: temporal (no discrete moment of decision survives continuous parameter drift), institutional (the entity that authors the decision logic is not the entity legally accountable for it), and evidentiary (the "reasons" that due-process doctrine demands do not correspond to any reconstructible chain of inference). Using a comparative method spanning the Netherlands' SyRI litigation, France's algorithmic-transparency regime, the European Union's AI Act, Australia's Robodebt scheme, the United States' Michigan MiDAS litigation, and Brazil's pending AI bill, the article demonstrates that existing accountability instruments-explanation rights, human-in-the-loop requirements, risk classification-treat the symptom of unreviewable automated power without addressing the underlying attribution failure. It proposes the Algorithmic Sovereign Attribution Standard, a three-part institutional mechanism requiring decisional-moment certification, vendor-inclusive accountability extension, and mandatory reconstructability logging, and tests this proposal against institutional-capacity, cost, and federalism objections. The article's contribution is doctrinal and institutional rather than purely empirical: it reframes the automation-of-government-power debate around the precondition-attributability-that must hold before any of the rule of law's familiar guarantees can operate at all.

detail.abstract: Institutional portfolios now hold assets that legacy classification systems were not built to describe: model weights held apart from their developer, tokens carrying cash-flow or governance rights, tokenised claims on off-chain assets, autonomous agents that hold resources and transact, and compute capacity that is priced daily and moving toward listed futures. Single-code schemes misfile these exposures or drop them, and both failures are silent. This paper presents the DAP Standard, an original classification standard that places any economic entity on six independent layers: economic domain, sector and segment, asset form, geography, secondary themes, and risk, governance, and policy tags. Sixteen domains and 223 defined leaf segments cover traditional economic activity in full, checked only against public-domain government activity concepts, and extend first-class coverage to model assets, autonomous agents, protocols, data assets, and traded compute. Five special modules resolve the hardest cases deterministically, so that a human analyst and a machine agent reach the same label from the same facts. The standard is versioned with forward maps, ships with a machine-readable schema generated from the text, and is published for review under an open schema licence.

title: AI-Driven Vehicle-Loan Underwriting as a Growth Strategy: Speed, Conversion, and Market Share in Consumer Lending

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) in lending is often justified as a means of reducing labor cost. This study argues that its greater strategic value may be speed: protecting approved loans, member relationships, and market share before borrowers finance elsewhere. Using four years of de-identified operational data from a mid-sized credit union, the analysis focuses exclusively on vehicle lending, the institution's largest consumer-lending product and an important source of new-member relationships. Only about 12% of vehicle applications received an instant decision in the operational process, and the project artifacts report an instant-approval share of only 1.2%. Funded vehicle loans had a median application-to-funding time of nine days. Across 2019-2022, 10,158 applications that had been approved were ultimately declined by the member, representing approximately $290 million in requested vehicle demand. The cumulative opportunity curve rises rapidly early in the funding window and then flattens, consistent with a saturating logarithmic/logistic shape; however, member-decline events were not timestamped, so this pattern is descriptive rather than a causal time-to-fallout estimate. A tuned Decision Tree reproduced the institution's historical overall vehicle-loan approve/disapprove decisions with 97.76% accuracy, 98.44% precision, 93.94% recall, 99.37% specificity, and ROC-AUC of 0.9897. These metrics measure consistency with historical underwriting decisions, not credit performance. Because repayment and default outcomes were unavailable, the study cannot claim that AI makes better risk decisions than human underwriters. The business implication is narrower and more important: when approval policy is highly reproducible, automation can be used to shorten decision queues and increase conversion capacity. For vehicle lending, where dealer relationships and point-of-sale competition strongly shape outcomes, speed can be a differentiator in preferred-lender status and new-member acquisition. The principal value of AI underwriting is therefore not headcount reduction, but faster loan conversion, retention, and growth.

title: Long-Run Dependence and Network Topology in European Equity Sectors Across Changing Inflation Conditions

detail.title: Long-Run Dependence and Network Topology in European Equity Sectors Across Changing Inflation Conditions

detail.abstract: Inflation is a major source of macro-financial uncertainty, with potentially heterogeneous implications for sectoral equity risk and co-movement. We examine whether inflation is associated with low-frequency volatility in European equity sectors and document how estimated long-run dependence and network topology vary across changing inflation conditions over 2000–2025. Using indices for Energy, Financials, Industrials, Consumer Discretionary, and Consumer Staples, we estimate sector-specific GJR-GARCH-MIDAS models in which inflation enters the low-frequency variance component. We use the resulting standardized residuals to estimate long-run correlations through a DCC-MIDAS model. We then derive an Average Correlation Index (ACI) from the estimated correlations and construct minimum spanning trees (MSTs) from the corresponding correlation-based distances. Inflation is positively associated with low-frequency volatility in the Energy, Financials, Industrials, and Consumer Discretionary sectors, but the association is not statistically significant in the Consumer Staples sector. The estimated long-run correlations are highly persistent, reflecting an extended history of realized dependence. We map the ACI and MSTs onto inflationary and disinflationary episodes identified ex post. The ACI varies across changing inflation conditions but does not exhibit a monotonic relationship with inflation. Network topology adds information beyond average correlation, with Industrials central in most episodes, cyclical sectors forming a tighter core during the 2021–2023 energy-shock episode, and the network becoming more chain-like during the 2024–2025 disinflation period. These findings show that similar levels of average correlation can mask materially different configurations of persistent sectoral dependence, with implications for diversification, risk budgeting, stress testing, and the monitoring of shock-transmission channels.

detail.abstract: Anarkulova, Cederburg, and O'Doherty (2025) find that lifecycle investors should hold nothing but internationally diversified equities: a fixed 33/67 stock portfolio, with no local bonds. We reproduce that ranking from fully public data (the Jordà-Schularick-Taylor Macrohistory Database (Jordà et al., 2023) for 16 developed markets, 1927-2025, in each household's own currency and purchasing power) and extend the opportunity set to global fixed income, gold, and a managed-futures sleeve. At 200% gross exposure, two pre-specified diversified families, whose weights and leverage are chosen without reference to in-sample moments, match the all-equity benchmark's 17.4% annual volatility but cut retirement ruin from 7.4% to 1.8-2.5%, and match its lifecycle utility at a 5-6% saving rate rather than 10%. The ranking survives risk aversion from 2 to 10 and varied contribution and withdrawal assumptions, and weakens only beyond a sustained 200-basis-point financing spread. In this extended historical design, diversification, not stock concentration, is favored once the opportunity set is broad and strategies are compared at a common risk budget rather than at a common gross exposure.

keywords: Tendency of the Rate of Profit to Fall

detail.abstract: Firms adopting AI to substitute for labor face a coordination problem that recurs across two theoretically incompatible traditions: demand-side models, where aggregate demand depends on the same wage income that firms are cutting, and Marxian value-theoretic models, where the rate of profit depends on a capital-composition ratio that competitive automation drives in a self-undermining direction. We define a latent labor-intensity variable and channel-specific mappings into each tradition's own state variable, rather than assuming the two traditions share a state variable, and ask a narrower, computationally checkable question: under what conditions does decentralized, competitive automation converge on a labor intensity below the level that maximizes each channel's own aggregate outcome, a condition we call automation overshoot. Computed independently across a shared parameter space, the two channels show substantial but incomplete agreement (95% and 84% of the swept region show overshoot in the demand and Marxian channels respectively, 83% show it in both), a result that survives a fifteen-specification robustness check across alternative functional forms and internalization strengths (intersection fraction range 0.57-0.94, mean 0.82). Market concentration moves both channels toward less overshoot under fully independent native-parameter sampling that removes any shared coordinate system, a directional claim that survives four targeted falsification tests, one of which an earlier version of this model failed: a mechanical scale artifact in the demand channel, where more competing firms mechanically implied more aggregate automation activity regardless of any internalization behavior, is identified, derived away analytically, and corrected, with every result in this draft reported post-correction. A follow-up generalization addresses a further concern directly: firm count is not the same thing as market concentration. Removing the symmetric-firm assumption and re-deriving the demand channel's internalization term for heterogeneous market shares shows the correction scales as s_i^2 for each firm's own share s_i, so that aggregate internalization is governed by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, HHI = sum over i of s_i^2, with the earlier N-based results recovered as the symmetric-share special case. Holding firm count fixed at N=10 while redistributing shares from equal to one dominant firm moves demand-channel overshoot by a factor of 37; plotting demand-channel overshoot against HHI directly across firm counts from 5 to 50 collapses the resulting curves onto one relationship to within 5%, indicating HHI, not N, explains the concentration dependence in this channel substantially better than firm count alone, within the heterogeneous-share configurations tested and the isolating-benchmark design described in Section 4a. Separately, an analysis of the demand and Marxian channels' concentration relationships under independent sampling shows the two channels do not differ in "magnitude" on a single shared scale so much as in shape: the demand channel exhibits a sharp threshold effect concentrated at low firm counts, while the Marxian channel exhibits a shallow, gradual effect spread across the full sampled range of market structures. We extend the model with a hysteretic labor-effort function motivated by, but formalized independently of, Byung-Chul Han's account of the achievement subject: workers sustain effort under a belief that individual strategy can secure their position, a belief that collapses abruptly once a recognition threshold is crossed and recovers only past a lower threshold than the one that triggered the collapse. Wired into a simulated output trajectory, this produces a counterfactual output shortfall that persists after visible layoffs have already subsided; it is reported as an extension, not as co-equal with the core overshoot and concentration results.

detail.abstract: International climate negotiations focus on three distinct climate change costs: mitigation, adaptation and loss and damage. This paper measures voters' fairness views about how these costs should be allocated between nations, and investigates whether fairness views and beliefs about a country's responsibility matter for policy support. In an online survey experiment, the paper finds that fairness views vary with the type of cost, that voters underestimate their country responsibility, and that fairness views and beliefs jointly predict voters' climate policy preferences. The paper also implements tailored treatments to test whether fairness views and beliefs causally affect policy support, but it finds no evidence of a causal link. The results highlight that, to be consistent with citizens' fairness ideals, the international distribution of mitigation costs should differ from the one of adaptation and loss and damage.

title: A Comment on "Graphical Potential Games"

detail.title: A Comment on "Graphical Potential Games"

detail.abstract: Babichenko and Tamuz (2016) demonstrate that an exact potential game with a graphical structure has a potential that can be decomposed as a sum of "local" potentials.  Moreover, any player's payoff function can be written as the sum of a non-strategic term together with the local potential for every clique of which they are a part. Their proof relies on a sophisticated argument that connects graphical potential games to Markov random fields and applies the Hammersley-Clifford theorem. In this note, I provide an elementary proof that also allows us to compute the local potentials.

detail.abstract:
This Strategy Note diagnoses the gap between the EU's digital rulebook and its enforcement, and sets out a sequenced institutional reform path. It argues that enforcement failure is structural rather than incidental, resting on five root causes: geopolitical exposure, politicised accountability, governance fragmentation, resource shortfalls, and national interests. Reviewing the reform proposals currently on the table in Brussels, it finds that coordination mechanisms are legally sound but institutionally weak, while independent authorities remain constitutionally fragile without treaty change.

The Note proposes three steps in strict sequence: first, an EU Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum modelled on the UK DRCF and built on existing EDPS infrastructure; second, the transformation of HaDEA into a Digital Enforcement Agency within the 2028-2034 MFF, founded on Article 114 TFEU and bounded to satisfy the Meroni doctrine; third, treaty-level reform anchoring fully independent enforcement across the Digital Single Market. It is intentionally published ahead of the Commission's Digital Fitness Check, expected in Q1 2027, aiming to trigger a larger policy debate on enforcement.

title: Is the IMF Conditionality Model Obsolete? An Empirical Analysis of Selected Developing Countries

detail.title: Is the IMF Conditionality Model Obsolete? An Empirical Analysis of Selected Developing Countries

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Once a country is in debt distress, the relevant question not only is whether it can pay, but who will decide what payment looks like in terms of ‘fair’. Through much of the 20th and early 21st centuries, this answer was rather clearly defined. The IMF would assess the macroeconomic situation, while the Paris Club would coordinate official bilateral debt restructurings, thus providing the sovereign debt restructuring some recognisable structure (Club de Paris, 2025; International Monetary Fund, 2019; European Central Bank, 2021). Nowadays, this framework has become much more complex though. China has evolved into a large bilateral creditor to developing countries, and is ill at ease within the former Paris Club approach that had guided the workout of public loans. The IMF conditions are still very important because the plan for restructuring depends on a way of handling the economy. At the time the old way of working which was based on the Paris Club no longer had enough money to meet today's needs. This is because there are now new lenders, especially China and that means a new way of dealing with them is needed This paper raises the following question: has the IMF’s conditioning on sovereign debt restructurings been made redundant by this evolutive landscape?

title: The Unsettled Side of Unanimity: Jury Verdicts after Ramos

detail.abstract: Ramos v. Louisiana requires unanimity to convict a defendant of a serious offense, but it did not decide whether acquittal must also be unanimous. Most American jurisdictions require unanimity for both verdicts, while Oregon permits acquittal by a vote of 10-2 or 11-1. This Article applies a Blackstonian framework to compare the two-sided and one-sided unanimity rules. We retain the unanimity requirement for conviction, but allow the number of votes required for acquittal to vary. The analysis yields three main results. First, larger juries strengthen the case for one-sided unanimity because two-sided unanimity makes correct acquittals increasingly difficult, leaving factually innocent defendants without a clearing "not guilty" verdict. Second, an increase in the loss that deadlock imposes on factually innocent defendants, such as the stigma of an unresolved accusation, lowers the desirable number of votes required for an acquittal. Third, the stigma attached to a hung jury is itself endogenous to the voting requirement for an acquittal. Third, the stigma attached to a hung jury is itself endogenous to the voting requirement for acquittal. Making acquittal easier causes the deadlocks that remain to convey a more adverse signal about the defendant. However, under our linear specification the reduction in the incidence of deadlock more than offsets the increase in its conditional severity. The results identify the institutional tradeoffs left unsettled by Ramos and rendered even more compelling by Kian without attempting to resolve the constitutional question.

detail.title: Antitrust as Metaphor? The Political Battle Against the Proxy Advisor Duopoly in the United States

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none

detail.abstract:
This Article analyzes recent U.S. antitrust initiatives against the duopoly in the proxy advisory industry. The two leading international proxy advisors—Institutional Shareholder Services and Glass Lewis—have been accused of standardizing corporate-governance voting recommendations around ideological commitments to ESG and DEI principles, thereby violating U.S. antitrust law. The two firms, which are also controlled by “foreign” entities, allegedly influenced the votes of large U.S. funds improperly, affected the governance of American corporations, and reduced the wealth of millions of U.S. citizens.

An examination of the various initiatives shows that antitrust in the United States has operated primarily as a rhetorical and political-regulatory instrument rather than as a genuine means of protecting competition. The allegations of collusion, anticompetitive standardization, tying, and monopolization seem weak and, at least thus far, unsupported by persuasive evidence.

Although poorly grounded, these initiatives have placed enormous pressure on proxy advisors and the funds and asset managers that manage most equity wealth. To avoid political pressure and potentially substantial sanctions and damages, proxy advisors have begun to alter their products and services significantly, diluting pro-ESG and pro-DEI positions. Institutional investors have likewise begun changing their voting practices by developing in-house analytical models, relying on artificial intelligence, or returning decisions to ultimate beneficiaries.

detail.abstract: We ask whether misperceptions about the time investment required for stock market participation act as a barrier to entry. In a survey experiment fielded to 70,000 randomly selected Danes, we show that non-investors expect to spend far more time on a hypothetical investment than investors actually report spending: only 30% think 15 minutes a week suffice to manage a broad-market investment, against 71% of investors who report spending less than that. We randomly assign participants to a short video on market efficiency, diversification and passive index funds. Treatment significantly lowers expected preparation time for a hypothetical investment from 9.5 to 8.5 hours, expected monitoring time falls from 60 to 48 minutes per week on average, and preferences shift towards funds over individual stocks. Investment intentions rise significantly by 3.7 percentage points. Treated respondents are also more than twice as likely to voluntarily download further information. Our results suggest that misperceived time requirements are an important barrier to asset market participation.

detail.title: Policy Sabotage and the Competence Curse

detail.abstract: Can a more competent government produce worse policy outcomes? In a dynamic two-party model, an office-motivated opposition can sabotage reform. Greater competence improves policy selection but also makes successful reform more electorally threatening, inducing more sabotage. Voter welfare therefore depends on effective competence: the incumbent's informational advantage multiplied by reform's survival probability. When sabotage responds sufficiently elastically near full competence, welfare is maximized at an intermediate level; this result ranks informational environments rather than prescribing lower competence. For sufficiently impatient parties, the competence-failure ordering survives jointly more precise signals for both parties and asymmetric priors; it also holds locally under weak partisan motives. Imperfect detection by voters can sustain a no-sabotage equilibrium when the detection probability reaches a competence-dependent threshold, but the threshold rises with competence. Voter ignorance can therefore both reward sabotage and make competent governments harder to protect from sabotage.

title: Institutional Alignment with ESG Disclosure Standards in BRICS+ Countries and the Cost of Sustainable Capital
affiliations: Moscow State University of International Relations (MGIMO University)

detail.title: Institutional Alignment with ESG Disclosure Standards in BRICS+ Countries and the Cost of Sustainable Capital
detail.abstract: This paper examines the institutional risks arising from the uneven alignment of national ESG disclosure standards and sustainable finance taxonomies across BRICS+ countries, focusing on Russia, China, India, and South Africa. As the grouping has expanded to ten members (with the addition of Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates), regulatory heterogeneity has increased: member states are at markedly different stages of convergence with international sustainability reporting standards (IFRS S1/S2), possess taxonomies of varying maturity, and are unevenly engaged in international regulatory networks such as the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS). The paper proposes an ESG Regulatory Alignment Score (ERAS) to quantify a country's institutional distance from the international disclosure baseline, together with a risk-premium function linking this score to the cost of capital for issuers of sustainability-labelled instruments. The analysis shows that incomplete alignment with the international disclosure baseline constitutes an independent barrier to capital mobilization, regardless of the scale of a country's domestic ESG initiatives.

title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Development of RegTech and SupTech: New Approaches to Financial Risk Management
affiliations: Moscow State University of International Relations (MGIMO University)

detail.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Development of RegTech and SupTech: New Approaches to Financial Risk Management
detail.abstract: Regulatory technology (RegTech) and supervisory technology (SupTech) have moved from experimental pilots to core infrastructure in financial oversight, with artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly embedded in compliance automation, anti-money laundering (AML) monitoring, anomaly detection, and predictive risk analytics. This paper examines how AI is reshaping the tools available to both regulated institutions and supervisory authorities, and how the pace and pattern of adoption differ between advanced economies and developing countries. Drawing on recent survey and policy work from the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the Financial Stability Board (FSB), the Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI), the World Bank, and the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the paper argues that AI-enabled RegTech and SupTech offer significant gains in supervisory efficiency and risk detection, but that these gains are conditioned on data governance capacity, human capital, and the management of third-party technology dependencies. The paper concludes with a set of practical recommendations and a phased implementation roadmap for financial regulators.

title: Dependence-Order Reversal from Early Default Feedback in Interbank Clearing

detail.abstract: In interbank stress testing, individual banks' marginal path laws may be fixed while their joint dynamic dependence remains a model-risk choice. This choice matters because anticipated counterparty failure can mark down current interbank claims, alter present solvency, and trigger absorbing default before liabilities mature. We study dependence-robust expected transformed societal shortfall on finite trees with multicausal couplings. The uncertainty set varies cross-bank dependence while preserving every marginal path law. Under the explicit conditions of an asymmetric two-bank construction, the upper Fréchet coupling is uniquely worst under terminal-only clearing, whereas the lower Fréchet coupling is uniquely worst under feedback-active clearing. For linear shortfall, terminalonly clearing is dependence-neutral, while the lower Fréchet coupling is uniquely worst dynamically. More generally, under weak default, canonical maximal clearing is well defined at positive and null histories, the robust objective is upper semicontinuous, its maximum is attained, and its value has an exact representation by finitely many linear programs over coupling-space sign cells. As a feedback-inactive benchmark, under Markov marginal transitions satisfying stochastic monotonicity and a terminal payoff satisfying supermodularity, the stagewise common-quantile multicausal law is worst. Network-level conditions make terminal supermodularity explicit. For every fixed strictly convex nondecreasing payoff Φ, strict upper-to-lower Fréchet reversal persists on a nonempty relatively open set of asymmetric primitives.

detail.abstract: Providing liquidity on decentralized exchanges earns fees but exposes liquidity providers (LPs) to impermanent loss from price movements. With concentrated liquidity, LPs control this risk by choosing how narrowly to deploy capital around the price. Using option prices, we quantify the cost of liquidity provision by developing measures of implied impermanent loss for concentrated liquidity and define the associated impermanent loss risk premium. Empirically, higher expected impermanent loss widens liquidity ranges, while higher risk premia re-center and tighten liquidity around the spot price, highlighting opposing effects of risk and compensation.

detail.abstract: We document strong co-movement in firm-level idiosyncratic skewness. We show that the common component in idiosyncratic skewness (CIS) is a powerful non-linear predictor of market returns, in and out of sample; it is not subsumed by existing predictors, and adds economic value for mean-variance investors after transactions costs. Results are robust across observation frequencies and evaluation periods. Within a standard valuation framework, CIS forecasts through the discount rate channel. Using a simple stochastic discount factor formulation, we infer that the predictability evidence is consistent with a state-dependent SDF. Further analysis suggests that the state-dependence may originate from investor recency bias induced by fading memory, offering a new channel to illustrate the impact of experience-based learning on asset prices.

detail.abstract: We study whether machine learning and finer intraday information improve next-trading-day realized-variance forecasts. Four HAR-family specifications provide classical benchmarks, while a locally estimated PBRV implementation is the most accurate benchmark in the common sample. We estimate positive multiplicative corrections under QLIKE and compare nested Boundary and Gaps information sets through chronological validation. A validation-weighted Gaps ensemble lowers pooled QLIKE by 4.0892% relative to PBRV. Allowing learners to use two additional one-minute frequency-gap variables lowers QLIKE by a further 1.5246% relative to the Boundary ensemble. The design distinguishes gains from flexible residual learning from those associated with finer intraday information.

detail.abstract: Azerbaijan's oil revenues are conventionally understood as a function of two variables: production volume and world oil price. This article shows that this two-factor model is no longer sufficient to explain the country's fiscal trajectory. During the first half of 2026, Azerbaijan's oil and gas revenues continued to decline even as global oil prices rose sharply amid instability in the Strait of Hormuz-a combination the standard model cannot account for. Drawing on a sixteen-year dataset (2010-H1 2026) covering national production, price, and revenue, together with field-level data for the BP-operated Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli (ACG) block and SOCAR's own operations, the article identifies two structural forces operating beneath the price-and-volume surface: a sustained decline in the capital efficiency of ACG's investment (output generated per dollar of capital and operating expenditure) and a parallel decline in the drilling productivity of SOCAR's own fields (output generated per metre drilled). Both indicators point to the same underlying phenomenon, field maturation, but through different mechanisms and with different implications for producers, regulators, and fiscal planners. The article concludes that continued reliance on price and volume alone as explanatory variables for Azerbaijan's oil revenue trajectory will systematically misstate the country's fiscal outlook, and it proposes a set of institutional and technical responses to the productivity decline documented here.

title: The Retraction Economy Needs Its Own Watchdog: A critical audit of Ivan Oransky’s ‘Retractions Are Increasing, but Not Enough’

detail.abstract: Ivan Oransky’s 2022 Nature World View argues that retractions are rising but remain radically below the level allegedly justified by the evidence. Its pivotal numerical proposition is that approximately one in 50 papers would satisfy at least one Committee on Publication Ethics retraction criterion, compared with an actual rate below 0.1%. The essay supplies no reproducible derivation for that estimate. A widely cited pooled survey estimate near 2% measures respondents who admitted an act at least once, not papers; lifetime admission, not publication-level prevalence; and a narrower misconduct category, not every COPE ground for retraction. This article audits the essay’s arithmetic, cited examples, incentive proposal, disclosures and subsequent institutional context. It argues that absolute retraction counts are unsuitable as a performance indicator, that two narrow citation studies cannot carry a global claim about a missing retraction volume, and that a pay-per-detection model risks metric-target distortions unless rewards are separated from outcomes and subject to independent verification. Public tax filings report no reportable compensation to Oransky from the Center for Scientific Integrity in 2022 or 2024; allegations of personal enrichment are therefore not established. The defensible concern is structural: journalism, advocacy, database classification, publisher services and editorial roles can converge around the same actors. The proper response is not a counter-campaign against individuals, but auditable provenance, recusal, correction, appeal and independent oversight for the watchdogs themselves.

detail.abstract: The need to implement language capabilities in environments with changing language barriers, limited connectivity, and constraints on resources-such as bandwidth and compute power-has created a structural deficiency with today's language-enabled assistants: they require cloud-based inference, and rely on static parameter sets. This review highlights recent advancements in edge LLM, Mixtures of Experts routing, parameter efficient fine-tuning methods, Federated learning and self-evolving agents and introduces a conceptual framework of self-evolving edge LLM under reinforcement-based parameter routing. The framework integrates a lightweight, back-propagable "multilingual backbone" with a bank of lightweight adapters, each dependent on a specific linguistic context and specific device metrics such as reward value and/or telemetry, and selected by a reinforcement learning policy during inference. The review draws evidence from over fifty peer-reviewed and archival sources, mostly published between 2019 and 2025, that were selected and summarised to synthesise the reported evidence on quantisation, pruning, distillation, low-rank adaptation and learned routing and position these techniques in the context of offline, multilingual, resource-constrained IoTs assistants. According to comparative synthesis, there is no solution that meets all above requirements in a single solution, motivating the proposed reinforcement-guided routing paradigm. The review also highlights several outstanding issues regarding (1) routing instability in the presence of sparse reward signals, (2) catastrophic forgetting in the case of continual on-device adaptation, (3) energy budgets on microcontroller-class devices, and (4) the lack of multilingual benchmarks for evaluation on an edge device. This paper suggests that a reinforcement-guided parameter routing (RP) framework might be a valuable empirically grounded approach to the evolution of local assistants that are respectful of user privacy and reliable when offline.

detail.abstract:
Policy discourse on digital economy development in emerging economies is organised, largely without argument, around a developmental ladder: Web 1.0 to Web 2.0 to Web 3.0, or an equivalent maturity sequence, with countries positioned on rungs and progress defined as ascent. This paper argues that the ladder is the wrong instrument, and that its persistence has a measurable cost — it directs attention to a country's position rather than to its binding constraints, and it bundles the capability its terminal stage names with one particular implementation of that capability.

We make three moves. First, we show that stage models of information systems development have been empirically contested since Lucas and Sutton (1977) and repeatedly disconfirmed since, that the e-government maturity literature reached the same verdict by 2008, and that the Web 1/2/3 ladder inherits every one of these defects while adding a further one. Its terminal capability — ownership — differs from reading and writing: technology cannot confer it unaided, because ownership is created by law and merely represented on a ledger; and in practice the discourse binds that capability to a single implementation, self-custody, which a country may rightly decline while still wanting the capability. Second, we propose a constraint-based alternative in which a small set of institutional facts selects the admissible architecture, and we derive four such constraints for a dollarized, low-inclusion economy. Third, we test the framework against evidence from a publicly deployed sovereign blockchain running a single validator and carrying test assets — one boundary is measured on that chain, the others reached analytically, and we mark which is which throughout — and report a finding the stage model cannot express: the components of a digital economy are not equally governable by a single architecture. A sovereign perimeter secures custody of a regulated asset and fails to secure exposure to it; it governs a natively digital asset completely and an asset representing something off the ledger only where a statute makes the entry decisive; it cannot confer data ownership by holding data, and can support it only by holding wrapped keys and consent records it is unable to read, alongside a statute and an encryption layer — an arrangement on which a data market built from copies leaks by the same mechanism, leaving selective disclosure as the missing and unbuilt instrument; and its most durable contribution is supervisory visibility rather than supervisory control.

We draw the case from Cambodia, where the constraints are unusually sharp — foreign currency deposits at 90.7 percent of total deposits, mobile phone ownership at 81.3 percent against account ownership at 39.0 percent, device access at parity across the survey's urban and rural strata while account ownership differs across them by thirty-one points, and reported barriers among the unbanked that are economic and administrative rather than technical. The paper concludes that sovereignty over a digital economy is component-specific; that code and statute divide the work between them, code alone failing outward and law alone failing late; and that policy sequencing should follow the components rather than the ladder. It also corrects, on the evidence, a position the present authors advanced in earlier unpublished work.

title: One Bucket, Many Harms Correlating JCI's Workplace Violence Terminology with the ASIS/SHRM Standard, the Modified Overt Aggression Scale, and OSHA/NIOSH Source-Type Taxonomy

detail.abstract: The Joint Commission International (JCI) Accreditation Standards for Hospitals, 8th Edition, address workplace violence (WPV) through two standards-GLD.07.02 and SQE.02.02-both of which define WPV as a single, undifferentiated category spanning verbal aggression through physical assault, and require hospitals to report and analyze incidents without specifying how those incidents should be classified by source or severity. Three independent, well-established frameworks already address adjacent pieces of this problem in isolation: the NIOSH/OSHA Type I-IV typology classifies workplace violence by the relationship between perpetrator and victim; the ASIS/SHRM WVPI.1-2011 American National Standard, jointly developed with the Society for Human Resource Management, prescribes organizational protocols for preventing, detecting, and resolving workplace violence; and the Modified Overt Aggression Scale (MOAS), a validated clinical instrument, assigns a weighted numeric severity score to aggressive behavior. None of the three, individually or in combination, gives a hospital a single reportable field capturing both who a workplace violence incident involved and how severe it was. This paper proposes a correlated two-axis Source × Severity classification, adapting NIOSH's source categories and MOAS's weighted severity logic into a documentation field compatible with JCI's existing reporting requirement, illustrated with a short hypothetical worked example.

detail.abstract: This chapter examines the mechanisms through which China engages with the international arbitration community and develops cross-border cooperation in commercial dispute resolution. It analyzes four principal dimensions of collaboration: the international expansion of Chinese arbitration institutions and the growing presence of foreign arbitral institutions in Mainland China; cooperation agreements between Chinese and foreign arbitration bodies; summits, forums, seminars, and other professional exchanges; and the cross-border recognition and enforcement of arbitral awards. The chapter shows how Chinese institutions have expanded overseas offices, internationalized their arbitrator rosters and procedural rules, and entered into extensive cooperation agreements involving information exchange, arbitrator recommendations, training, administrative assistance, and joint research. It also examines China’s gradual liberalization of market access for foreign arbitral institutions, particularly in free trade zones and other designated regions. Regional and international forums have further institutionalized cooperation through joint initiatives, hearing centers, and collaborative platforms linking China with partners in Asia, Africa, Europe, Latin America, and the Middle East. Finally, the chapter considers the mutual recognition and enforcement of Chinese and foreign arbitral awards as an important indicator of international judicial trust. It argues that these overlapping mechanisms of institutional presence, formal cooperation, professional exchange, and enforcement are strengthening China’s integration into the international arbitration system and supporting its emergence as an increasingly influential hub for cross-border dispute resolution.

detail.abstract: China’s arbitration regime has undergone a decade of incremental liberalization through a distinctive process in which local experimentation often precedes nationwide legal reform. This article analyzes that process by tracing reforms involving Pilot Free Trade Zones, foreign arbitral institutions, ad hoc arbitration, court-arbitration cooperation, and the 2025 Arbitration Law. It shows how Shanghai, Beijing, Hainan, and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area have functioned as regulatory laboratories in which policymakers have tested greater institutional openness, procedural flexibility, and international participation before incorporating selected innovations into the national framework. Particularly significant developments include progressively expanded market access for foreign arbitral institutions, the emergence of ad hoc arbitration from the “three specifics” framework to express statutory recognition, judicial assistance with evidence collection and interim measures, and formal adoption of the seat of arbitration in foreign-related cases. The analysis identifies a recurring reform pattern: controlled experimentation, assessment through arbitral and judicial practice, and selective legislative normalization. This approach has enabled China to move toward internationally familiar arbitration norms without abandoning incremental regulatory control. Significant challenges nevertheless remain, including uneven regional rules, limited operational guidance for ad hoc proceedings, and incomplete mechanisms for judicial-arbitral coordination. China’s experience illustrates a model of arbitration reform in which institutional opening is achieved not through wholesale transplantation of foreign rules, but through gradual adaptation, localized experimentation, and subsequent national consolidation.

detail.abstract: The perceived ethical environment of an industry-the meso-level normative infrastructure between the individual entrepreneur and the state-has rarely figured in tax morale research. We examine its role among 1,513 entrepreneurs across Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia, using an industry-level adaptation of the Corporate Ethical Virtues (CEV) framework focused on tax compliance. The dimensions divide sharply: governance-like features (supportability, transparency, clarity, norm enforcement) are associated with lower acceptance of tax cheating and lower estimated shadow economy activity, while exemplar-based features (role modelling, feasibility) are not. Mediation evidence, supported by an individual-level panel design, is consistent with a pathway in which perceived industry ethical culture partly accounts for the well-established association between institutional satisfaction and entrepreneurs' tax morale. For policy, this localises a tractable target between the state and the individual entrepreneur: an industry's perceived governance infrastructure is more closely associated with entrepreneurs' tax compliance attitudes than the exemplar-based features that practitioner literature often emphasises.

detail.abstract: This study reconstructs the historical development of religious life and cultural diversity in Caraycaray, Naval, Biliran, Philippines, with particular attention to religious transformation during and after the Spanish colonial period. The study responds to the limitations of interpreting local religious history as a linear transition from an assumed “first religion” to Roman Catholicism. Instead, it examines religious change as a historical process shaped by Indigenous traditions, Spanish colonial missionization, migration, settlement, cultural interaction, local agency, and collective memory. A qualitative historical research design integrating oral history and documentary analysis was employed. Community narratives were considered alongside available historical accounts and secondary sources concerning the early history of Biliran and Naval. Historical triangulation was used to distinguish documented evidence from community memory and subsequent interpretation. The reconstruction indicates that Caraycaray developed within a historically significant landscape associated with the early Spanish presence on Biliran Island. Historical accounts place a possible early Spanish-associated settlement near present-day Sitio Ilawod of Caraycaray, although this localization remains a historical hypothesis requiring further documentary and archaeological verification. The study further demonstrates that Roman Catholicism became an important institutional and cultural force but that religious transformation was neither uniform nor uncontested. The Biliran Religious Revolt of 1765–1774 illustrates the complexity of religious change and the capacity of local actors to reinterpret, contest, and reorganize religious authority. Cultural diversity likewise developed through migration, linguistic interaction, settlement transformation, and intergenerational transmission of community traditions. The study contributes to Philippine local history by demonstrating how religious identity and cultural diversity were historically produced through interaction rather than simple cultural replacement. It also highlights the value of combining oral history, documentary evidence, and critical source analysis in reconstructing under documented community histories.

detail.abstract: We consider a model of network formation in which agents benefit from intermediation insofar as they are the only bridge between agents who would otherwise be unconnected. Their payoffs depend proportionally on their frequency as intermediaries. We analyze two types of payoffs: global, based on the intermediation across the whole network; and local, based on an agent's perceived centrality in a subnetwork, measured within a fixed radius around the agent. These capture two measurements of network importance: objective and perceived (subjective). Agents have an incentive to form links so that they become key intermediaries in their (perceived) network and to bypass other key intermediaries in it. However, because payoffs are determined relative to other agents' contributions, an agent might refrain from forming links if this would expose them to relatively more essential players. In case agents' payoffs are global, the pairwise stable networks are connected and have at most one (central) agent with a nonzero payoff. In the case where agents' payoffs are local, we describe the pairwise stable networks and some characteristics of the individual payoffs within them. A class of networks we call augmented stars (stars in which spokes may be connected but no cycle encompasses all spokes) is pairwise stable for both global and all possible local payoffs.

detail.abstract: Authoritarian elite management is often framed as a trade-off between loyalty and competence, but this obscures the fact that regimes must balance multiple loyalties, to party, patrons, central institutions, and leaders. Strategies such as vertical and horizontal rotations and age-based reforms can therefore be combined to strengthen different loyalties simultaneously. These tensions are especially visible during leadership succession, when new rulers must consolidate personal authority while preserving institutional control. This study exploits an irregular case of presidential succession in Kazakhstan to contrast singular and hybrid elite management logics. Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, hand-picked by Nursultan Nazarbayev in 2019, initially governed from a protected position that allowed him to pursue institutional centralization. A coup attempt in January 2022, however, pushed him toward a hybrid strategy combining institutional controls with consolidation of personal power. Using an original dataset of 227 appointments from 2013 to 2024, the study shows how shifting threats reshape elite management.

detail.abstract: Organizations frequently rely on repeated interventions to promote the adoption of innovative practices and behaviors. However, repeated exposure can generate intervention fatigue, making employees progressively less responsive to subsequent interventions. Existing research on innovation diffusion typically treats receptivity as a fixed individual characteristic, whereas in practice it evolves with accumulated exposure. In this paper, we specify an agent-based network model in which innovation adoption occurs through two channels: direct managerial intervention and peer influence. While the effectiveness of direct intervention declines with repeated exposure, peer influence operates through routine interactions and does not erode receptivity in the same way. We evaluate this model using three targeting strategies on a set of synthetic and real-world interaction networks under three settings: a fatigue-free benchmark, a fatigue-blind setting in which managers ignore fatigue, and a fatigue-aware setting in which exposure history informs targeting decisions. Our results show that ignoring intervention fatigue can cause managers to substantially overestimate innovation adoption, while accounting for fatigue in targeting decisions can improve adoption by broadening intervention coverage and reducing the concentration and redundancy of intervention effort. We further show that the cost of fatigue and the benefits of fatigueaware targeting both depend on the underlying network structure. They are greatest in hub-dominated networks, where repeated targeting rapidly exhausts influential employees, and smaller in dense networks, where peer influence plays a stronger role in promoting adoption. This study highlights the under-discussed role of intervention fatigue in innovation network studies and offers a flexible framework for evaluating intervention outcomes when receptivity evolves with exposure.

title: A Carr-Madan Type Projection Method for Evaluating Multidimensional Real Options
