detail.abstract: Multidimensional optimal stopping problems arise in applications including the valuation of American and Bermudan-style derivatives, real options, and sequential investment decisions under uncertainty. Although simulation-based dynamic programming methods have substantially extended the range of tractable problems, their computational performance depends critically on the approximation space used to represent continuation values. Existing approaches typically rely on generic function spaces, including polynomial regression, splines, kernel methods, and neural networks, whose conditional expectations must be estimated numerically. This paper proposes a projection framework based on a tensor-product basis of European contingentclaim payoff functions. Rather than using generic approximation architectures, we construct an approximation space whose basis functions are analytically tractable contingent claims. The proposed basis reflects the option-like nonlinearities inherent in optimal stopping value functions while exploiting the analytical structure of the stochastic model. Motivated by the static replication methodology of Carr and Madan, the resulting approximation space coincides with the classical truncated-power spline basis, combining established approximation properties with analytical tractability. Consequently, the Bellman recursion separates into an analytical valuation step and a numerical projection step. We derive semi-closed-form continuation-value representations under correlated GBM using exponentially tilted multivariate lognormal moments and extend the framework to affine Gaussian statespace models. Numerical illustrations include three-dimensional Bermudan geometric put and basket call options, and a forestry harvesting problem with stochastic timber prices, convenience yields, and biological growth. By establishing a direct connection between static option replication, spline approximation, and dynamic programming, the proposed methodology opens a new direction for constructing approximation spaces in multidimensional optimal stopping and advocates designing approximation spaces that jointly exploit the geometry of value functions and the analytical structure of the underlying stochastic model.

title: On the Nature of Capitalist Equilibrium

detail.title: On the Nature of Capitalist Equilibrium

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: As a neoclassical school of thought, Austrian economics has an essentially moneyless conception of market equilibrium, and their producer theory is mono-causal: social time preference determines both the length of production and the pure rate of interest (PRI), and these do not depend on the demand for money. While this framework may be acceptable for analyzing pre-capitalist economy-that is, production for direct use-it is unsuitable for understanding capitalist economy-that is, production for sale. Under capitalist modes of production, there are monetary constraints-namely, the requirement of positive aggregate profit-that do not exist under generic market orders. Building on earlier work (Mahoney 2025a, b) I will argue that capitalist equilibrium is characterized by a tri-causal nexus: social time preference (determining the length of production), production for direct use/consumption by terminal capitalists (determining the PRI), and the demand to hold money by intermediate capitalists (determining the number of stages of production). A coherent construct of an equilibrium demand for money will thus be established, distinguishing capitalist from non-capitalist economies.

title: Local Slope Estimation under Position-Localized Contamination

detail.title: Local Slope Estimation under Position-Localized Contamination

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
A trailing-window slope is one of the simplest real-time features used in quantitative finance, but its statistical behavior changes when measurement errors are concentrated near the newest observations. This paper studies a fixed logistic-weighted local-linear slope and ordinary least squares (OLS) on the same finite trailing window. The logistic estimator is not presented as a new regression class: it is exactly a weighted least-squares local-linear slope with a logisticshaped weight profile. We first prove exact affine reproduction and show that OLS is the unique minimum-variance linear affine-reproducing estimator under independent homoscedastic level noise. For the benchmark window N = 50, the logistic slope pays a 65.0% variance penalty relative to OLS, while its coefficient on the newest observation is about one third as large. We then introduce a position-localized contamination model. If the clean error has covariance Σ, a centered contamination of variance τ 2 occurs with probability ρ, and the contaminated position is j with probability p j , every affine-reproducing linear slope w has the exact finite-sample risk MSE(w) = w ⊤ Σw + ρτ 2 j p j w 2 j .
This identity yields a closed-form cross-over contamination amplitude between OLS and the logistic slope. For contamination uniformly distributed among the most recent m positions, the logistic slope can beat OLS only when the contamination is sufficiently localized and sufficiently large. A deterministic sensitivity study over N ∈ {25,50,100} and U ∈ {2,4,6} shows that this qualitative conclusion is stable: stronger endpoint downweighting reduces immediate sensitivity but increases clean variance. A locked synthetic Monte Carlo implementation check passes its pre-specified tolerance. A separate semi-empirical BTCUSDT/ETHUSDT one-minute stress test preserves the same qualitative geometry but requires much larger contamination amplitudes for the fixed logistic profile to overtake OLS. Earlier directional and tail-risk forecasting tests are retained as negative evidence; no return-predictability or trading-profit claim is made.

title: Nomic Learnability as Evidence for a Cognition-Aligning Creator: A Bayesian Variant of the Intelligibility-of-Nature Argument

detail.title: Nomic Learnability as Evidence for a Cognition-Aligning Creator: A Bayesian Variant of the Intelligibility-of-Nature Argument

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: This paper develops a variant of the traditional argument from the intelligibility of nature. The core observation is not merely that the universe is law-governed, nor merely that it is comprehensible, but that its law-structure can be learned by finite, resource-bounded, embodied cognizers whose inductive biases were fixed by a process (evolution under ancestral survival pressure) that had no causal contact with whatever process fixed those laws. I argue that this specific mismatch sharpens the classical puzzle associated with Wigner, Polkinghorne, and the broader "book of nature" tradition, and that it permits a more precise, formally grounded statement of why the fit should be considered improbable on naturalism, drawing on the No Free Lunch theorems from computational learning theory (Wolpert and Macready 1997). I present the argument in Bayesian confirmation form, following the methodology standard in contemporary natural theology (Swinburne 2004, Collins 2009), rather than as a deductive proof. I am explicit throughout about what in this treatment is inherited from existing literature and what, if anything, is a distinct contribution. The argument type itself is not new. What may be new is the attempt to derive the naturalist's low prior probability from a specific theorem rather than from unformalized intuition. I close by identifying what I take to be the argument's most serious vulnerability, a concentration-of-measure objection, and by being candid about the extent to which the argument's success depends on an independently motivated theological premise that could otherwise look ad hoc.

title: From Ex-Ante to Ex-Post: Introducing Empiric Mortality Pooling for Retirement Income

detail.title: From Ex-Ante to Ex-Post: Introducing Empiric Mortality Pooling for Retirement Income

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The mortality pooling architecture introduced in this paper is the conceptual foundation of a mortality pooling method and process described by the author in United States Patents No. 11,468,514 B2 (2022) and No. 12,106,373 B2 (2024), and corresponding patents granted in Canada, India, Japan, and Singapore between 2019 and 2024. The author filed the underlying patent application in 2013. The author has given the name empiric mortality pooling to the class of methods described in this paper and the related research series. The method is the sole invention of the author, who is the sole applicant and owner of all patent rights. No assignment has been made. All research and development activity related to this work from 2013 has been self-funded by the author. The author has a direct financial interest in any future potential commercial application of this method. No other competing interests exist.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Retirees face three competing objectives, funding income throughout retirement, preserving access to savings, and maintaining a legacy for their beneficiaries. Mortality pooling is theoretically beneficial for addressing the first objective, yet relatively few retirees own annuities or other pooling products. The conventional approach requires a payment at entry for the benefit of pooling, typically through a premium that commits savings upfront and removes those funds from the retiree's directly accessible savings. Products whose calculations rely on probabilistic estimation of future mortality experience typically require this entry commitment. This paper identifies an alternative, drawn from a class of mortality pooling products termed empiric, whose calculations rely only on observable realized values. The pooling contribution is paid at exit rather than at entry. This ex-post contribution architecture preserves the retiree's access to savings throughout retirement while still delivering the longevity protection of mortality pooling. The paper derives three necessary conditions that any such self-funded product must satisfy and shows by construction that these conditions can be met by an empiric product. Modern financial infrastructure, unavailable when conventional products were developed, makes this ex-post approach operationally feasible today.

title: Except for a Physician: How Illinois Wrote the Standard for Consent to Clinical Artificial Intelligence and Exempted the Profession Most Patients See

detail.title: Except for a Physician: How Illinois Wrote the Standard for Consent to Clinical Artificial Intelligence and Exempted the Profession Most Patients See

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: In August 2025 Illinois became the first state to regulate artificial intelligence in therapy. The statute defined consent, named the precise defect that a general intake form containing a line about artificial intelligence amid unrelated material represents, required that the specific tool and its specific purpose be disclosed, and then removed physicians from the definition that triggers all of it. The exclusion is so structured that the statute reaches the advanced practice psychiatric nurse and not the psychiatrist. This Article argues that the resulting condition is not a gap left by legislative silence but an exemption written by a legislature holding the standard in its hand, and that nothing else fills the space. Federally, a single characterization, health care operations, eliminates the consent requirement, closes both independent exclusions in the Illinois biometric statute, and defeats the accounting a patient might otherwise obtain, while an affiliated-entity designation the provider documents for itself sets how far the record then travels. The one Illinois statute that unambiguously conditions a clinical recording on the patient's agreement is the criminal eavesdropping Article, and its reach ends where disclosure begins; its doctrine of implied consent, developed entirely in custodial settings, treats continued speech as assent in precisely the room where continued speech is least voluntary. Common law is the ordinary residual, and its instrument is calibrated to a hypothetical undifferentiated patient. That calibration is the difficulty. A routine visit to a general practitioner is where psychiatric history is recorded, where anxiety is described aloud, and where psychotropic medication is adjusted, and the empirical record now shows that consent to ambient documentation falls from 81.6 percent to 55.3 percent when patients are told what the tool is, where the audio goes, and who is commercially involved. For a patient whose diagnosis is one that people do not wish to have circulating, an unspecific disclosure does not fail to inform; it prices the visit. The Article grounds a disability civil rights claim in that pricing, develops five disclosure questions as an evaluative instrument, measures Illinois, Texas, and California against them, and finds that no regime answers all five, that Texas has expressly blessed for its public hospitals the same boilerplate line Illinois defined as not consent, and that the carve-out is drawn along a clinical line ambient documentation technology has already erased.

title: Restoring the Margin

detail.title: Restoring the Margin

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any individual or organization that influenced this study. This is independent, self-directed research conducted without external sponsorship.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author without financial support from any institution, organization, or grant.

detail.abstract: This paper develops a policy framework for restoring household financial margin — the gap between what work pays and what a household must spend to participate securely in housing, healthcare, childcare, and other necessities — using current data on wages, rents, and cost burdens (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Zillow, U.S. Census Bureau) alongside comparative institutional evidence from other wealthy democracies. Rather than treating affordability as a single problem with a single ideological solution, the paper diagnoses eight distinct cost categories — housing, healthcare, childcare, wages and bargaining power, utilities, groceries, higher education, and household debt — and argues that each requires a different institutional response depending on the underlying market failure: competitive markets where genuine consumer choice and market entry exist, regulation where market power is concentrated, public or cooperative provision where natural monopoly limits competition, and social insurance where households cannot efficiently self-insure against catastrophic risk. Comparing U.S. outcomes against mechanisms used in other wealthy democracies, the paper evaluates specific policy options — housing supply liberalization paired with targeted subsidy, competing paths to universal health coverage, expanded childcare capacity, antitrust enforcement, public and cooperative utility models, and bargaining-power reforms — against evidence, cost, and implementation tradeoffs rather than ideological label. The paper concludes that a mixed, institution-by-institution approach, chosen by empirical results rather than by whether a mechanism is public or private, offers a more defensible path to restoring financial margin than any single-model reform agenda.

title: Paying for the Margin

detail.title: Paying for the Margin

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any individual or organization that influenced this study. This is independent, self-directed research conducted without external sponsorship.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author without financial support from any institution, organization, or grant.

detail.abstract: This paper analyzes the fiscal sustainability of the federal government alongside the debt burden of American households, arguing that a serious affordability agenda must track both balance sheets simultaneously rather than treating them as separate questions. Using Congressional Budget Office projections, Federal Reserve Bank of New York household debt data, and KFF medical-debt estimates, the paper documents a federal deficit of $1.9 trillion in fiscal year 2026 (debt held by the public projected to reach 101 percent of GDP in 2026 and 120 percent by 2036) alongside $18.771 trillion in aggregate household debt, including $1.651 trillion in student debt and at least $220 billion in medical debt. The paper evaluates specific revenue and spending options — including defense reductions, tax-base reforms, and healthcare cost control — against CBO's own published estimates, and finds that no single source closes the federal gap; a credible fiscal path instead requires stopping debt growth relative to the economy, reaching primary balance, and sequencing reform in phases rather than through a single comprehensive package. On the household side, the paper argues that student and medical debt relief should target unaffordable payment structures and preventable cost drivers rather than broad-based cancellation, and proposes a ten-year scorecard for measuring whether reform genuinely repairs both the household and federal balance sheets rather than improving one by transferring cost to the other. The paper's central claim is that policies which move an existing private cost onto the federal budget do not necessarily make a service more affordable, and that federal deficit reduction achieved by increasing household financial strain is not a net improvement in national fiscal health.

title: Narrative Capital and Asset Prices: Search-Based Attention, Portfolio Returns, and Factor Exposure

detail.title: Narrative Capital and Asset Prices: Search-Based Attention, Portfolio Returns, and Factor Exposure

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The research was conducted independently and was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
This paper develops and empirically investigates a search-based measure of narrative intensity, termed the Narrative Capital Index (NCI). The central premise is that investor attention is not allocated exclusively according to fundamentals: narratives can concentrate attention, alter expectations, and potentially generate temporary deviations between prices and fundamental value. We construct NCI from Google Trends search intensity and examine its relation to monthly equity returns using a no-look-ahead portfolio-sorting design. The empirical workflow proceeds from aggregate NCI-return analysis to stock-level NCI, sector-based NCI, long-short portfolios, decile sorting, and factor-adjusted time-series regressions with heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent (HAC) standard errors.

The project's preliminary monthly specification uses approximately 82 usable monthly observations. In the final factor regression available from the project, the long-short portfolio has an estimated intercept of 0.0048 per month (t = 0.91, p = 0.364), a market loading of −0.2019 (t = −2.10, p = 0.035), and a momentum loading of −0.1895 (t = −1.70, p = 0.090). Thus, the evidence does not establish statistically significant alpha, while it indicates statistically meaningful negative market exposure and weaker evidence of a negative momentum loading. Earlier exploratory specifications produced different coefficients, illustrating the sensitivity of the signal to universe and NCI construction.

title: Digital Gold and Programmable Money: Which Cryptocurrencies Suit Which Investor

detail.title: Digital Gold and Programmable Money: Which Cryptocurrencies Suit Which Investor

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No personal and no financial relationship influenced this study
declarations.funderStatement: No funder

detail.abstract:
Eighteen years after Nakamoto's (2008) white paper, cryptocurrencies form an asset class of their own, worth USD 2.73 trillion and reaching governments, central banks, pension funds, insurers, university endowments and sovereign wealth funds. This paper introduces the major cryptocurrencies-from Bitcoin and Ether through XRP, Solana, BNB, TRON and Cardano to the stablecoins Tether and USD Coin-naming their creators, their supply rules and their economic uses beyond speculation: cross-border remittances at a fraction of traditional cost, contracts that execute themselves on the blockchain, and the tokenisation of money market funds and bank deposits.
The paper documents who invests at the institutional level: the United States with a strategic reserve of roughly 200,000 forfeited bitcoin, El Salvador and Bhutan with sovereign holdings, the Czech National Bank with the first direct purchase by a Western central bank, BlackRock's bitcoin fund holding 777,666 bitcoin, and pension funds, insurers and university endowments from Wisconsin through MassMutual to Harvard. It also shows the other side of the ledger: peak-to-trough losses of 52 to 94 per cent per market cycle, volatility running at three to four times that of major equity indices, and a correlation with equity markets that has risen markedly since 2020.
From supply rules, usefulness, valuation and risk, the paper derives which currency suits which investor: Bitcoin as a scarce store of value for patient investors holding across full market cycles of at least four years; Ether and selected platform currencies for investors able to bear technology risk; stablecoins as payment and liquidity instruments without upside; small currencies at most as a side bet funded from money whose total loss would be bearable. The paper recommends combinations built on a Bitcoin core plus a small number of platform currencies, capped at a few per cent of liquid wealth.

title: Dubstrata: A Cryptographically Verified Causal Knowledge Graph and Decentralised Prediction Market Microstructure Architecture for Forward-Looking Financial Risk Intelligence

detail.abstract: Quantitative risk modelling in financial institutions has historically depended upon backwards-looking econometric models and statistical assumptions of stationarity that deteriorate during rapid macroeconomic regime shifts, geopolitical disruptions, and non-linear tail-risk shocks. Concurrently, decentralised prediction markets aggregate forward-looking collective intelligence with continuous state-contingent pricing, yet their direct utility for institutional risk systems remains impeded by thin-market illiquidity, Sybil manipulation, whale concentration, and unstructured narrative dispersion. Furthermore, emerging generative artificial intelligence and Large Language Model (LLM) narrative analysis tools frequently exhibit hallucinations, lack cryptographic grounding, and suffer from lookahead bias during quantitative backtesting.

title: Policing, Punishment, and the Public Trust

detail.title: Policing, Punishment, and the Public Trust

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any individual or organization that influenced this study. This is independent, self-directed research conducted without external sponsorship.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. It was conducted independently by the author without financial support from any institution, organization, or grant.

detail.abstract: This paper develops an evidence-based framework for evaluating American criminal-justice policy, organized around a single standard: whether an institution reduces the number of future victims while preserving liberty and legitimacy, rather than how much punishment it administers. Drawing on Bureau of Justice Statistics correctional population data, randomized and quasi-experimental studies of policing and sentencing interventions, and international comparisons, the paper documents an unusually large American baseline (5.53 million adults under correctional supervision, 1.85 million incarcerated) alongside evidence that specific alternatives to conventional punitive escalation improve safety outcomes — including de-escalation training, community-oriented policing, environmental design, and targeted social-support interventions. The paper separates deterrence from incapacitation as distinct mechanisms with different and contested magnitudes of effect, examines wealth-based disparities in the burden of enforcement, courts, and confinement, and traces a documented case of institutional stress-testing through the 2020 false-elector prosecutions to illustrate the limits and complexity of legal accountability mechanisms. It develops a reform agenda built on paired evidentiary standards for both reducing and increasing state coercive power — including police professionalization, sentencing reform, private-prison accountability, and a public-safety scorecard measuring outcomes rather than institutional activity — and evaluates the cost and implementation feasibility of each proposal against the available evidence rather than ideological position. The paper's central argument is that public safety is not measured by how much punishment a society can administer, but by how little harm its people are required to endure.

title: Beyond the Linear Gradient: Non-Monotonic and Spatially Clustered Property Tax Assessment Gaps in Greater Santiago, Chile

detail.title: Beyond the Linear Gradient: Non-Monotonic and Spatially Clustered Property Tax Assessment Gaps in Greater Santiago, Chile

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study, as it relies exclusively on secondary, anonymized administrative datasets (cadastral tax records and census cartography) and involved no human subjects, clinical trials, or primary personal data collection.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or external funding from any agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Property tax equity is typically tested for a linear relationship between the assessed-to-market ratio and socioeconomic status. Using a hygienized panel of 282,530 residential transactions matched to fiscal records across the 34 municipalities of Greater Santiago, Chile (2018–2025), we show that this linear framing conceals the true pattern. Assessed values are 51% of market value at the median—well below the statutory target of 60%—with an aggregate coefficient of dispersion of 43.6, indicating poor overall calibration. Regressing the assessed-to-market ratio on a territorial socioeconomic status index built via principal component analysis from 2024 census block cartography, we find no significant linear relationship (p = 0.245) but a highly significant inverted-U relationship (p < 0.001): the ratio rises then falls as status increases. Local Moran’s I on the fiscal–market gap reveals significant spatial clusters of under-assessment concentrated in higher-status territory and over-assessment clusters in lower-status territory (Kruskal–Wallis p < 0.001)—a spatially explicit, regressive pattern invisible to the linear specification. Doubly robust selection correction and a gradient-boosted hedonic cross-check confirm these results are not artifacts of model choice. Extending the analysis to administrative mechanisms—excess-mass bunching at the exemption threshold, an event-study test of reassessment capitalization, uncaptured land-value anticipation near transit infrastructure, and generalization to nonresidential land uses—we find that some mechanisms are robust across specifications while others are fragile, and that the municipal-level incidence of statutory compliance is itself regressive even though the aggregate fiscal impact is close to revenue-neutral. We discuss the findings through both equity and efficiency lenses and outline implications for reassessment policy.

title: Regulation, Risk, and Knowledge Production in contemporary AI
affiliations: and Peace Research Institute Oslo

detail.title: Regulation, Risk, and Knowledge Production in contemporary AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Authors have nothing to declare.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Forthcoming in Alice Martini and Susana de Sousa Ferreira eds (2026) Routledge Handbook of Security Studies and AI. Critical Insights, Routledge

detail.abstract: Alongside prominent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology, we are currently witnessing increased efforts to curb its potential harm on safety and security grounds. In different regulatory instruments around the world, "risk" becomes a central regulatory category, serving as the reference point against which responsibilities are allocated, proportionate gains are assessed, and discussions are framed. However, risk-based approaches are heavily influenced by the complex knowledge production dynamics that shape how risk and its levels are conceptualised. Risk categorisation is not an objective endeavour and is rather a product of different influences. Moreover, these dynamics have more than regulatory impacts; they produce security effects with uneven consequences. We explore them by building on Critical Security Studies' (CSS) literature on risk and uncertainty, as well as Science and Technology Studies (STS) concepts of co-production and situated knowledge. Using riskbased approaches in the EU AI Act and the AI Safety Report as examples, the chapter unveils a monolithic perception to AI, asymmetrical representation, and instrumentalisation of risks prevailing in international efforts to ensure safe AI. All in all, we show the added-value of actively combining regulatory studies with critical insights from CSS and STS to unveil key challenges of regulating emerging technologies.

title: Geopolitical Risk, Oil Rents, and the Financial Stability of Banking Systems: Global Evidence from Brent Crude Oil Price Uncertainty

detail.title: Geopolitical Risk, Oil Rents, and the Financial Stability of Banking Systems: Global Evidence from Brent Crude Oil Price Uncertainty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest to be declared.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding received.

detail.abstract: Employing global coverage of banking systems, the study investigates the impacts of global Brent crude oil price on financial stability through the lens of oil rents across geopolitical risk episodes. Our baseline dynamic panel estimates present the robust adverse impacts of oil price volatility on bank stability risks, including the buffer, financial profitability, and non-performing loans. The effects are heterogeneously conditional on stages of growth, financial development pyramid, and geopolitical uncertainties. The global oil price impacts on financial stability are unevenly dependent on the levels of oil rents as the important driver of the buffer levels of banking systems. The treatment effects of oil rents on bank stability are pronounced in times of heightened geopolitical risk that are sensitive to the global volatilities of Brent crude oil price. The difference-in-differences (DID) estimates show the robust treatment of oil rents to global banking stability under oil price uncertainty. Banking systems adjust their risk-taking buffers accordingly to the direct impacts of oil-related risks. The difference-in-differences in differences (DDD) estimates highlight the drivers of global geopolitical risk extreme scenarios to the treatment effects of oil rents on global financial stability. Our study offers novel evidence on the sensitivity of economies to the price of global brent crude oil supplies with the treatment effects of oil rents on the financial stability of banking systems worldwide. Oil supplies and oil price uncertainties are the important channels for which financial systems could adapt with heightened geopolitical risks for inclusive growth and sustainable development goals.

title: A Dynamic Structural Model of the Japanese Economy

detail.title: A Dynamic Structural Model of the Japanese Economy

declarations.declarationOfInterest: なし
declarations.funderStatement: なし

detail.abstract:
This paper applies the author's Endogenous Regime-Switching Model of Capitalist Economic Dynamics (A Disequilibrium Comparative Statics Model) to the Japanese economy and analyzes the dynamic structure of the Japanese economy in the 2020s.

The model shows a structure in which "stagnant demand" and "supply-constrained inflation" occur simultaneously, accompanied by a decline in the labor share and an increase in income inequality. A mechanical simulation for 2019–2030 reproduces the coexistence of low economic growth and inflation.

By incorporating demand stagnation, supply constraints in the service sector, the distribution structure, the labor market, and foreign investment within a unified dynamic framework, this paper presents an analytical perspective for explaining the coexistence of low growth and inflation characteristic of the Japanese economy.

The analysis also illustrates why, in the author's Endogenous Regime-Switching Model of Capitalist Economic Dynamics (A Disequilibrium Comparative Statics Model), some factors are treated as exogenous variables and their mathematical formalization is deliberately limited.

title: Normalization, Convergence, and Speed in Demand and Gravity Inversion
affiliations: University of California, Irvine

detail.title: Normalization, Convergence, and Speed in Demand and Gravity Inversion

declarations.declarationOfInterest: There is no conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Many demand-estimation and gravity-type models in industrial organization, spatial, trade, and urban economics recover fundamentals by inverting observed allocations. These inversions share a common fixed-point structure and are typically solved by iteration. Because fundamentals are identified only up to a constant, the iteration imposes a seemingly innocuous normalization, which differs across fields: demand estimation fixes one alternative, the outside good, and drops its equation; gravity-type applications often update all equations symmetrically and normalize afterward. I show that both algorithms converge globally but can differ sharply in speed. The symmetric update is theoretically faster and avoids the well-known slow-convergence problem in demand estimation when the outside-good share is small. Simulations and standard benchmarks show substantial speed gains. For example, in the Nevo (2000) cereal application, the symmetric update reduces market-share function evaluations by more than 50%. It requires only minor changes to existing code.

title: Human-Centered Cybersecurity: Integrating Artificial Intelligence, Zero Trust, and Security Awareness to Defend U.S. Institutions
affiliations: Seattle University

detail.title: Human-Centered Cybersecurity: Integrating Artificial Intelligence, Zero Trust, and Security Awareness to Defend U.S. Institutions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: The increasing sophistication of cyber threats presents significant challenges for U.S. institutions responsible for protecting sensitive information, critical infrastructure, and essential services. Traditional cybersecurity approaches that rely primarily on technical controls may be insufficient against threats that exploit human behavior, compromised identities, and rapidly evolving attack techniques. This paper examines a human-centered approach to cybersecurity that integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and continuous cybersecurity awareness. Through a qualitative review of cybersecurity research, government guidance, and industry practices, the study examines how these three capabilities can complement one another to improve organizational cyber resilience. AI can enhance threat detection, behavioral analysis, automation, and incident response; Zero Trust can reduce unauthorized access and limit attacker movement through continuous verification and least-privilege principles; and cybersecurity awareness can strengthen employee preparedness and reduce human-related security risks. Based on this analysis, the paper proposes a Human-Centered Cybersecurity Framework that integrates technology, governance, and people into a unified defensive strategy. The framework emphasizes continuous monitoring, adaptive defense, risk reduction, and workforce participation as interconnected components of cyber resilience. The study concludes that U.S. institutions can strengthen their cybersecurity posture by treating technological innovation, security governance, and human awareness as mutually reinforcing rather than independent security functions. The proposed framework provides a foundation for future empirical research examining the effectiveness of integrated cybersecurity strategies across different organizational and critical infrastructure environments.

title: The Hidden Hand: Minority Shareholder Expropriation in China's Split Share Reform
affiliations: , The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen - School of Management and Economics and The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen - School of Management and Economics

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Declaration
declarations.funderStatement: No Funder

detail.abstract: We examine China’s split share reform, a setting where controlling shareholders compensated minority tradable shareholders to convert nontradable shares into tradable ones. We find that controlling shareholders minimized total compensation by transferring private benefits—proxied by abnormal perk expenses—to a subset of tradable shareholders in exchange for their support of low-compensation plans. These private benefit transfers were more prevalent in firms with strong incentives to complete the reform expeditiously, those facing difficult negotiations, and those with weaker corporate governance. Furthermore, nontradable shareholders were strategic in their targeting: they utilized these transfers more aggressively in firms that subsequently exhibited significant operating improvements and superior stock returns.

title: Implementation of Tumour Boards in Romania: An Austrian Perspective

detail.abstract: Multidisciplinary oncology meetings, commonly known as "tumour boards," are viewed in Romania as a key aspiration of the healthcare system-proof of collaboration between specialties, a guarantee of high-quality care for cancer patients, and, in general, a source of improvement in public health. However, an imprecise understanding of how genuine collaboration is possible in medicine-as in any other field with an economic component, both at the individual and institutional level-has led to a deeply painful systemic problem that has been described in Romania for nearly 200 years: the well-known phenomenon of "forms without substance". We propose the perspective that true multidisciplinarity will expand gradually, influenced by broader systemic factors, especially incentive structures and patterns of healthcare provision. From this viewpoint, reliance on regulatory approaches may be insufficient for adequate implementation.

detail.abstract: As forecasts of 18 FOMC decisions, the CME FedWatch tool and a prediction market that prices each decision outcome directly are statistically inseparable, yet the two name a different most likely decision in 2.08 percent of minutes, in episodes of up to 64 hours. The difference lies in what each can express. FedWatch carries exactly one number per meeting, the expected policy change; every published probability follows mechanically from it, and its step size is fixed by the futures contract and the FOMC calendar before any trading occurs. A single price step can shift the published probability by up to 4.4 percentage points. The prediction market prices the outcomes themselves, every minute, around the clock. The disagreements are real. The two markets price different means, and the tool's arithmetic creates almost none of the disagreements. We publish the market series, the code that rebuilds the standard tool, and every disagreement with its timestamp.

detail.abstract: This article presents a comprehensive product and business framework for modernizing enterprise pricing engines by combining deterministic rule-based control with agentic artificial intelligence (AI). Modern multi-channel manufacturers and retailers face significant operational complexity managing global currencies, hierarchical buying structures, customized discounts, and tiered rebate programs. While mature rule-based pricing engines excel at executing deterministic contract logic, maintaining margin guardrails, and providing auditable price calculations, they struggle to adapt dynamically to fast-moving market disruptions, dynamic bundling, and competitor price shifts. To address these limitations, the framework introduces a multi-agent AI architecture operating as an autonomous reasoning layer above the core rules engine. Specialized agents perform multimodal visual and specification matching, calculate landed unit economics considering freight and holding costs, and strictly enforce compliance with established policy guardrails. By combining rule-based governance with bounded agentic autonomy, organizations can achieve real-time competitive arbitrage, prevent margin erosion, and streamline decision workflows. The framework emphasizes system governance, explainable pricing logic, and progressive rollout strategies moving from shadow execution to controlled autonomy to build commercial trust and maximize contribution margins across complex global selling environments.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how the low-carbon transition interacts with persistent excess capacity in the global steel industry. It distinguishes cyclical overcapacity caused by temporary demand weakness, structural overcapacity associated with distorted entry or exit incentives, and transitional overcapacity that can arise when low-carbon capacity expands faster than incumbent high-emission capacity is retired and demand grows. The capacity-demand gap widens when net capacity creation, i.e. low-carbon additions less incumbent retirement, exceeds the growth of effective demand. The quantitative analysis combines OECD steel-capacity benchmarks, worldsteel apparent-steel-use data, a Wood Mackenzie long-run demand extension, and BloombergNEF technology-transition pathways. The simulations show that low-carbon investment paths can have different market-balance effects depending on the pace of incumbent retirement. Slow retirement makes the transition more capacity-additional, whereas faster retirement shifts it toward capacity substitution. Monte Carlo simulations further show that stronger positive dependence between low-carbon entry and incumbent retirement substantially reduces the dispersion of capacity-demand outcomes while leaving the mean change in the capacity-demand gap broadly unchanged. Therefore, the relevant transition measure is net capacity creation, not gross low-carbon investment alone.

title: Danantara and the Return of the Shareholder State

detail.abstract: Indonesia’s Danantara represents more than the creation of a new sovereign wealth fund: it marks the return of the state as an active shareholder in the economy. Established in 2025 to consolidate and manage Indonesia’s state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and their assets, Danantara raises a fundamental question about what governments should seek from the companies they own. Unlike private shareholders, states may pursue objectives extending beyond financial returns, including infrastructure development, strategic industries, national resilience, and broader economic development. This article examines how Indonesia can reconcile these public objectives with the commercial discipline required for effective corporate governance. It compares Singapore’s Temasek, which emphasizes professionalized and commercially disciplined state ownership, with China’s more closely integrated model of state ownership and industrial policy. The article argues that Indonesia should adopt neither model wholesale, but instead develop its own approach to state ownership. Danantara’s success should ultimately be measured not by the size of its portfolio or the profitability of its enterprises alone, but by whether Indonesia can clearly define which companies the state should own, what those companies are expected to achieve, and who is accountable when commercial and public objectives diverge.

detail.abstract: Rich democracies finance the modern state through labour taxation. If artificial intelligence (AI) reduces the labour share, governments will have to replace lost revenue, especially through consumption or capital taxation. AI rents arise from intangible assets with hard-to-observe transaction prices. Taxing them requires digital fiscal capacity, the legal and administrative resources for identifying and valuing AI returns and distinguishing rents from normal returns. In its absence, blunt capital taxation disproportionately burdens conventional, non-AI firms. With digital fiscal capacity, targeted taxation becomes possibleand shifts part of the burden to AI firms, making conventional firms pivotal in the conflict between voters favouring such taxation and AI firms opposing it. Our model examines investment in this capacity as the transition to an AI economy empowers AI firms politically. Declining revenue from labour taxa- tion and greater inequality strengthen conventional firms’ support; their fiscal stakes, the speed of transition, and political power relative to AI firms determine whether and when investment occurs. The extent to which technological change transforms the tax state thus depends crucially on intra-business conflict over the incidence of capital taxation.

title: The Shareholder State Is Making a Comeback

detail.title: The Shareholder State Is Making a Comeback

detail.abstract: Governments are increasingly returning as shareholders, particularly in strategically important industries, challenging the long-standing assumption that privatization and shareholder primacy represented the endpoint of corporate governance evolution. This article argues that the central corporate governance question is no longer whether governments should own corporations, but how they should govern them. Revisiting the convergence debate following Henry Hansmann and Reinier Kraakman's The End of History for Corporate Law, the article contrasts the post-Cold War emphasis on privatization with the contemporary rise of strategic state ownership. It examines developments in China, the United States, Indonesia, and Singapore to demonstrate that governments with different political systems and legal traditions are increasingly using state ownership as an instrument of economic policy. The article contends that the success of state ownership depends on institutional arrangements that separate the state's roles as shareholder and regulator, thereby preserving board independence, managerial autonomy, commercial discipline, and accountability. It concludes that the future of corporate governance will be shaped not by a choice between market capitalism and state capitalism, but by governments' ability to exercise strategic ownership through governance institutions that preserve competitive markets while advancing long-term national interests.

detail.abstract: Predictive models are often validated against post-deployment outcomes even when modelguided decisions help produce them. In a multi-lender refinancing model, greater assessment commonality turns diversified false rejections into joint rejection. Induced defaults then raise measured accuracy while unanimous negative assessments become less informative about borrower fundamentals. More accurate but more common technologies can therefore improve validation while increasing refinancing fragility. Controlled model-diversity exercises and lender-state evidence support the covariance and rescue mechanisms. The result extends beyond credit to consequential prediction systems in which multiple decision makers use correlated technologies and jointly affect the outcomes used for validation.

detail.abstract: We apply the Volume Price Confirmation Indicator (VPCI) to the Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP) portfolios sorted by volatility. Our results indicate that the VPCI yields annual returns as high as 60% in the top decile and 16% in the bottom decile, with low risk and accuracy ranging from 58% to 62%. detail.abstract: Measuring ambiguity attitudes for a natural source of uncertainty requires the analyst to carve that source into events, and the method of Baillon et al. (2018) is usually implemented with events that are approximately equally likely. How the distribution from which those events are cut should be estimated is disputed: one position holds that only a long historical window identifies a distribution rather than a regime, the other that a recent window matches the information environment of respondents. I test both on the Moroccan All Shares Index, using an authorcompiled series of twelve annual returns for 2014-2025 and six monthly returns for the first half of 2026, and I then ask, by Monte Carlo simulation of a neo-additive elicitation, whether the resulting imbalance reaches the recovered indices. The long window delivers a partition within two percentage points of equiprobability; the short window delivers one of 52, 30 and 17 per cent. Imbalance is nearly innocuous for moderate attitudes but censors a third of respondents with strong ones, and choice-list coarseness matters more than either. The analysis is diagnostic and associational rather than causal.

detail.abstract: For decades U.S. electricity demand barely rose at 0.1% per year, but it now grows 1.7% a year since 2020. Equipment and interconnection pipelines are years long. The largest new customers in history are impatient enough to consider building their own power where connection is slow. The installed fleet is aging, and its measured reliability is slipping. Customers are frustrated with bills and legislators are responding to that frustration. Each of these is manageable but their arrival together makes this the most complex time to run an electricity business since the industry started. The main recommendation in this document is to build a portfolio of strategic options. Eleven “foundation” moves hold up in all “plausible but extreme” futures examined, thus are worth starting now. Six “triggered bets” pay off in some futures, so each is viewed as an option until key signals indicate starting them. Worksheets that can be operationalized are also included.

detail.abstract: This study aims to analyze the effectiveness of the implementation of the 7P marketing mix in increasing the distribution of multipurpose loans in PT BPD Sulawesi. Using a qualitative approach with a case study method, this study evaluates how the integration of seven marketing elements-product, price, promotion, place, people, process, and physical evidence-contributes to the growth of credit volume. The results of the study show that a flexible product strategy allows customers to access credit for various needs such as consumptive housing, home renovation, and working capital. Competitive pricing through competitive interest rates has successfully attracted the interest of a wider market segment. Active promotion through various communication channels increases public awareness of multipurpose credit products. The strategic location of the branch facilitates access for prospective customers throughout the Southeast Sulawesi region. The support of professional human resources ensures quality and responsive service to customer needs. An efficient credit application process reduces waiting times and bureaucracy, while physical evidence in the form of adequate office facilities strengthens the bank's image as a trusted institution. The integrated implementation of these seven elements has proven effective in driving consistent growth in multipurpose credit volumes from 2023 to 2025. This success not only expands PT BPD Sulawesi's credit portfolio, but also strengthens local people's confidence in the role of regional banks as inclusive financial institutions. These findings provide practical implications for regional banking management in designing holistic marketing strategies to increase market penetration and competitiveness amid increasingly fierce competition in the banking industry.

detail.abstract: For sixty years, a serious tradition-Debord, Baudrillard, Zuboff, Hui, Stiegler-has diagnosed how algorithmic mediation captures the human capacity to specify, for oneself, what to attend to and what the next thought should be about. The tradition's diagnosis is accepted here in full. What is disputed is the prescription that follows from it: that the only response is withdrawal from algorithmic mediation as such. This prescription rests on a further, unargued premise-that algorithmic systems cannot in principle be designed to preserve rather than capture the reference-setting function. This paper distinguishes two architectural classes of algorithmic system by the runtime rule each follows when it meets an unfinished human thought. Substitutional systems complete the user's next act of reference-setting. Revelatory systems hold the reference slot open until the user closes it themselves. The distinction is not intentional and not ethical; it is architectural, in the runtime-rule sense. The paper defends the distinction with a working reference implementation, Clara Nexus, whose Direction Check (a runtime gate) and Vulnerability-Pluralism Model (a constitutional runtime layer) instantiate the revelatory category. Placing the distinction against Stiegler's pharmakon, the paper argues that revelatory design is pharmacological care exercised at the architectural level, not only at the level of the user's noetic capacity. It then draws out the implications for responsible technology: the commercial pressures currently pulling AI toward substitutional autonomy, an emerging case record on the discoverability of AI-generated reasoning (United States v. Heppner, Noel Anthony Clarke v Guardian News & Media Ltd, the Ninth Circuit's June 2026 sanctions ruling), and the EU AI Act's compliance trajectory for high-risk systems. Substitutional architectures are on a compliance path that revelatory architectures architecturally sidestep. The paper closes with implications for procurement (buyers should specify architectural class), evaluation (measure runtime rules, not only outputs), and governance (organisations should constrain the architectural class of systems they build or deploy).

detail.abstract: Government procurement of AI is evolving from systems that generate information to systems that can also invoke tools and execute government transactions. This requires institutional capabilities beyond traditional AI governance and creates new pressures on small states that must preserve strategic choice while relying on infrastructures and providers that cannot realistically be replicated domestically. The purpose of this paper is to develop agentic AI exitability as an integrated procurement-governance capability for constraining delegated agency, preserving accountability evidence, moving government-controlled operational assets, substituting material dependencies and facilitating an orderly transition without unacceptable disruption to public services. The paper introduces the Agentic AI Exitability Framework (AAEF) and, through structured policy-document analysis of Jordan's SANAD AI pre-qualification documentation, shows strong visibility of domestic data control, government integration, cybersecurity and institutional capacity-building requirements. Other safeguards associated with reversible agentic dependence are not explicit at the pre-qualification stage. It argues that, for small states, AI sovereignty should be understood as strategic choice under interdependence rather than technological self-sufficiency. The paper also introduces the Agentic AI Exitability Drill as a means to demonstrate critical exit capabilities rather than merely promise them.

detail.abstract: This paper tests whether an online Wasserstein stress coordinate transports beyond the markets in which its tail-routing behavior was developed. Eight equity indices are evaluated strictly out of sample from January 2007 through June 2026 under a design frozen before outcome access: three volatility filters, three tail probabilities, four memory rules, 22-trading-day updates, and a single authorized run. The primary estimand is the FZ0 loss differential between Soft-DRP routing and matched filtered historical simulation. Universal portability fails because every cross-market prediction interval has a positive upper endpoint. Under the prespecified hierarchical model, the Europe-domain gate passes in five realized-volatility cells: all four European markets have favorable signs, pooled FZ0 differences remain negative after Holm correction, and Soft-DRP does not add a DQ rejection in those cells. No EWMA(0.94) or frozen-GARCH cell passes, and the non-Europe domain fails. The limited European result does not survive conservative wider-heterogeneity stress tests. Absolute calibration also remains weak: DQ rejects 258 of 288 Soft-DRP cells and 257 of 288 matched historical-simulation cells. The robust finding is therefore a boundary on universal portability; the European evidence is conditional on realized-volatility scaling and the prespecified hierarchical specification.

detail.abstract: The proposition that "institutions matter" bundles together claims of very different strength: correlation with development, within-country predictive content, and causal effects of institutional change. We separate these claims using Quality of Government and World Development Indicators in a global country-year panel and subject them to an adversarial identification ladder. Corrected country wild-cluster inference rejects the joint null for the six Worldwide Governance Indicators and five-year per-capita growth (𝑝 𝑤𝑖𝑙𝑑 = 0.010), the only primary hypothesis in the four-test family that survives Holm adjustment (𝑝 𝐻𝑜𝑙𝑚 = 0.040). V6 adds falsifications targeted at the remaining identifying assumptions. The joint result replicates with independent GDP series from Maddison (𝑝 𝑤𝑖𝑙𝑑 = 0.0067) and Gleditsch (𝑝 𝑤𝑖𝑙𝑑 = 0.0133) and is generally stable to omitting individual calendar years, although excluding 2006 moves the bootstrap probability to 0.053. By contrast, abrupt WGI changes fail a full pseudo-date rank test: the observed date is not exceptional for either improvements (𝑝 𝑟 𝑎𝑛𝑘 = 0.273) or deteriorations (𝑝 𝑟 𝑎𝑛𝑘 = 0.409) under the five-year donut estimand. Only 9 of 22 strict WGI breaks receive same-direction support from V-Dem or ICRG within two years, and only two are certified by both providers. AR(1) null simulations generate nearly as many strong single breaks as observed, while the observed concentration of breaks in the same calendar year is unusual (𝑝 ≈ 0.032), reinforcing concern about common measurement or global timing. Long-horizon democratization remains positive in calendar-matched balanced samples and among sustained-regime transitions, but Rosenbaum-style sign sensitivity is weak: the 20-and 25-year conclusions can be overturned by hidden odds ratios of only about 1.09 and 1.05. A not-yet-treated group-time DID shows an early post-transition increase but also a visible pre-treatment deviation and little precision after five years. Equivalence tests further show that most coup nulls are imprecise rather than evidence of economically negligible effects. The resulting conclusion is deliberately narrower: institutional measures carry reproducible economic information, but causal effects of measured institutional changes are local, treatment-definition-sensitive, and substantially less robust than the predictive institutional gradient.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This conceptual paper examines how Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) functions as a mediating mechanism linking corporate climate strategy, digital transformation, and financial performance. While prior literature has treated GHRM, climate finance, and HR digitalization as largely separate research streams, this paper argues that their convergence is increasingly material to firm value. Design/methodology/approach: Drawing on a structured review of the GHRM, sustainable finance, and digital HR literatures, the paper develops an integrative conceptual framework that positions digitally-enabled GHRM practices, including e-recruitment for sustainability competencies, HR analytics for carbon-relevant workforce metrics, and digital green training, as capability-building mechanisms that reduce climaterelated financial risk and support ESG-linked financial outcomes. Findings: The proposed framework suggests that digital HR infrastructure acts as an enabling condition rather than a peripheral tool, strengthening the translation of green HR practice into measurable financial and disclosure-related outcomes. Research limitations/implications: As a conceptual contribution, the framework has not been empirically tested; propositions are offered to guide future quantitative and case-based research. Originality/value: The paper contributes a novel integration of three literatures, GHRM, climate finance, and digital HRM, that are rarely theorized together, and offers testable propositions for scholars and a practical reference model for HR and sustainability practitioners.

detail.abstract: When the SADC Parliamentary Forum wrapped up its 57th Plenary Assembly, delegates representing thirteen member states put their weight behind something that has been building quietly for a couple of years now. The resolution called on the region to enact enabling legislation that allows Southern Africa to adopt artificial intelligence while safeguarding users and national security. It was one line in a much longer set of resolutions, but it named a gap that has sat largely unaddressed across the region. Sixteen member states, sixteen different starting points, and so far no shared rulebook for a technology that moves across borders far faster than law does. This paper looks at where SADC countries currently stand on AI-related regulation, where the gaps and the unevenness lie, and what a regional framework or model law might reasonably contain if the Parliamentary Forum's call is to go anywhere. Given the timing, with the Forum's resolution landing just as the SADC Secretariat is reportedly drafting its own regional AI model policy, this is a good moment to lay the arguments out plainly.

detail.abstract: 现有的组织变革理论常常将试点成功和全面失败视为两个独立的现象，将其归因于组织惯性或个人抵抗。本研究通过引入战略意图稀释（SID）概念，探讨了这一悖论背后的结构机制。通过对通用汽车NUMMI合资企业（1984-2009）的理论构建单一案例研究，研究追踪了改革意图在高级、中层和一线组织层面的传递。分析识别出三阶段的连续稀释链：（1）高级认知分歧，使改革源头不稳定;（2）中层管理的转化简化，将核心战略逻辑剥离为可复制的程序形式;以及（3）前线信号失效，这削弱了反馈循环，理论上有助于促进习得性无助感。该框架通过强调战略意图逐步削弱的层级过滤过程，将SID区别于信息扭曲和组织惯性。提出四项治理措施以减轻这些影响，为制造组织和地理分布广泛的跨国子公司提供实用指导。

detail.abstract: A low Hurst estimate from realized volatility can describe latent variance, measurement error, or both. This paper asks a narrower empirical question: does the apparent roughness of realized volatility align with a directly observed leverage-related state in cryptocurrency perpetual futures? Using public Binance Vision data for BTCUSDT and ETHUSDT from January 2020 through July 2026, I estimate a rolling increment-variance exponent from hourly realized variance and match it to perpetual-futures funding and the perpetual-spot basis. In six-hour update samples, a one-standard-deviation increase in absolute funding is associated with a 0.010 decrease in apparent H for Bitcoin and a 0.006 decrease for Ether. The association survives month fixed effects and alternative 1-, 5-, and 15-minute realized-variance meshes. It does not survive the inclusion of lagged apparent H, and funding does not explain changes in apparent H. Non-overlapping 14-day blocks retain the relation for Bitcoin during extreme funding episodes but not for Ether. Recursive forecasts show no daily gain; an Ether one-hour gain is statistically detectable but economically small and does not generalize. The evidence therefore supports a persistent state association, not a transition signal, structural estimate of spot regularity, or trading rule. The distinction clarifies what a rolling roughness estimate can and cannot identify in noisy high-frequency markets.

detail.abstract: Problem Definition. Hard-to-abate sectors such as aviation, chemicals, and plastics are under increasing pressure to substitute fossil-based feedstocks with low-carbon alternatives. We study three emerging technologies (sustainable aviation fuel, low-carbon hydrogen, and chemical recycling) that are central to this transition and share a common substitution logic: each replacing a fossil-based input within an existing production system. Because they occupy the same structural position in their respective industries, we posit that a common set of operational and policy challenges governs their scaling. We adopt a comparative perspective to identify these challenges and the research opportunities they present for operations management. Methodology and Results. We synthesize the existing literature across the three technologies, identifying dimensions that are relevant to all and that expose gaps in existing operations management (OM) literature. This approach yields six issues that we organize into two groups: operational, technological, and supply chain considerations, and informing policy design. In the former group, we highlight four key issues: (i) process efficiency and yield variability; (ii) commodity price uncertainty; (iii) infrastructure & supply chain requirements; and (iv) technical feasibility and integration. On the policy side, we observe common issues pertaining to (i) mandates and incentives and (ii) allocation and attribution policies. We argue that existing models treat these topics incompletely, if at all, and identify a series of open research problems that address this gap. Managerial Implications. For firms, the results reframe adoption as a joint decision over feedstock sourcing, pathway-specific capacity, and network design under coupled price, quality, and yield risk, where near-term feasibility and abatement can conflict, and early commitments can strand capital. For policymakers, they clarify how uniform mandates interact with regional heterogeneity, how reversal and stringency thresholds affect scale-up, and how attribution rules steer investment.

title: Faqr, Scholarly Authority, and Non-Transferable Responsibility

detail.title: Faqr, Scholarly Authority, and Non-Transferable Responsibility

detail.abstract: This article develops a revelation-bounded Sunni conceptual-normative architecture for relating divine normativity, juristic expertise, moral agency, and collective consultation without collapsing one into another. Its point of departure is faqr: the creaturely condition of dependence upon God. The argument reconstructs faqr as an epistemic discipline as well as a spiritual truth. Revelation is not fallible, but human reception, interpretation, contextualization, and institutionalization remain creaturely acts. The article therefore distinguishes revelation from juristic readouts, scholarly epistemic authority from adjudicative and political authority, and all of these from the agent's answerability for action. Drawing on Qur'anic passages, the authoritative Prophetic Sunnah as accessed through Sunni hadith transmission and authentication, classical uṣūl al-fiqh, distinctions among fatwā, qạā', ijtihād, and taqlīd, and modern scholarship on Islamic legal authority, the article advances five linked claims: Faqr Symmetry, Juristic Non-Identity, Non-Transferable and Additive Responsibility, Ethical Self-Deliberation under Revelation, and Shūrā as Distributed Corrigibility. Its foundational thesis is deliberately strong: fiqh is a human juristic determination of divine normativity, not revelation itself. This does not secularize fiqh or diminish its authority; it states the very condition under which ijtihād can be rewarded when correct and still rewarded when it errs. The framework preserves the need for qualified scholars while resisting the conversion of expertise into a soft religious caste or an unreviewable proxy for divine voice. It further proposes a seven-stage decision architecture for family, legal, policy, and social-practice settings. The paper's central claim is not that lay Muslims should perform unauthorized ijtihād, but that consultation cannot extinguish the moral responsibility of the person who acts. Responsibilities may accumulate across scholars, rulers, judges, institutions, and agents; they do not simply substitute for one another. The resulting architecture places every human authority inside a revelatory perimeter: waḥy governs the field, while fiqh, adjudication, policy, consultation, and action remain differentiated human trusts answerable to it. A structured global evidence review of socio-legal, comparative-legal, anthropological, and survey scholarship further identifies a recurrent transregional mechanism that this article terms functional sacralization of fiqh: human juristic determinations may acquire practical attributes of sacred normativity when religious attribution is combined with legal, political, organizational, or communal mechanisms that make dissent costly, deviant, or institutionally inaudible. Malaysia functions as an index case because it combines unusually direct evidence on popular legal consciousness with codification and statutory fatwā institutions. Cross-national survey signals and comparative studies of Brunei, Pakistan, northern Nigeria, Egypt, Morocco, Indonesia, Bangladesh, and Muslim-minority settings show that component mechanisms recur across markedly different political and legal regimes. The claim is therefore global in the sense of a recurrent transregional mechanism, not a claim of universal prevalence or identical Muslim belief. Counter-literatures and contrast cases show that religious authority can also cultivate ethical agency, remain contestable, or fragment rather than harden. This offers a Sunni route toward stronger ethical agency, institutional humility, and peaceful governance of juristic plurality.

detail.abstract:
Purpose: Business analysis centers of excellence (BACoEs) are governed by maturity model assumptions of linear progression through developmental stages, yet longitudinal observation reveals a substantial gap between prescribed progression and organizational reality. This study examines the critical junctures that determine successful phase transitions versus indefinite stagnation.
Design/methodology/approach: A longitudinal comparative case study tracked 16 BACoEs over 48 months, drawing on 178 interviews and 811 documents. Within-case temporal bracketing, event sequence coding, and cross-case configurational comparison identified juncture patterns across successful, plateaued, and dissolved cases.
Findings: Sixty-two percent of BACoEs did not advance beyond Phase 1 of a three-phase maturity framework. Five critical junctures emerged (Launch Credibility, Vulnerability Window, Scope Decision, Authority Crystallization, and Strategic Elevation), with the Vulnerability Window accounting for 80% of dissolutions. BACoEs meeting all five readiness indicators achieved an 86% transition success rate (6 of 7 cases). None of the seven cases meeting fewer than three transitioned. Deliberate plateau emerged as a strategically rational outcome rather than a developmental failure.
Originality/value: This study extends punctuated equilibrium theory to internal capability unit development, introduces an evidence-based readiness diagnostic replacing calendar-based progression assumptions, and identifies deliberate plateau and phase-skipping as legitimate developmental pathways that contradict maturity model prescriptiveness.

detail.abstract: Conventional financial diagnostics provide powerful assessments of financial position, vulnerability and individual financial decisions, but reveal less directly how financial consequences are transmitted, absorbed and carried forward across connected financial functions over time. This study examines the Finance Flywheel as a complementary longitudinal financial diagnostic, applying it to Pegasus Airlines and Ryanair over more than a decade. Using audited company disclosures, the analysis combines Reinforcing Drivers Analysis (RDA), Loop Velocity (LV) and Recursive Feedback (RF), supported by longitudinal financial analysis, lagged-transmission tests and radar comparison. The results reveal markedly different patterns of financial transmission. Ryanair records five Reinforcing and two Contained RDA relationships, with Medium-high Loop Velocity and Stronger Recursive Feedback, producing Financial Accretion and broader financial manoeuvrability. Pegasus records no Reinforcing relationships, four Contained and three Weakening relationships, with Medium but uneven Loop Velocity and Partial/contained Recursive Feedback, producing Emerging Financial Compression despite remaining profitable, liquid, investment-active, and financeable. Lagged tests provide no robust evidence of a stable one-or two-year recursive mechanism, limiting causal interpretation. The study shows that the Finance Flywheel complements conventional strategic and financial diagnostics by identifying where financial capacity is preserved or absorbed, where transmission bottlenecks arise, how continuously financial capacity flows through the system, and what remains available for subsequent financial choices. It therefore distinguishes financial position from financial motion while providing a bounded rather than predictive forward diagnosis of firms' financial room for manoeuvre.

title: Why Organizations Can Know What Is Wrong and Still Fail to Correct It

detail.abstract: Organizations do not fail only because they cannot see, learn, adapt, or implement. They can also fail after the relevant error has become visible and the diagnosis has been accepted. This article develops the Correction Gap as a theory of post-recognition organizational failure: the distance between accepted diagnosis of a consequential architectural error and a legitimate, coordinated, executable, and verifiable intervention against the architecture that produced it. The article deliberately enters a crowded theoretical field. Organizational learning already explains revision of beliefs and governing variables; dynamic capabilities explain sensing, seizing, and transforming; readiness and implementation theories explain commitment, efficacy, and enactment; unlearning addresses the discarding of obsolete knowledge structures; structural inertia explains resistance to organizational change. The proposed contribution is therefore narrower. It identifies a conversion problem that remains after recognition: whether an organization possesses correction rights and an Error-to-Intervention Architecture capable of translating recognized structural error into redesign. That architecture comprises acceptance, architectural attribution, correction rights, resource mobilization, coalition protection, redesign, transition, verification, and reversibility. The theory predicts that organizations may become more knowledgeable about their own failure while remaining structurally unable to stop reproducing it. This possibility becomes more important as AI increases diagnostic resolution faster than organizations redesign authority. The paper develops eight propositions, boundary conditions, falsification tests, operational measures, and an empirical research agenda. The core claim is simple but demanding: organizational intelligence is incomplete when a system can recognize architectural error but lacks an institutional route from evidence to redesign power.

title: Coastal Climate Hazards Pose Material but Uneven Financial Stress Across India's LNG Terminals

detail.abstract: India’s growing reliance on imported liquefied natural gas (LNG) makes coastal terminals important to energy security, yet their exposure to extreme weather and financial disruption remain poorly understood. We develop an open, reproducible component-level framework that follows disruption through three core functions: unloading LNG from ships, storing it, and converting it back into gas for delivery. It captures how stored LNG buffers short interruptions and translates component damage and downtime into financial loss. To isolate location effects, we compare a 5-million-tonne-per-year terminal across nine sites. Risk varies sharply by hazard and location: flood produces high-loss cases on the west coast, while surge and wind create hotspots on both coasts. At the 10-year return level, aggregate financial stress is US$390 million for flood, US$175 million for surge and US$117 million for wind, equivalent to mean site-level stresses of 1.21%, 0.55% and 0.36% against a US$3.57-billion 30-year profit baseline. More frequent hazard levels create greater long-term pressure, while rarer events cause larger losses. Future conditions can increase severe losses locally, and tank and jetty assumptions can alter the leading hazard. The framework supports screening and resilience planning for comparable onshore LNG terminals, not engineering approval, insurance pricing, annual-loss estimation or joint-event forecasting.
